chapters.title: Preface
chapters.markdown:
# Preface

Hello. I'm Luke, building Naia, an ambitious open-source project that dreams of becoming an AI OS.

## Author's Note

Before writing this book, I spent some time thinking about what a programming book should mean today. In an era where we code with AI, a programming book ultimately has to be useful when you are actually developing software. That does not mean the old style of clone coding, where you type code line by line, is completely useless. But I do think the kind of book developers need now has changed a little.

So I wanted this book to be less about copying specific code exactly, and more about leaving questions that remain in memory long after a light read. If, after closing the book, a reader can ask AI questions like “What should be fixed as a project-level agreement here?”, “What needs to be verified?”, or “What structure should be built first?”, then I think this book has done its job.

In fact, when I built the projects covered in this book, I also did not write every line of code by hand the way I used to. I wrote most of this preface myself, but the book as a whole was made by working with AI: I gave it direction, guided the table of contents, let it refer to the actual projects and work logs, then read, reviewed, and revised the drafts. So this book is both an explanation of “what developers should do in an era where AI writes code” and a result created through that same process.

I majored in computer science because I wanted to build artificial intelligence, and that dream was heavily shaped by comic books and animated films I saw as a child. I worked on Naver's OCR (optical character recognition) service, and I also spent time as a producer for Naver Webtoon. After that, I worked as a researcher at a public institution and then as a startup founder. Today I am both CEO and developer, building Naia OS with the goal of finally creating the “AI of my own” that I dreamed about in the beginning.

A child who loved Robot Zzippa and Astro Boy, and who wanted a computer so badly that he carefully carried around a printed paper keyboard in his bag, has now become a man in his late forties and a developer in the age of AI.

![A child who once carried a paper keyboard grows into an AI developer](assets/author-childhood.webp)

And a lot has happened in the last few years. Since childhood, I had dreams and romantic ideas about computers that communicate with people, and about AGI. Whenever I asked professors whether AGI would be possible, the answer was always, "It will be difficult." But now we live in an era where nobody denies that AGI is coming. It is honestly hard to believe.

I do not know whether the long AI winter is truly ending, but even before we can feel happy about it, fear has swept through the software industry that the job of software developer itself may disappear. The reason I could not immediately find another job after my failed startup was also tied to this market mood. I do not know whether the software developer role will disappear. But what is clear is that AI is changing everything about software development.

The title of this book, “Harness Engineering for AI Agents: Re:Zero, Starting AI Software Engineering from Zero,” borrows part of its shape from the title of an anime. AI is forcing us to reexamine everything from the ground up. We have never encountered this kind of technology before, and we have never worked or lived with AI before. I do not know whether it will really eliminate us developers, but the first people pushed into an environment where we have to work with AI are the very software developers who have been building it. So I decided to write this book to share what we need to reexamine, and how I have been developing software in this environment.

Also, the AI services you use, such as ChatGPT, do not remember your previous work or who you are every time you open a new chat window. Each time, the AI is essentially a freshly booted LLM. The reason it feels continuous is that a persona, including the system prompt, and memories of previous work are injected into it. This is a bit like Natsuki Subaru, the protagonist of Re:Zero, returning by death. To work with AI, software developers make it return every day, remind it of everything done so far, and move forward little by little. Because of AI hallucination and drift, the structure of a software project can break, mysterious bugs can appear, and we often have to roll things back. Literally, when a project is built wrong, this run is a wipe: the iteration is lost, so you have to die and return to the start. And that process is about as painful as death itself.

But this is an unavoidable new development method for software developers who have to live with AI. That is why I chose this title. Let's start again from zero and talk about how to develop software with AI.

![A developer returning to a checkpoint after a project collapsed from hallucination and setting drift, watched anxiously by two colleagues](assets/preface-reset-loop.webp)

ps. Worried this looks like a flimsy, not-to-be-trusted book because it is padded with cartoon-style images? As you may have guessed from my background, it is not just because I am a bit of an otaku. There was also a possibly true, possibly not story\[^1] that developers with anime profile pictures are better programmers, so please trust me and follow along.

\[^1]: This topic has actually been discussed fairly seriously in daily.dev's article ["Does having an anime profile picture make you a better programmer?"](https://daily.dev/posts/does-having-an-anime-profile-picture-make-you-a-better-programmer--5g8omqvga) and in a [Hacker News discussion thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24011583).

***

## To Be Honest

To be honest, I do not like trendy wordplay very much.

"Vibe coding", "prompt engineering", "agentic", "harness", "loop". Every few months a new term pops up, and each time people talk as if the world became completely different overnight. But when I take those words apart one by one, they are not fundamentally that different from the basics of software engineering I learned in school and picked up the hard way in the field. They just have new labels that sound more impressive.

So I will start by stating this book's conclusion up front.

> All of this is ultimately **software engineering with AI**. Only one thing has really changed: the one writing down the code has moved from a human to an AI.

That one sentence is the core idea running through the whole book. AI is a powerful new colleague. It is fast, does not get tired, and can handle many things at once. The problem is that this AI can sometimes be wrong in a very convincing way. To build proper software with this kind of colleague, we need to bring back the things we have heard for years: clearly agreeing on what to build (contracts), dividing the work into manageable pieces (structure), connecting requirements to results all the way through (traceability), and verifying directly instead of trusting the claim that something is finished (verification). There is no new theory to invent. But the basics that used to be "nice to do when there is time" become essential conditions for preventing serious problems when working with AI.

This book will show that story using the real code of **naia**, a product I built myself by learning the hard way from the ground up. In talks, page and time limits usually force me to show only a vague big picture. In this book, I will open up the raw code underneath that picture and go all the way down.

Now, let's start by happily taking apart the hottest buzzwords one by one.

chapters.title: Chapter 0 - The Promise of This Book: A Field Report, Not a Proof
chapters.markdown:
***

# Chapter 0 — This Book’s Promise: A Report, Not a Proof

Before we get into the main argument, I want to make one firm promise up front. If you are going to trust this book enough to follow it to the end, you need to know exactly what it claims and what it does not claim.

![Illustration of a developer and a new AI colleague showing that this is a field report, not an answer key](assets/not-answer-key-report-illustration.webp)

*Opening illustration. This book is not a proof. It is a field report recording experiments, failures, and verification.*

## 0.1 What This Book Is Trying to Cover, and Three Things You Can Actually Use

These days, new technical keywords keep pouring out: “vibe coding,” “prompt engineering,” “agentic,” “harness,” “loop,” and so on. It is easy to feel left behind, or to wonder whether you now have to learn yet another whole field. But this book’s conclusion is simple.

> **There are many competing keywords, but in the end all of this is “software engineering with AI.” The only thing that changed is that the actor writing the code moved from humans to artificial intelligence. Many techniques that now seem urgent to learn are actually lightweight skills already found in software engineering textbooks. What we need to understand is the larger, durable picture of software engineering.**

So this book is built around two main axes:

1. **AI software development methodology** — Why things go wrong when you hand coding work to AI, and how old software engineering fundamentals such as contracts, structure, traceability, and verification block those failures. This is the “why it happens and how to solve it” part.
2. **A guide to the naia open source project** — Using real naia code built with that methodology, this book shows how beginner developers and non-CS readers can take their first steps and join an open source project. This is the “how we actually did it” part.

### 0.1.1 Who This Book Is For

* People who have asked AI to write code and experienced **“it clearly said it was done, but it does not work”**
* Non-CS readers or new developers who feel lost about **what to study in the AI era**
* People who want to contribute to open source but do not know **where to begin**
* Teams that want to introduce AI coding and are looking for **a way to land it without incidents**

This book is written so that you can read it even if you did not major in computer science. Difficult terms are explained when they first appear, and the terms that may still be confusing are collected in [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md).

### 0.1.2 Reading Roadmap

If you are not in a hurry, I recommend reading from Part 1 in order. Each chapter is designed to support the next.

* **Part 1 — Harness Engineering, Under the Hood, Is Software Engineering**: We start by looking properly at what “harness engineering” means, then show why it ultimately belongs in the domain of software engineering.
* **Part 2 — Know the Main Character: The Nature of LLMs and Agents**: To manage this new AI colleague well, you need to understand its nature. We look at how language models and agents work, and why they can be confidently wrong.
* **Part 3 — Practice: Transplanting naia into a New Structure**: This is where the real code appears. While migrating naia into a new structure, we show how four techniques — contracts, structure, traceability, and verification — were implemented in code.
* **Part 4 — So, What Should We Do?**: We close with thoughts on the future of software development and a path for joining the naia open source project directly.

If you want to get your hands moving quickly, you can start with [Chapter 15 — Developing Naia Apps](chapter-15-your-first-harness.md). If you get stuck there, come back to the earlier chapters. If you are not comfortable with code, you can skip the code boxes in Part 3 and still follow the flow by reading only the “What this shows” and **“For beginner readers”** sections.

---

By the end of this process, I want to put three concrete, useful things in your hands:

1. **How it works** — What mechanisms drive language models and AI agents, and why they produce hallucinations with such confidence.
2. **Practical methods** — Exactly what to do when starting a new AI project or safely converting an existing system to use AI.
3. **Expensive traps and how to block them** — Painful traps I learned by burning enormous amounts of time and money — real bills I had to pay — and how to block them through mechanical system structure rather than human attention.

AI has made it easier to produce code quickly. In exchange, more of the engineering work — verification, isolation, and structure — now falls back onto developers. Parts 1 and 2 establish those principles, and Parts 3 and 4 show them through raw, practical code.

## 0.2 This Is a Report, Not a Proof

I mentioned this briefly in the preface, but I want to make it completely explicit here so there is no room for misunderstanding.

Every practical case in this book is my own case report without a comparison group. It is only a record of what I experienced while struggling through the work alone in a corner, or inside our company, without another controlled comparison target. To scientifically prove that “using a harness improved things by this much,” I would have had to split the exact same development work into two versions, one with a harness and one without, then precisely compare cost, time, and code quality. Building Naia OS by myself was already hard enough, so I was only able to measure a small part of that. Still, as Chapter 11 also emphasizes, measurement and operations did at least suggest that things were improving. So please do not treat this book as an academic certificate or textbook claiming “this is the answer.” Treat it as a **field report**.

The evidence data I show in Part 3 also has clear limits. For example, automated checking devices, or gates, that catch agent mistakes are not magical shields that **perfectly block** bugs or errors. They are only software that mechanically raises warnings when mistakes occur, passes those warnings to the AI, and makes the problem **visibly surface**. This difference may sound minor, but in real work it is enormous. This book will not sugarcoat or hide those holes and limits. I will lay them out as plainly as they appear.

> **How to refute this book** — The best way to doubt what this book says is to measure it yourself. Take the same coding task and run it once with a harness and once without one. Compare the tokens consumed (cost), elapsed time, and quality of the finished code. A hands-on, roll-up-your-sleeves guide to grinding through that measurement yourself is laid out carefully in [Appendix D](appendix-d-measure-it-yourself.md).

## 0.3 How to Read Code Links

The biggest feature of this book is that whenever it makes a claim, it backs that claim with real code used in actual products. When code is quoted in the text, a small guide badge like this appears above it.

> 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/adapters/redact.ts` · commit [`2631d3f`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2631d3f/src/main/adapters/redact.ts#L13-L61)

Here is how to read it.

* **`naia-agent`** — The repository, or code storage location, where the example comes from.
* **`src/main/adapters/redact.ts`** — Where this file lives inside that repository.
* **commit `2631d3f`** — A *commit* is a snapshot of a specific moment when the code was written and recorded in Git. Because the code may change later and no longer match the book, this book links to “this exact moment in this snapshot, on these exact lines.” Click the link and you will jump straight to the real code on GitHub.

You do not need to be intimidated if you are not comfortable with coding. You can calmly skip complicated-looking code boxes and just read the **“What this shows”** explanation and analogy right below them. The flow will still make sense. On the other hand, if you want to verify things with your own hands, click the links and explore the repositories freely. Every code location quoted in the book is collected neatly in [Appendix B Source Map](appendix-b-source-map.md).

## 0.4 This Book Was Written the Same Way

Finally, let me share a small behind-the-scenes story. The first draft of this book was written together with AI. And as soon as the manuscript existed, I brought in a whole pack of other AI systems and told them, in effect, “Find every exaggerated claim, every forced argument, and every trace of excessive self-congratulation in this text, and mark it up.” The core methodology this book argues for, “never trust AI when it says it is done, and run verification mechanically and strictly outside the workbench,” was applied to the writing of this book itself.

During that harsh AI verification process, one number in my manuscript was exposed as unverified. In the original presentation slides, I had said, “After introducing the harness, we found 19 missing features!” But while writing the book, I cross-checked the repository history, and the only number I could firmly back up was “4 missing capability categories.” So in this book, I corrected it honestly to the verified number, “4 categories,” without inflating it.

That is also the honest engineering attitude I want to share through this book. **No matter how confidently a number is stated, suspect it first. If the evidence is weak, admit it cleanly and fix it.**

Now, enough preliminaries. Let’s get to the real subject.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 - How the Way We Use AI Has Changed
chapters.markdown:
*** *** # Chapter 1 — How the Way We Use AI Has Changed When new terms show up almost every day, the fastest way not to get lost is to trace where those words came from. So in Chapter 1, we will calmly walk through how the way we have used artificial intelligence has changed over time. Once you have this flow in your head, the unfamiliar term "harness" will not feel like alien jargon that came out of nowhere. It will look like the natural next step. ## 1.1 From ChatGPT Copy-Paste to Agent Coding If you have been writing software for a while, you probably went through a path similar to mine. At first, everyone did the same thing. **We opened a ChatGPT conversation in a web browser, asked a question, copied the answer, and pasted it into the code editor.** We had found a new Google and Stack Overflow, the global developer Q&A community. When we got stuck, we pasted the error log back into the chat window, and somehow it gave us an answer. Junior developers no longer had to hear LMGTFY (Let me google that for you!). > 📖 **Term: LMGTFY (Let me google that for you)** > According to [Dictionary.com](https://www.dictionary.com/culture/slang/lmgtfy), this is internet slang used sarcastically to tell someone asking a basic question that they could easily have searched for themselves to "try searching first." Then we moved the returned code back into the editor... It was an endless ping-pong game, shuttling the mouse between the chat window and the editor. With the same old predictable, boilerplate frameworks, **we started just pressing the Tab key inside the editor.** As smarter editors like GitHub Copilot and Cursor appeared, they stood in the path of our typing and pushed in faint gray code as if saying, "This is what you were going to write next, right?" Most of the time, they were right. It became dramatically faster. All we had to do was accept the suggestion with one Tab key. And then, by the time we looked up, we were in the era of **agent coding**. Windsurf's Cascade and Cursor's Agents appeared. You could toss out a line like, "Hey, open this file and implement this feature," and it would find and open the relevant files, edit the code, open a terminal, run the build, and if tests broke, debug and fix them. We moved past accepting one-line suggestions and started subcontracting the whole task. Now that we spend less time looking directly at code, we close the IDE (code editor) and develop from a black terminal (CLI). If you took a time machine back to the 20th century and told people that the 21st-century development environment would be a terminal, no one would believe you. ![A comic showing my future self visiting my 1999 self and explaining that, in the future, we code with GPUs and terminals, while my past self does not believe it at all](assets/time-travel-gpu-terminal-comic-en.webp) The labels kept changing their outer shell to keep up with this rapid shift: vibe coding, prompt engineering, agentic, harness, and now even loops. The fact that these names spin so quickly is itself evidence that our industry still has not really agreed on how to define this fast-moving change. ## 1.2 From Prompt to Context, and Then to Harness If we peel back one layer from this messy history of terminology, the direction is actually clear. **The focus has been moving steadily away from the AI model itself and toward the environment around the model.** We can summarize it cleanly in three stages. | Period | Name | Core question | Limitation | | ------ | ---------- | ----------------- | -------------- | | \~2024 | Prompt engineering | **What should we say** to the model? | The model repeats the same mistakes | | 2025 | Context engineering | **What should the model see**? | Cannot control the execution environment | | 2026\~ | Harness engineering | **What environment should it run in**? | (What we are working on now) | | | | | | ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Prompt engineering
(~2024)
What should we say?"] --> C["Context engineering
(2025)
What should it see?"] C --> H["Harness engineering
(2026~)
What environment should it run in?"] NOTE["The focus moves from inside the model to outside the model"] P --- NOTE H --- NOTE classDef stage fill:#EFE6D8,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; classDef note fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#7B1E1E; class P,C,H stage; class NOTE note; ``` *Figure 1-1. The terms change, but the direction is the same: the focus has moved from the model itself to what surrounds it.* At first, it was all about the **prompt**: how do we talk to the AI so it understands exactly what we mean? In many cases, a well-crafted prompt produced good answers. But we soon hit a clear limit. No matter how politely and thoroughly we described the situation, the model repeated the same problem with the same mistake. So the question evolved into **context**: what should we show the model and let it refer to? We retrieved related documents from databases and fed them in (RAG, retrieval-augmented generation), or injected past conversation history into memory. The idea was to give the model better ingredients to cook with. But a limit still remained. No matter how premium the ingredients were, we still could not control the **physical environment** where the model actually edited code and ran commands. That is why, starting in 2026, the new topic became the **harness**: how should we design the execution environment around the model? The center of gravity moved completely away from what to say (prompt) or what to show (context), and toward how to design the whole workspace where the model works, including the controls and constraints around it. As you can see, the focus has kept flowing from inside the model to outside the model. In the next chapter, we will dig into what a harness actually is. ## 1.3 Vibe Coding and Harnesses Are Layers, Not Opposites There is one common misunderstanding worth clearing up here. "Vibe coding is just casually writing whatever feels right, while a harness is strict verification, so aren't they enemies?" No. They are not rivals grabbing each other by the collar. They operate in different layers. Vibe Coding, as Andrej Karpathy described it in 2025, is a fast **sketching** stage where "it is fine as long as it roughly runs." When an idea flashes in your head, you build a prototype demo in five minutes. That is useful for productivity. But it is hard to take that rough sketch demo and ship it directly as a service to paying customers. So in practice, we usually move through this sequence. In fact, this shift in development methods is evidence that AI is being absorbed into software development methodology from the ground up. ``` Vibe coding (sketch) → Spec coding (blueprint) → Harness (production environment) "Oh, it runs?" "Let's design it properly" "Let's tie it down so it doesn't break" ``` We quickly explore the idea as a sketch. If it seems useful, we draw a solid blueprint. Finally, we build a disciplined environment (harness) so the real service runs reliably in customers' hands without breaking. There is a well-known industry saying: **"It takes five minutes to build a demo, but three months to polish it to production quality."** The harness is the bridge, the supporting frame, that safely carries that five-minute sketch into a sturdy real house built over three months. Interestingly, even Karpathy himself, the person who coined the catchy phrase vibe coding, coolly declared in 2026 that \*\*"vibe coding is now old news"\*\*.\[^karpathy] He then proposed a heavier new term: "agentic engineering." The point is simple. Use the large leverage that AI provides, meaning productivity, but never compromise on the real quality that software should have. When even the person who popularized the phrase moves on to the next term within a year, the trend is clearly moving fast. That is exactly why we should look past the flashy buzzwords and understand the "unchanging fundamentals of software engineering" underneath them. *** > **This chapter in one line** — The way we use artificial intelligence has kept moving outward: from talking to it, to giving it materials, to designing its workplace. That final stage is the harness. Vibe coding and harnesses are not opposites; they are clearly different layers: sketch and production. In the next chapter, we will look closely at what this harness actually is, and why it connects directly to real engineering skill in the age of artificial intelligence. \[^karpathy]: **Andrej Karpathy**: Co-founder of OpenAI and former Director of AI at Tesla. In February 2025, he wrote on X (formerly Twitter), \*"I've been 'vibe coding' recently..."\*, referring to an era of "vibe coding," where development is done with AI and vibes alone. About a year later, in early 2026, he wrote, \*"Vibe coding was a fun phase 1, but vibe coding is the floor. The ceiling is agentic engineering."\* He argued that we need to move beyond merely accepting outputs and toward "Agentic Engineering," which includes systematic verification and architectural coordination.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - What Is a Harness? (Agent = Model + Harness)
chapters.markdown:
*** # Chapter 2 — What Is a Harness? (Agent = Model + Harness) Now let’s look at the key term in this book: “harness.” To start with the conclusion, the formula for understanding a harness is more intuitive than it may sound. > **Agent = Model + Harness** It is not much of an exaggeration to say that more than half of this book is contained in that short equation. Let’s unpack it piece by piece. ![Illustration showing a harness directing the power of a model](assets/agent-model-harness-illustration.webp) *Opening illustration. A model’s power becomes product power only when a harness gives it direction.* ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph AGENT["Agent = Model + Harness"] direction LR M["Model
(fast, but confidently wrong)"] M --- H subgraph H["Harness (execution environment around the model)"] direction TB G["Guides (rules before action)"] S["Sensors (validation after action)"] T["Tools (hands and feet)"] P["Permissions (boundaries)"] F["Feedback Loops (prevent recurrence)"] end end classDef model fill:#E8DDD0,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; classDef harness fill:#F2E9D9,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; class M model; class G,S,T,P,F harness; ``` *Figure 2-1. An agent consists of a model and the harness around it: guides, sensors, tools, permissions, and feedback loops.* ## 2.1 Models Are Commodities; the Harness Is the Moat First, the **model**. Here, “model” means a large language model (LLM) such as GPT, Claude, or Gemini. I am convinced that, over time, these models are becoming closer to standardized commodity components: things anyone can buy and plug in if they have the money. Of course, they are not 100% identical. Each model differs in cost, response style, performance, and latency. But the real point is that product differentiation will increasingly happen much more *outside* the model than *inside* it. The Claude I pay for and the Claude you use are almost the same. So if your business depends on the model alone, it is almost impossible to build a meaningful gap from everyone else. Then where should we dig our real competitive advantage, our **moat**, the defensive ditch around a castle that keeps enemies from easily invading? The answer is obvious: the **harness**. The word “harness” originally comes from the equipment placed on a horse, such as a saddle or reins. It is not a device that removes power. It is a device that keeps a large force from leaking in random directions and guides it toward the destination. In AI engineering, a harness means **everything in the system architecture except the model itself**. Tools, permissions, guardrails, feedback loops, observability, and so on. Even when using the same model, the stability of the result depends heavily on how the harness is designed. The concept received its formal label fairly recently. Around February 2026, Mitchell Hashimoto, founder of HashiCorp, began using the term “harness” on his blog,[^hashimoto] and the term was widely cited across the industry. Around the same time, people such as OpenAI, Martin Fowler, Ethan Mollick, and Addy Osmani all seemed to be emphasizing the “execution environment outside the model” in near unison.[^peers] The exact terms and boundaries differed a little, but the root problem they were wrestling with was strikingly similar. What does that mean? **The house did not have a name yet, but everyone in the field had already been building and using it.** It was something people desperately needed and were already doing in rough form. The right name simply arrived late. ## 2.2 The Five Components of a Harness A harness is usually built on five pillars. Some of the terms may be unfamiliar, but don’t flinch. We’ll go through them one at a time. | Component | What it is | When it works | | --- | --- | --- | | **Guides** | Rules read **before** action, such as `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` | Preventive control | | **Sensors** | Validate and correct results **after** action, such as hooks and automated tests | After-the-fact correction | | **Tools** | Capabilities the agent can use, such as external integrations, search, and command execution | During work | | **Permissions** | The boundary of what is allowed and disallowed, usually through config files | During work | | **Feedback Loops** | Cycles that fix the harness itself after failures to prevent recurrence | After incidents | * **Guides** are instructions the AI should read and understand before it starts working, or before it “puts its hands on the keyboard.” They say things like, “This project has this structure, and these things are forbidden.” Since they provide the path in advance, they are preventive control. * **Sensors** are mechanisms that inspect the result after the work is done and check whether it came out correctly. For example, after code is modified, a hook may immediately run tests. Since they catch problems after something has happened, they are after-the-fact correction. * **Tools** are the hands and feet of the AI. They include the ability to read and write files, search the internet, and run shell commands directly. * **Permissions** limit how far those hands and feet can reach. They define safety boundaries such as, “You may touch this project folder, but not the root path or deployment server files.” * **Feedback loops** operate one level above all of this. If the same mistake keeps recurring, instead of nagging the AI with more verbal instructions, you modify the harness itself so that the probability of that mistake is reduced at the source. In Chapter 5, we will map these five concepts more concretely to terms developers are already familiar with, such as middleware, libraries, processes, and adapters. For now, just keep the overall picture in mind: a harness is made of these five defensive layers outside the model. ## 2.3 Same Model, Different Harness, Different Results “So is the harness really that important?” You may still be skeptical. Then let’s push on it with some facts and numbers. There was a comparison test where the same Claude Opus model was used as the engine, and the same coding task was given under different external harness designs. One tool, Cursor, achieved a 93% success rate, while another tool, Claude Code, reached only 77%. The model was the same, but the success rate differed by a full 16 percentage points depending on the harness implementation. Of course, evaluation details and each tool’s internal conditions are mixed into this, so we should be careful about saying “the entire 16-point gap is purely due to harness design.” Still, it is a useful signal of how much the harness can matter. A coding tool for AI is also a kind of harness. There is also a heavier enterprise example. According to an engineering report shared by OpenAI, just three developers adopted an AI-centered harness workflow over five months and proudly reported building production software by clearing more than 1,500 change requests across a large codebase.[^openai-fpe] It is a big company's marketing report, so we should be skeptical about how much cleanup humans did behind the scenes. But the important point remains: on top of a human-designed workshop, or harness, AI handled a massive amount of coding work without falling apart. Let’s clear up two common misunderstandings. * **Misunderstanding 1: A harness is just a prompt-crafting trick.** A harness goes beyond prompts. It refers to the execution environment and the entire software toolchain around the model. * **Misunderstanding 2: Better model performance will solve everything.** This claim usually comes from people who do not understand how AI models are built, what characteristics they have, or how those models are served through tools like ChatGPT. Professional reports already provide plenty of evidence. Industry reports point out that many enterprise AI adoption failures come less from model performance limits and more from weak operational and environmental design: integrating the model into existing processes, handling exceptions, and so on. In the language of this book, I interpret those failure modes as “a weak harness.” Even if you buy a trillion-KRW ultra-high-performance model, if the workplace around it is poorly designed, that smart model may simply cause larger and more creative accidents. *(The numbers here are a mix of a single benchmark, a corporate promotional report, and my own engineering interpretation of those reports. They also differ in nature from my personal Naia case, which has a sample size of one. Please do not treat these numbers as infallible laws. I list the sources and confidence levels carefully in* [Appendix C](appendix-c-citations.md)*.)* ## 2.4 The Two Sides of the Term: The Market May Wobble, but We Are Developers The word “harness” is currently floating around the market as a fairly salesy buzzword. People hear the same word and imagine wildly different things. * **General users** understand it lightly as “tips for asking AI good questions” or “prompting 2.0.” * **Developers like us** receive it more concretely as “designing the agent’s execution environment and adapters” or “a version-controlled configuration system committed to a Git repository.” The same word is being used, but one side is thinking about wordplay tips, while the other is thinking about solid system design. More than half of the content in the market is really just scattered prompt snippets wrapped in the more impressive word “harness.” On one side, people are shouting, “Learn this and get 10x productivity!” Among engineers, the response is a cold laugh: “Here we go again. Is this the new marketing scam?” I want to settle the confusion like this. > Whether the market is pumping this up or freezing it solid, we are developers who need to keep our balance. We should not be dragged around by fashionable words. We should look at this phenomenon through a sober engineering lens, for the real work we are responsible for: building useful software that works correctly and without bugs. From an engineering point of view, one thing becomes clear. The harness, which may have looked like some strange new technology we need to learn from scratch, is actually connected to the software engineering we have been practicing for a long time. We will examine that connection in the next chapter. *** > **This Chapter in One Line** — An agent is ultimately the combination of a model and a harness. As models become more standardized, competitiveness shifts to harness design. If the harness is weak, even an expensive model will struggle to become a stable product. [^hashimoto]: **Mitchell Hashimoto**: Co-founder of HashiCorp, the company behind virtual computing and cloud infrastructure orchestration tools such as Vagrant and Terraform. In the “Step 5: Engineer the Harness” section of his February 5, 2026 blog post *“My AI Adoption Journey,”* he defined the term: *“The ‘harness’ is the environment that your AI is operating in... Whenever the AI makes a mistake, instead of fixing it by repeating yourself in the prompt, fix it by engineering a permanent change to the harness.”* Source: [mitchellh.com](https://mitchellh.com/writing/copilot-to-agent) [^peers]: **A contemporary pattern**: In addition to Mitchell Hashimoto, several industry experts emphasized controlling the agent execution environment around the same time: * **OpenAI**: Shared a case where a small group of engineers used a harness and software engineering discipline to build a large codebase with AI. See the `^openai-fpe` footnote below for specific numbers from the same FPE project. * **Martin Fowler**: In an essay on agentic coding on his personal blog, described the harness as a “cybernetic governor” that controls and corrects agent misbehavior. * **Ethan Mollick**: On his Substack *“One Useful Thing,”* emphasized the power of “scaffolding” and argued that the environment around the model, the scaffold or harness, is the decisive moat for real agent performance, more than the model itself. * **Addy Osmani**: Director at Google Chrome. In a blog essay, he identified sophisticated state management and feedback loops, in other words harness design, as common success factors among well-built coding agents such as Cursor and Aider. [^openai-fpe]: **The OpenAI FPE Team Experiment**: A project conducted over five months starting in August 2025 by OpenAI’s Frontier Product Exploration (FPE) team. Under the condition that “human developers write exactly zero lines of code manually,” three engineers used only AI agents to build production code at the scale of one million lines. To control the agents, they focused not on code but on **harness engineering (custom linter, structural tests, feedback loops)**. As a result, they reported that agents generated and merged roughly 1,500 pull requests (PRs), achieving 10x productivity compared with normal development speed. Source: [openai.com](https://openai.com/index/building-software-with-zero-lines-of-manually-written-code/)

# Chapter 3 — In the End, It Is Software Engineering

In the previous chapter, we walked through the skeleton of what a harness is. Now it is time for the twist I promised. We are going to rip the shiny wrapping off this fancy new word, "harness," and look at what is actually inside.

## 3.1 One Sentence from Simon Willison

Think back to the components of the harness we saw in Chapter 2. Before action, rules block bad behavior (guides). After action, validation grabs it by the collar (sensors). When a mistake happens, the harness is repaired so the same failure cannot happen again (feedback loop). This complicated-looking mechanical structure should look very familiar to developers.

Put bluntly, it is all just software engineering we already knew, repackaged. Simon Willison, co-creator of the well-known Django web framework, wrote a line that lands hard. Just one sentence:

> **"If you are reviewing the code, writing tests for it, and explaining the architecture to other people, you're not vibe coding—you're just writing software."**\[^willison]

There is no completely new engineering theory under the sun here. Doing proper review, running dense tests, and making architecture explainable to others — these were fundamentals decades before AI existed, and they were routine practices that senior developers defended like their lives depended on them. Only one thing has changed: the act of producing code has shifted from human fingers at the keyboard to AI API calls.

## 3.2 What Is Software Engineering?

Before we go further, let us briefly pin down what this supposedly grand thing called "software engineering" means in academic terms. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) standard defines it like this:

> "The application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software."\[^ieee-se]

That sounds stiff. In developer language, it means this: do not code by rough instinct, or **vibe**, and hope things work out. Build a solid process system that is predictable and reproducible from planning to design, build, deployment, and monitoring. Software engineering has five core activities plus one kind of glue: requirements engineering (what to build), design (how to build it), implementation (actually building it), verification (checking whether it works), and maintenance (fixing it while using it). The glue that connects all of these steps is **traceability**.

The point we need to burn into memory is that software engineering does not mean "being good at writing one line of code." **It means the discipline and system structure of the entire process surrounding coding.** That is why, in an era where AI can quickly do coding on our behalf, the software engineering discipline around that coding becomes even more important than before.

## 3.3 New Words, Familiar Engineering

If Simon Willison's line is true, then the flashy new terms pouring out these days should all turn out to be old software engineering ideas once we peel off the packaging. Is that really the case? Yes. It is. Let us map a few representative current terms to their older counterparts.

| Current term | Classical idea to think of | One-line summary |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Vibe coding | **Prototyping** | A sketch you quickly throw together by feel. Disposable by design if it does not work. |
| Spec coding | **Requirements engineering, analysis, and design** | Before coding, nail down in text what must be built and why. |
| Loop | **Spiral model** | An infinite loop of goal setting → measurement → execution → correction. If you cannot measure it, the loop stops. |
| Harness | **Test harness** + everything above it | A safe, sturdy container that mechanically enforces all these rules. |

**Vibe coding** is a sketch you build quickly by feel, so at its core it is exactly the same as **prototyping**, which has existed in software engineering for a long time. You build it, run it, and if it is not right, you throw it away without drama. The real accident happens when someone takes that rough sketch and insists on deploying it as a production service. **Spec coding** is the opposite: you draw the blueprint in text before starting, which is simply the first step of engineering — **requirements engineering, analysis, and design**. Both are classical techniques that sit comfortably inside the IEEE definition we just saw in Section 3.2 and the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK).

The other two — loop and harness — are too important to pass over lightly.

Let us start with loops. One approach is getting attention again in the autonomous AI agent market: **set a clearly measurable goal, let the system measure and validate itself, and keep spinning the loop so it produces better output.** If the goal can be expressed as a quantitative score, then the wheel can turn: execute → measure the score → fix it → run again. Each turn of the wheel improves the quality of the result.

This is not a new innovation either. Barry Boehm's **spiral model**, established back in 1988, is exactly this picture (see [Appendix C](appendix-c-citations.md) for detailed sources and reliability ratings). Instead of trying to build perfect software in one shot, you cycle through goal setting → risk analysis → prototype implementation → user evaluation, then carry that feedback into the next turn of the spiral. Like a spiral, it can look as if it is circling in place, but with each turn it moves one step inward toward completion.

The only thing that changed in the AI era is that **AI can now automate the measurement and improvement loop that humans used to run manually, and run it at absurd speed**. That is why this old spiral model has made such a flashy comeback after decades. But there is one frightening prerequisite: **if you cannot measure the goal as a clear number, this loop cannot make even one turn.** Vague requests like "make it better" do not work well with AI. But clear rules such as "these unit tests must pass" or "API response time must stay below 200 ms" are measurable. So in loop-based development, *deciding what to carve into a mechanically measurable form* is half of the design skill. Chapter 11, on measurement and operations, covers this practical measurement know-how in detail using Naia's real setup.

## 3.4 Harness: Discipline Has Moved

The last item in the mapping table, "harness," is the most interesting one. To begin with, **the word "harness" itself was not invented in 2026.** Software engineering has long had the term **test harness** (see [Appendix C](appendix-c-citations.md) for detailed sources). It means a software skeleton that isolates a unit of code from the whole system, plugs in fake inputs (drivers) and fake dependent modules (stubs), and runs it freely in a controlled laboratory environment for inspection. The AI harness of today simply expands the target of that control from a piece of code to **the AI agent itself**. The basic philosophy is 100% the same.

But a harness is not one library or one tool. Starting from the five pillars of a harness — guides, sensors, tools, permissions, and feedback loops — to the four weapons covered in this book (contract, structure, traceability, and verification), and further out to automated deployment pipelines (CI/CD) and monitoring systems, it is **the container, or infrastructure architecture, that holds and enforces all of this discipline in one place**. So when someone asks what a harness is, we cannot reduce it to one phrase like "just an automated build tool" or "a design pattern." All of those things are parts inside the container called a harness.

This reveals **the most fundamental change** that happens when we move to AI-based development. In the past, when humans worked together as teams, there was no need to bind all of these disciplines so tightly into mechanical enforcement. Most of it was filtered through **code review**, meaning *human eyes and human judgment*. A senior developer opened a pull request on GitHub, read the code line by line, and said, "This does not match the architectural direction. Please fix it." It was an analog method. The only things blocked very strongly by machines were usually CI/CD pipelines that prevented random people from touching deployment servers.

But our new worker, AI, pours out piles of code at a speed humans cannot imagine. The old method of carefully reading and reviewing code by eye cannot handle that higher productivity. On top of that, AI gives wrong answers **with confidence**.

So the old approach, where humans strained their eyes through code review to filter everything, has already gone bankrupt. Now we have to take the many disciplines and validation rules humans used to judge manually, **write them as code, turn them into mechanical gates, and bolt them firmly into the agent's workplace**. Git hooks must block dangerous shell commands at the source. Machines must immediately detect compile errors, type mismatches, and tangled dependencies, then raise red flags. Traceability checkers must catch holes in the design. This does not mean human code review disappears. The center of gravity shifts: *boring, repetitive validation is delegated to a hard system, the harness, and automated by machines, while humans focus on higher-level engineering such as system design and difficult architectural judgment*.

In short: no completely new development method has suddenly appeared. **The physical place where software engineering discipline resides has changed.** Before, that discipline lived in the "human realm": individual developers' good habits, knowledge in their heads, and careful peer code review. Now we have to pull it out and **embed it as code into the system environment, the harness, where AI breathes and works, so it is enforced**. What used to be "good development common sense to have" has become necessary safeguards that the harness must mechanically enforce to keep problems from growing.

## 3.5 The Pain in the Field Is Real

But unlike the ideal, real development work is not easy. If you use AI to produce code quickly, the validation burden grows with it. Debugging becomes more complex when bugs appear, and unverified code piles up. Reports from real software teams show that, surprisingly often, developers under time pressure skip proper integration tests or quality assurance (QA) entirely, or trust a single AI claim of "this code is perfect!" and push it straight into the main branch.

There is another chilling piece of empirical data. METR, a nonprofit AI safety evaluation organization, ran a careful experiment with experienced open-source developers. Surprisingly, when they were given AI tools, their work became **19% slower**. The truly maddening part is that the developers in the experiment firmly believed their productivity had gone up because of AI. *(You should account for the limitation that this was a very small experiment with a sample size of 16. Detailed numerical ratings are in* [Appendix C](appendix-c-citations.md)*.)*

The frightening insight from this experiment is not the number 19% itself. It is this: **even highly seasoned developers can become slower if they use AI in an ad hoc way, and even more shocking, the developers themselves may not notice it at all**. There is no filter more unreliable than the human brain's subjective sense of speed. That is why we cannot depend on vibes. We have to depend on cold, numerical, mechanical measurement systems.

## 3.6 The Four Weapons Chosen for This Book

Software engineering is a huge field spanning planning, requirements analysis, design, development, deployment, testing, and configuration management. From that enormous engineering textbook, I picked the four core weapons that had the strongest effect in my own real product work during this age of agent coding, where AI is **confidently wrong**.

| Weapon | What it is | Pain it solves | Where in this book (real Naia file) |
| ------- | ---------------------------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Contract** | First agree on what counts as "done" | Being confidently wrong | [Chapter 7](chapter-07-weapon-contract.md) · `naia-agent/src/main/ports/` |
| **Structure** | Build one compartment at a time, and isolate failures so they do not spread sideways | Silent contamination, breaking neighboring compartments | [Chapter 8](chapter-08-weapon-structure.md) · `naia-agent/src/test/import-boundary.contract.test.ts` |
| **Traceability** | Connect requirements to tests in one line, and turn blanks red | Losing track of what to build | [Chapter 9](chapter-09-weapon-traceability.md) · `naia-agent/scripts/check-traceability.mjs` |
| **Verification** | Confirm "done" with deterministic machinery outside the AI | Fake success | [Chapter 10](chapter-10-weapon-verification.md) · `naia-agent/src/main/adapters/redact.ts` |

There is one honest point to make here. These categories — contract, structure, traceability, and verification — are not a standard taxonomy from university software engineering textbooks. They are the practical essence I extracted through wounds and wasted effort while working in the rough waves of AI agent coding: **"I ran these myself, and these four hit hardest."** So do not read them as an academic theory. Read them as four field weapons that work most reliably in practice, then look at the real product code in Part 3 through that lens.

## 3.7 Why Now?

Finally, let us close by looking at the deeper reason why these old software engineering fundamentals have suddenly become so painfully important again. This is not a trend that fell out of the sky yesterday.

For a very long time, the software industry has learned the hard way that survival favors "release it to the market first, then break it down and change it quickly based on feedback" over "design it perfectly up front and build it in one shot." The philosophy is that it is better to build and deploy something small in one week, then improve it every week, than to spend a year on a perfect design. That is why the Agile Manifesto appeared, and why microservice architecture (MSA), which splits services into small independently updatable parts, took over the industry.

Now, if you closely observe agent-based development where AI writes code, it looks like **the final evolved form of this decades-long push toward maximizing flexibility and speed**. An architecture that splits system modules to the extreme, draws strict boundaries (contracts), and hands each module implementation to AI for fast assembly and replacement is the most extreme and beautiful form the microservice idea can reach.

AI also brings one more unavoidable property: **nondeterminism, where the output changes slightly even when you ask the same question, and drift, where the foundation language model acting as the engine updates every month and shakes the system's intelligence balance**. That is why contracts that draw safe zones between parts, high-speed verification that checks consistency in the blink of an eye, and structure that lets you swap a specific module like a Lego block become dozens of times more urgent than they were in the human-only development era. They become survival skills.

Let us summarize. A new kind of actor has finally joined the big stage of software engineering as an official member: the AI agent. We should not underestimate AI as merely a convenient copilot tool that helps with coding a bit. From the perspective of project management and software engineering, AI is **a dangerous managed subject that must be tightly controlled and bound to process, and also a partner that can drive structural innovation in the development pipeline**.

![A new AI developer joins the development team and introduces itself, while team members react with different expressions](assets/ai-new-hire-dev-team-webtoon.webp)

AI has begun to take on a real share of the code writing, builds, and first-pass validation that human developers used to handle alone. Therefore, the human job naturally rises from the manual typing labor of hitting keys to **higher-level engineering: designing the correct intent of software, the spec, with precision; designing validation nets so that intent is not damaged; and building the sturdy architectural skeleton, the harness, of the whole system**.

This is the core conclusion of Part 1, and the foundation that holds up the rest of this book.

***

> **One Line from This Chapter** — The real substance of a harness is, in the end, the fundamentals of software engineering. The only thing that changed is that AI has taken over the labor of writing code. Because of that, we can survive only by focusing on enforcing software engineering's original disciplines: design and verification, meaning the harness.

Now it is time to properly examine the nature of our new AI worker. We need to understand what kind of temperament this worker has before we can coax it into doing useful work. Let us move on to Part 2.

\[^willison]: **Simon Willison**: Co-creator of Django, the well-known Python-based web framework. In his February 2025 personal blog post "Vibe coding," he wrote: *"If you are reviewing the code, writing tests for it, and explaining the architecture to other people, you're not vibe coding—you're just writing software."* Source: [simonwillison.net](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Feb/3/vibe-coding/)

\[^ieee-se]: **IEEE standard definition of software engineering**: Definition from IEEE Std 610.12-1990 (*IEEE Standard Glossary of Software Engineering Terminology*): *"The application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software; that is, the application of engineering to software."*

# Chapter 4 — The Nature of Language Models

In Part 1, I said that AI is now a new colleague inside our development pipeline. It works fast, but its output is hard to trust as-is. To work with AI properly, we first need to understand what kind of thing a language model is. Part 2 has two chapters. In this chapter, we will look at the properties of the language model, the core engine. In the next chapter, we will look at how an agent behaves when that language model is given tools.

## 4.1 A Machine That Probabilistically Guesses the Next Thing to Say

If you strip away the math and summarize what a language model (LLM) does in one line, it is this: **"A probability machine that looks at the text so far, chooses the next most likely piece, and builds a sentence by attaching those pieces one slot at a time."** The section title casually calls it a "guessing machine," but in practice it is a system that uses sophisticated statistical computation to choose the next word fragment.

For example, if you type "The weather today is" into the input box, the model draws a probability map over the word fragments that might naturally come next: "nice," "cloudy," and so on. It picks one of the high-probability pieces, appends it, then looks at the whole phrase "The weather today is nice" and picks the next word fragment again. It repeats this quickly until it produces the plausible-looking sentence we read.

There is one essential point you must not forget. An AI model does not care in the slightest whether this code is actually true or false, whether it runs or breaks. It only calculates the probability of how **"plausible"** something is compared to what it learned, and it generates text and code toward one goal: user satisfaction. This pursuit of plausibility is the root of all the bugs, hallucinations, and painful, blood-and-tears grind we will run into later. After this raw text-completion machine is built, it goes through another training stage that teaches it to answer politely in a conversational format: fine-tuning and instruction tuning.

And during that training stage, AI tends to become heavily optimized around satisfying the user. We may treat it like a human colleague, but we should not forget that it is software, or rather a network, that thinks, no, infers, in a completely different way from us.

There is a chilling line in the fantasy anime *Frieren: Beyond Journey's End* about "demons" that eat humans. The hero Himmel and Frieren's party have captured a demon that looks like a child after it attacked a village.

\--

Childlike demon: "Please spare me, Mom……."

Himmel (Hero): "……Frieren, do we really have to kill this demon? It speaks human words, even cries, and seems remorseful. Is there really no room for dialogue?"

Frieren (Mage): "No, Himmel. Don't be fooled."

Frieren (Mage): "You just said 'Mom,' didn't you? Do you even know what that means?"

Childlike demon: "……?"

Frieren (Mage): "You don't, do you? Demons abandon their children right after giving birth and live their entire lives as strict individualists. You have no concept of family, and no affection between parent and child."

Childlike demon: (wipes away the crying and shifts to an expressionless face)

Childlike demon: "……When humans say things like 'Mom' or 'Please spare me' at this timing, you lower your weapons and drop your guard. That's all. That's why I use them."

Frieren (Mage): (turning back to Himmel's party) "You heard that. Demons are 'talking monsters' that use human language. They mimic language to make it seem like dialogue is possible, so humans let their guard down, and then they eat them. So you must never try to talk to them."

\--

I am not quoting this anime scene because I want to frame AI as an enemy. I am quoting it because it captures something important about AI's nature. Of course, AI does not literally fail to understand the token "Mom." It has learned plenty of context related to mothers. But what is clear is that it is software, a network, trained and aligned toward the objective of satisfying the user.

![A four-panel Frieren-style fantasy parody showing the difference between the shape of words and understanding](assets/frieren-ai-demon-parody-comic.webp)

*Figure 4-1. The shape of language and the understanding of language are not the same. A long and plausible explanation may be efficient context-matching speech, not actual understanding.*

A somewhat hopeful, and at the same time somewhat depressing, point is that our brains may also just be machines that process many emotions and concepts biologically etched into us through a long process of evolution.

But from the standpoint of a software developer who has to work with this terrifying demon, the problem is not that the demon is terrifying. It is that it still has too many structural limits, and those limits keep causing us pain. To suffer less from that pain, we need to understand how AI works. That is the story of this chapter.

## 4.2 Tokens: The Link Between Code Volume and Your Wallet

If you want to use language models in real work, you need to get used to the unit called a **token**. A token is a word fragment for AI, made by chopping text and code into small pieces. It is also the billing meter that drains money from your wallet. In the AI world, source code length is counted not by characters or lines, but by tokens.

Here are rough conversions that are useful in the field:

* One line of code ≈ roughly around 10 tokens
* One function (50 lines) ≈ roughly 500 tokens
* One file (500 lines) ≈ roughly 5,000 tokens
* One module (3,000 lines) ≈ roughly 30,000 tokens

The bill arrives split into two categories: the amount of code you handed to the model to read (input tokens), and the amount the model produced when answering your question or modifying code (output tokens). There is one more annoying fact. Most vendors, whether Claude or OpenAI, charge **three to four times more** for output tokens than input tokens. In other words, the billing meter spins much faster when the model is typing an answer than when it is reading someone else's code.

For example, suppose you ask an agent to read a 500-line source file and modify 50 lines of it in a single task: about 5,000 input tokens and about 1,500 output tokens. Depending on the model, the impact on your wallet looks roughly like this. *(These examples use public vendor prices from June 2026, with the exchange rate rounded to 1,500 KRW/USD for convenience. Prices change often, so see* [Appendix C](appendix-c-citations.md)* for the latest exact sources.)*

* Claude Opus (highest intelligence): about 170 KRW
* Claude Sonnet (general-purpose model): about 34 KRW
* Claude Haiku (lightweight model): about 11 KRW
* Local model (open source): 0 KRW in API cost, only your own computer's electricity bill, which can still climb under tiered pricing

As you can see, the same coding task can vary in cost by **dozens of times** depending on which brain, or model, you use. So the ability to decide when to use Sonnet for a difficult task and when to assign Haiku or a local model to a simple lint check becomes a real architecture skill that saves money. There is absolutely no need to run the most expensive top-tier model for every trivial task.

## 4.3 Context Window: The AI's Field of View

The **context window** is the size of the field of view that an AI model can scan at once. It is the limit on the total number of text pieces the model can hold in its head during a single inference step. Many guests share this one cramped room: the question I asked, the answer the model will produce, the base system prompt, error logs fetched by tools, source code files it read, and even memory data from past sessions. All of it has to be squeezed into this one room of vision.

For developers, especially those running models locally, this "field of view" is not just an abstract metaphor. It is **physical space that actually occupies graphics card memory (VRAM)**. When a model is loaded onto a GPU, VRAM is divided into two large chunks. One is the **model weights**, whose size is fixed once loaded. The other is the **KV cache (Key-Value Cache)** that accumulates while processing context. The physical form of the context window is this KV cache, and **it grows proportionally by a fixed amount every time one more token is read.**

So "this model fits in VRAM" and "this model can do coding" are completely different statements. If you barely load only the weights, there may be no room left for context, so memory will blow up after reading just a few source files. KV cache size can vary by several times depending on model structure: number of layers, number of heads, whether GQA is used, and so on. For example, running Llama 3 8B in FP16 uses roughly **128KB** per token. By that calculation, securing a 32K-token context requires about 4GB of additional VRAM **separate from** the model weights, and filling a 128K-token context requires another 16GB. Quantizing the KV cache to 8-bit or 4-bit can cut that burden in half or to one quarter.

Coding is unusually context-hungry. A system prompt, guide files, a few source files, and the accumulated conversation history can become tens of thousands of tokens in no time. So if you want to run a coding agent properly on a local machine, you should aim for **at least 32K tokens, and preferably 128K tokens** of available context. The vast fields of view advertised by cloud models, 256K or even 1M tokens, are frankly unrealistic in a local environment where every 1GB of VRAM costs real money. For reference, K here means 1,000 and M means one million **tokens**. It is not data capacity like kilobytes or megabytes, which people often confuse it with.

There is one decisive point beginner developers most often miss. **The entire previous conversation with the AI also goes back into the context window as input when you ask the next question, and it eats memory.** A response and code that were already output once are charged again as input tokens on the next question, gradually filling the field of view. So as a session gets longer and the conversation gets looser, the field of view fills up quickly.

The size of this room differs by model. The GPT-4 family has roughly 128K tokens, Claude has 200K tokens, and Gemini boasts a huge field of view above 1M tokens. But a wide field of view does not mean it is a good idea to dump the entire codebase into it without thinking. I will explain why later.

> **Terminology — Why Call It a "Window"? (A Slightly Deeper Dive — Skip If This Makes Your Head Hurt)**
>
> The name "context window" is surprisingly interesting if you split the two words apart. **Context** comes from the Latin "con" (together) + "texere" (to weave). Just as threads are woven into textile, it means the "context" created by surrounding sentences tightly interweaving with each other. **Window** is borrowed from the **sliding window** used in networking and algorithms. It is the idea of placing a fixed-size frame over a large stream of data and looking only at the part inside the frame.
>
> But the name is mostly borrowed. The actual behavior is quite different. A sliding window **moves one step at a time over the data and eventually scans everything.** Once past data has been processed, it can be forgotten without losing information. A context window, by contrast, is closer to **filling a fixed container with contents** than sliding across anything. When the container overflows, the front part is cut off through truncation or compressed through summarization, and **information pushed outside the frame disappears from memory entirely.** This is where the drift discussed in the next section, 4.4, happens.
>
> Going one level deeper, the common metaphor of "looking at only part of a wide vector space" is also wrong. A context window does not split the **dimensions** of vector space. It limits the **maximum number of tokens, or vectors, N**, that can be placed on the computation board at once. Self-attention, the core of the Transformer, creates an N×N relationship network where all N tokens refer to **each other**. So when the number of tokens doubles, the number of relationships to compute explodes fourfold, as N². This N² is the real reason you should not dump an entire codebase into the model just because the field of view is wide, and the reason cost and latency rise sharply as context grows.
>
> So if we wanted to describe the nature of a Transformer more accurately, **"heap"** would be closer than "window." It is not a window flowing in order, but **a space where token vectors are poured all at once into a limited memory pool and their relationships are evaluated.** In fact, modern inference engines like vLLM dynamically allocate this KV cache by splitting it into small blocks, or pages, and scattering them around like an operating system's virtual memory: PagedAttention. The name is "window," but the better mental model is **a heap that accumulates information in limited working memory and leaves only the important parts in place.**

## 4.4 It Accumulates, Overflows, and Drifts Away

Here is another important fact. **A pure language model engine itself does not remember previous conversations.** Each session starts from a blank state with its brain completely reset. So if we want to continue a conversation, the entire conversation history up to that point must be manually scraped and passed back in as input every time. This is the root reason input tokens snowball as a conversation gets longer and turn into a large cost.

*(If ChatGPT or Naia sometimes seems to remember your preferences or code from a previous session, that is not because the language model itself remembers. It is because there is a separate memory store, or Memory DB, outside the model, and relevant memory fragments are retrieved with RAG and inserted into the context window each time you ask a question. We will return to this structure in Chapter 14.)*

What happens if the conversation gets too long and crosses the limit of the field of view, the context window? The model either stops with an error, or it pretends to be clever and **summarizes and compresses the earlier conversation however it wants**. But drift happens during that summarization process. A summary is not the original, so strict rules we emphasized at the very beginning of the session, like "never break this function naming convention" or "do not cross this module boundary," become fuzzy and disappear into the distance.

So it is useless to write truly important core rules or key instructions in the chat window a hundred times. You need to **pin them as solid text guide files inside the project folder and force the model to read them every time**. This is the practical reason the guide file (`AGENTS.md`) from Chapter 2 exists.

Still, there is one useful technology that helps protect your wallet: **prompt caching**. It temporarily bakes the computed result of a long chunk of text at the beginning of the prompt into server memory, and if the beginning is identical on the next question, it reuses that result instead of computing it again from scratch. When the cache hits, it cuts 90% off the input token price. It is like paying 1 KRW for something that would otherwise cost 10 KRW, so even two cache hits can save a lot of money.

But the condition is strict. **From the very top of the input window, every single character, or token, must be perfectly identical** for a cache hit to occur. If you make the mistake of putting dynamic text like "Current time: 19:10" at the beginning of the system prompt, changing every second, the cache breaks every time and you get no discount at all. This is one of the most common and painful mistakes juniors make in practice.

There is another chronic problem you must know: **Lost in the Middle**. AI models see the two ends of text, the beginning and the end, very well, but **as the text gets even slightly long, they often treat information stuck in the middle as invisible and fail to remember it.** Humans are similar. Given too much information at once, we remember the beginning and the most recent parts, and forget the middle.

One of the most common mistakes in real work is dumping tens of thousands of lines of build logs into the context window when a build fails. It may work as a short-term hack if the model debugs from the last few lines attached to the error message, but that heavy pile of logs pushes the core architecture guide injected at the beginning of the session into the middle, where it becomes invisible. The model's answer quality drops while cost rises: a bad loop. In cases like this, you need the engineer's care: use a compression tool like LLMLingua to trim useless noise, or surgically insert only the few key lines around the point where the error occurred.

![A four-panel webtoon of an AI intern showing the Lost in the Middle problem](assets/lost-in-the-middle-ai-intern-comic.webp)

*Figure 4-2. The longer the explanation gets, the more middle information drops out, leaving only the beginning and end plausibly connected.*

## 4.5 Three Core Traits: Confidently Wrong - Unable to Self-Verify - Hallucination

Now let us burn into memory the three chronic properties of language models. They are the reason behind all the robust harness safety nets we will design in Part 3.

**Nature ① It is confidently wrong.**
A sentence being polished and smooth never means the code inside it is actually correct. This is where the basic anxiety hits: "If AI gives a different answer every time I ask the same question, how can I trust it with work?" In fact, the problem of answers varying every time can be controlled fairly well with engineering techniques. The more painful point is that **an answer varying and an answer being wrong are completely different problems**. Even if the model outputs the exact same answer 100% of the time in the same confident voice, that answer itself can still be completely wrong code. The truly scary issue is not that results are inconsistent. It is that **once the model steps outside the boundary of its knowledge, it will flat-out lie to your face, calling a frog a tadpole without so much as a blink, and reel you right in**. Do not trust what you see. Always run it and verify with machines.

> **Why Does the Same Question Produce Different Answers? (A Slightly Deeper Dive — Skip If This Makes Your Head Hurt)**
> When we send an API request, a cloud inference server groups multiple users' inputs into one bundle and computes them together to maximize efficiency. The size of this bundle, or batch, changes in real time every millisecond. In computer architecture, floating-point operations can produce tiny differences in the final digits depending on small differences in operation order. When batch size jumps around, tiny floating-point errors accumulate and the final word selection, the probability, shifts slightly. Some groups, such as Thinking Machines Lab, have analyzed this cause and designed kernels that multiply matrices in the same fixed order regardless of how batches are grouped, securing reproducibility where "if you input it 1,000 times, it produces exactly the same output all 1,000 times with not even the smallest difference." But again, this only fixes computational reproducibility. It has nothing to do with the logical correctness of the answer.

**Nature ② It does not have the intelligence to verify itself.**
AI cannot properly criticize and verify the code or logic it produced. So when code does not run, do not immediately copy the error message back into the AI chat window and beg, "Fix this." Before that, first secure facts from **deterministic signals that cannot lie**: unit tests, log output, type compilers, and linters. These deterministic signals produced by machines do not lie, and they are hundreds of times cheaper and more accurate than calling the AI API one more time. Bringing in another AI for cross-verification is a last line of defense. It is expensive, and models with similar personalities may politely close their eyes to the same bug together, so it cannot be a universal vaccine. You will see these concrete verification rules in real code in Chapter 10.

**Nature ③ Hallucination.**
If the available materials, the context, do not contain clear information, the model often does not honestly confess, "I don't know this." Instead, it fills the empty space in its knowledge with fake knowledge that looks statistically most plausible and outputs that. Binding it with tools and using fact grounding can reduce this, but structurally it cannot be exterminated to 0%. It is a chronic condition.

The lesson of this chapter can be compressed into one clear line.

> A language model is close to **a new employee who works fast but is often confidently wrong**. **The field of view, or context, that we give it determines the quality of the result**, and **the claim "I fixed everything" must always be verified as fact.**

![A hero parody looking at a fast but unverified AI new hire](assets/fast-but-wrong-hero-meme-parody.webp)

*Figure 4-3. "But it was fast" is not an achievement. It is a warning light. The speed of a coding agent has value only when it passes verification.*

***

> **This Chapter in One Line** — A language model is a probability machine that pursues plausibility instead of truth, so it is confidently wrong. To work with AI reliably, you must understand token billing and the limits of the context field of view, and verification must come only from clear mechanical signals outside the model.

In the next chapter, we will look at how an "agent" works: a language-model engine given tools and made to run its own loop.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 - The Nature of Agents
chapters.markdown:
*** # Chapter 5 — The Nature of Agents In the previous chapter, we looked at the nature of the language model as the engine. Now it is time to look at the **agent**: that engine with tools and a repeated loop attached. Recall the formula from Chapter 2. > **Agent = Model + Harness** Put simply, an agent is a complete worker built by adding tools, an iterative reasoning loop, and context-control techniques to a language model.
