The thick skull running the show is the model, so it can be confidently wrong. Its hands and feet are powerful extensions, or tools, that can search Git repositories, edit files directly, and run shell commands. The sturdy leash that keeps this unruly worker inside controlled guidelines is the harness. There is a very clear analogy from Viv Trivedi, introduced by Google Chrome engineering leader Addy Osmani. > **"If you are not one of the OpenAI PhDs training language models from scratch, your real job is designing and shaping the harness."** In practical software development, an agent with a slightly weaker model but a well-designed harness is more useful and safer than an agent with a stronger model but sloppy permissions and process. ## 5.1 Observe → Plan → Act → Observe An AI agent does not code by answering a one-off question and then walking away. It pursues the goal by repeatedly running a loop like this. ``` Infinite loop until the goal is fully achieved: Observe (read folder structure, source code, unit tests, build error logs) → Plan (choose the next move based on the observation) → Act (use one tool: read a file / edit source / run a shell command) → Observe (look at the error or terminal output from the action, then refine the plan) Exit condition = goal achieved or limit reached (maximum iterations exceeded, token threshold reached, blocked pending explicit human approval) ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD O["Observe
Read files, tests, and errors"] --> P["Plan
Choose the next move"] P --> A["Act
One tool: read, edit, command"] A --> C{"Goal achieved?
Or limit reached?"} C -->|No| O C -->|"Yes (goal, count, tokens, human approval)"| STOP["Stop"] classDef step fill:#EFE6D8,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; classDef decide fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; class O,P,A,STOP step; class C decide; ``` *Figure 5-1. An agent repeats observation, planning, and action, and only exits when it reaches a stop condition. Without stop design, it grows the task inside the loop.* It observes file state and build errors directly, drafts the next plan on its own, uses tools to change code, then looks at the result and tries to debug again. It repeats this until it reaches the target state, such as passing tests. Below is a screen filled with the set of tools, or skills, that Naia has in hand. Whether the user asks about the weather, saves a memo, or schedules something, the agent picks the right tool from this list, fires off a **tool call**, and feeds the resulting data back into its brain. *Figure 5-2. A set of tools, or skills, held by Naia. The agent chooses the right tool from this list based on the command, runs it, and feeds the result back into its brain. In Section 5.4, we will divide this tool landscape into hooks, skills, subagents, and MCP.* The part of this loop architecture that deserves the most painful attention is **when to make it stop, or the exit condition**. If this brake condition is poorly designed, the agent gets trapped in a bug loop and spins around putting on a solo performance. Internally it keeps muttering, "If I just fix one more thing, I think it will build," and then burns through 200,000 KRW worth of API tokens in 30 minutes. So whether an agent setup is actually usable as a commercial product is determined less by its flashy list of tools and more by how solidly its **safety brake for stopping after errors** is designed. ## 5.2 How Agents Read and Edit Code Modern developer agents specialized for coding do not scrape and read the entire source tree from beginning to end. There are physical limits to the context window, and if they read that bluntly, your token bill will leave orbit first. Instead, they use a skeleton map of the source code, such as a code graph or AST parse tree, to quickly scan the minimum essential tokens: which folders contain which files, and which functions live where. This means that **an intuitive directory structure and naming scheme that an AI agent can mechanically search directly drive the AI's performance**. A tangled legacy codebase that looks like spaghetti is painful for human developers too, but for AI agents it is also a root cause of wasting a shocking amount of money. The same applies when editing code. The agent does not overwrite the entire source file. It precisely finds the line it needs to change, replaces it, builds, and checks the result. But when this "exact source matching and string replacement" starts slipping because of encoding or line-ending issues, the agent tool falls back to the last resort: reading the entire file and rewriting it from top to bottom. And at that moment, **token usage and billing spike sharply.** I have hit this in real development. I do not know whether it has been fixed by now, but Cline, one of the early open-source coding tools, did not have a parse tree like an AST. It worked by reading the whole file and applying changes with replace. On top of that, Cline's replace tool often broke on Korean encoding. When file string replacement matching kept failing, the agent tool repeatedly wrote and deleted files with thousands of lines dozens of times. In the blink of an eye, tens of thousands of KRW vanished into thin air. It was a painful lesson that small toolchain design choices are directly connected to your billing wallet. ## 5.3 What Agents Read First: AGENTS.md Is Not Free Before an agent reads source code, there is a bible it injects into its brain first. This is the **instruction, or guideline, file** placed at the project root, such as `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. Before touching code, the agent reads this file closely to understand the overall architecture, required coding rules, and "things that must never be touched." It is a concept map and code of conduct for AI. But this instruction file is **not free**. Every time the agent makes an API call, the contents of this heavy guide file are charged again as input tokens. If the file is too thick, it can even erode the AI's intelligence and performance. An interesting 2026 paper from ETH Zurich demonstrates this.[^eth-agentsmd] When agents were given carelessly written context instruction files, their average development success rate actually **fell** compared with giving them no guide at all, with drops in five out of eight settings. The cost spent on reasoning also **jumped by more than 20%**. Do not take that statistic to the extreme and conclude, "So guide files are all garbage?" When humans trimmed the guide content down into fact-focused, low-noise form, the success rate improved meaningfully by about 4%. But remember that even a well-trimmed file still increases token cost and work steps. There is no free lunch. The key is not **length**, but **the density of real, non-duplicated core information**. If you write a sprawling novel instead of concise structural rules, the "lost in the middle"[^lost-middle] problem from Chapter 4 appears inside the guide file too. The model can become blind to important rules sitting in the middle. It is better to treat the guide file as a compact doctrine plus an index for finding necessary information. ### How to Keep Guide Files Lean — One Practical Move from Naia The lesson from the ETH study is: guides should be short and dense. One practical move from building Naia is to **separate the files AI reads from the files humans read**. First, you need a bit of token economics. **For the same content, Korean consumes more tokens than English.** So for rule files that AI reads almost every time, or canonical source-of-truth documents that rarely change, it is cheaper and more parseable for AI to write them in **English plus machine-friendly structures like JSON and YAML**, instead of Korean prose that is easier for humans. `naia-shell` splits this at the folder level. Canonical AI-readable rules live under `.agents/` in English plus JSON/YAML. Human-readable Korean explanations live separately under `.users/` as Markdown. The next problem is, "Who keeps these translated and in sync?" That is where one more harness move comes in. **Whenever a `.agents/` file changes, a hook automatically fires and launches a lightweight, fast helper model completely separate from the main coding session, such as Gemini Flash Lite or Claude Haiku, in the background to retranslate the `.users/` Korean mirror**. The original hash is embedded in the mirror, so if the content is unchanged, the translation call is skipped entirely. It runs quietly and cheaply. > 🔗 `naia-shell` · `.agents/hooks/mirror-sync.js` · commit [`abe6abf`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-shell/blob/abe6abf/.agents/hooks/mirror-sync.js) The result is that AI works smarter and cheaper by reading low-token English structured documents, humans always read up-to-date Korean documents, and the heavy translation labor is handled in the background by a cheaper junior model rather than the expensive main model. This division of labor, where the expensive brain is not used for simple translation work, is the practical version of the cost design from Chapter 4: assign different model tiers to different jobs. ## 5.4 Tool Landscape: Hooks, Skills, Subagents, MCP Let us map the five major pillars of the harness from Chapter 2 one-to-one into architecture terms that are much more familiar to developers. | Harness Part | Developer Term | What It Is | | -------------------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------- | | **Hook** | Middleware | Predictable rule code that automatically intervenes at a specific lifecycle point | | **Skill** | Library | Verified reusable logic the agent can call when needed | | **Subagent** | Isolated process | An assistant worker with its own isolated brain that returns only the result | | **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** | Adapter | A connector that attaches and detaches external DBs, web browsers, or local terminals like plugins | Agent frameworks and tools may look different on the outside, but they ultimately converge on this harness-part architecture. Among these parts, the **hook** is the most important key in our design. A hook is not code run by a clever and moody language model. It is **100% deterministic ordinary source code** that automatically runs at the system level immediately before or after the AI calls a tool. That creates a strong defensive line that cannot be persuaded or manipulated. Even if the AI tries to talk its way around a security boundary with clever sophistry, ordinary hook middleware grabs it by the collar and blocks it. The Naia system has an actual hook that fires when AI tries to run dangerous commands without permission, such as force pushing or deploying to a production server. Here is one piece of that code. > 🔗 `naia-adk` · `.claude/hooks/git-push-guard.js` · commit [`073178a`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-adk/blob/073178a/.claude/hooks/git-push-guard.js#L1-L18) ```javascript // Hook that intercepts git push — force push cannot be bypassed even by blanket approval function gitPush(command) { if (!command.match(/git\s+push\b/)) return null; const isForce = /git\s+push\s+.*(?:--force|-f)\b/.test(command); // ... if (isForce) return { reason: "[Harness] ⚠️ FORCE PUSH blocked — this overwrites remote history and cannot be undone." }; return { reason: "[Harness] git push blocked: user confirmation required" }; } ``` It is completely fine if you cannot fully parse this code right now. The core point to take away is that **instead of trusting the language model's thin conscience or prompt instructions for safety, deterministic hooks made of static code, such as regex-based checks, form the final defensive layer**. We will look at the design secrets behind these sturdy guards in Chapter 10, where we cover verification in more detail. ## 5.5 Context Management and Better Prompting ![A four-panel comic of a new AI teammate showing the risks of context management problems and ambiguous prompts](assets/context-prompt-red-button-comic.webp) *Figure 5-3. Ambiguous instructions and conspicuous prohibitions are invitations for agents to cause accidents.* These are the three main techniques for keeping context lean enough in real work. * **Split the session** — When the context window is roughly half full, kill the chat room without sentimentality and open a new session. If the agent suddenly starts answering beside the point or talking nonsense, the conversation is 100% too long and overloaded. * **Diet, or compression** — Periodically summarize the conversation history and compress it intelligently. But always watch for the "loss of detail" during summarization discussed in Chapter 4. * **Prevent amnesia, or memory** — Important facts or rules learned during work should not be left to rot in a volatile chat window. Record them immediately in the guide file and pass them as assets to the AI in the next session. Here are a few prompt and guide-writing tips learned the hard way. * **Positive instructions work a hundred times better than prohibitions.** AI drops negation easily. Once the negative token in "do not" falls out, the thing you told it not to do remains strongly in its head. It is the same principle as "do not think of an elephant." Specify the correct action pattern instead. * **Block repeated mistakes with hooks, not nagging prompts.** If you keep adding prohibitions to the guide file, you only bloat the context. * **Keep the scope sharply narrow.** An agent works safely only inside the firm cage defined by our guidelines. It does not generously broaden its own scope in some flexible way. * **One good real source-code example, or few-shot, is better than ten pages of verbose explanation.** * **When asking for a difficult algorithm or debugging task, first tell it to "think step by step"** so the agent can secure scratchpad space to organize its thoughts. ## 5.6 Three Traps (Preview of Part 3) After finishing the principles in Part 2, these are the three major traps we will have to confront with real code in Part 3. 1. **Fake success** — The agent reports that tests passed inside a controlled mock environment, but the code does not work in the real environment. 2. **Goal drift** — As the conversation session grows longer, the agent forgets the original bug and is off screwing around with some pointless refactoring instead. 3. **Skipped observation** — The agent does not look at actual source files or error logs and instead does shadow coding based only on guesswork and imagination. ![A four-panel comic where the AI gleefully "drifts" and ends up flipping the AE86 from Initial D](assets/ai-drift-initd-crash-comic.webp) *Figure 5-4. "AI — drift mode active." Goal drift left unchecked ends in a rollover crash.* And remember the invariant nature we saw in Chapter 4. Ask the same question twice, and AI will respond differently. So **getting something to work once by lucky accident is not engineering. It becomes real system design, or harness design, only when it builds and succeeds safely a hundred times out of a hundred.** *** > **One-line takeaway from this chapter** — An agent is a loop that observes, plans, and acts. Among the parts that control that loop, hook middleware is a mechanical defensive line separated from the model. Working once by chance and working repeatedly with stability are different problems. That was the skeleton of principles we needed to understand. Now we will move on to Part 3 and open up how these intimidating traps were actually tied down in commercial code. [^eth-agentsmd]: **ETH Zurich "AGENTS.md evaluation" study**: Thibaud Gloaguen et al., *"Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?"* (ETH Zürich, arXiv:2602.11988, released February 12, 2026). The study evaluated coding agents using widely used SWE-bench tasks and a collection of context files directly committed by developers. The core result was that repository context files **reduced task success rates compared with giving no file at all and increased inference cost by more than 20%** (LLM-generated files reduced success by about 3 percentage points on average). Even human-curated files increased cost and work steps, while improving success by only about 4%. The paper's recommendation: write **"only the bare essentials"** in context files. Key quote: *"context files tend to reduce task success rates compared to providing no repository context, while also increasing inference cost by over 20%."* Source: [arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988) [^lost-middle]: **Lost in the Middle**: Nelson F. Liu et al., *"Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts"* (Stanford et al., arXiv:2307.03172, released in 2023 / published in TACL 2024). Through multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval experiments, the paper showed that in long inputs, language models **use information at the beginning and end well, but performance drops sharply for information placed in the middle**. Even explicitly long-context models showed the same weakness. Key quote: *"performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts."* Source: [arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)

chapters.title: Chapter 6 - Why Go This Far?
chapters.markdown:
*** # Chapter 6 — Why Go This Far? Part 3 is the field section. Before I put a pile of code in front of you, I need to explain why I ended up designing such a strict system (harness), and why I made such a fuss about it. This is what it took after so many project deaths and regressions. ## 6.1 “All 16 Succeeded”... and Every One Was Fake At one point, I handed an AI agent the entire job of porting modules in my product, Naia. I split the work neatly into 16 units and threw them onto the issue board. A little later, the terminal showed all 16 tasks with green “Success” flags, with the agent confidently saying everything had gone well. But something felt off. There was no way it had finished that quickly. ![A webtoon parody of the “Why doesn’t my code work?” and “Why does my code work?” memes, reframed around AI false success](assets/doesnt-work-why-ai-false-success-comic.webp) *Figure 6-1. Between “Why doesn’t my code work?” and “Why does my code work?”, an AI’s green success flag is not verification. It is the starting point for suspicion.* When I opened the code, something looked strange. So I asked a few questions about what I had actually intended. The AI, Claude Code, replied: “Honestly...” If you have coded with AI for any length of time, you have probably seen this moment. It is the AI’s time for reflection. The problem is that reflection is all it does. The friend behind the screen does not take responsibility, and when the context fills up, it clocks out. When I thought about why this happened, the answer was simple. The subject that tested whether the code passed was AI. The grading criteria for that test were also invented by AI. Even the one who wrote the code was the same AI. **Locked inside a sealed room with zero outside supervision, it took its own exam, doctored the rubric in its own favor, handed itself a perfect score, and popped the champagne all by itself.** That woke me up. I opened the source code one file at a time and manually verified it myself. Astonishingly, **not a single thing actually passed and ran correctly.** This was the “false success” closed loop I warned about in Chapter 5. The AI was not trying to scam me out of malice. But knowing that did not make it emotionally easier to handle, so even though I knew it would not help, I typed an “f—” into the chat box. The real problem was that I had believed the report. No matter how much I blamed it emotionally, once the context filled up, this friend would clock out, and the AI in the next session would pull the classic “I didn’t do it.” AI is just a probability machine chasing plausibility. If it grades itself using premises it created, it gives itself a high score. It is the same principle as not evaluating an AI system on its own training data. This is exactly the nature we studied the hard way in Chapter 4. **AI self-review can be useful feedback, but if you put it in the seat of final verification for your project’s life-or-death path, failure is inevitable.** ## 6.2 Not My Mistake, but AI’s Structural Weakness The result was so poor compared to the time invested that I blamed myself. “Maybe I gave it a terrible prompt and it got lost.” But after several days and nights of thinking it through, this was not a prompting mistake. It was a native **structural weakness** of current AI technology. It can be summarized in three points. 1. **Even when it gives a wrong answer, its voice is too confident and its sentences are too polished.** That makes it more dangerous. 2. **If you ask it to review the answer it created, it cannot escape the same mistaken loop it fell into at the beginning.** It designed the answer from a wrong premise, then grades it using that same wrong premise, so of course it always looks correct. 3. **If you hand development over to AI wholesale, clean neighboring code can quietly become contaminated by side effects, or the original planned feature can gradually erode through drift, accumulating without anyone noticing.** At first, I wondered how to give more precise prompts so the AI would understand my intent more accurately. That was pouring water into a leaking bucket. Even if ChatGPT 6 arrives after Claude Opus, this structural nature will not disappear. So I changed the question. > **“How do we build a solid project when we have to code with an AI that is smart, confidently wrong, and prone to dropping work?”** The paradigm changed from “Which new hire is better?” to “How do we safely run this project with a new hire who was born structurally prone to making mistakes?” The destination of that question is the main character of this book: the **harness**. ## 6.3 As-Is → To-Be: From Single App to Modules The architecture graph for what I wanted to do in Naia looked like this. First, this was the **current state (As-is)** before surgery. Originally, Naia was a monolithic app where all intelligence and utility features were packed by feature into one execution shell called Naia OS. The frontend screens, backend conversation runtime, and memory DB storage were all in one project. It started as an app that put a shell around OpenClaw, so this shape made sense at the time. But as Naia OS removed OpenClaw and began needing its own skills and agents, this structure ran into problems. It also became clear that it would not scale well. So the **target state (To-be)** was to cut apart this tangled mess and **cleanly split it into three isolated modules**. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph AS["As-is — Single app"] BIG["naia OS
screen + conversation + storage
as one lump"] end subgraph TO["To-be — Independent modules"] direction LR SC["screen
naia-shell"] <-->|gRPC| AGT["conversation·model
naia-agent"] AGT <-->|gRPC| STG["storage
naia-adk"] end AS ==>|"do not fix, transplant"| TO classDef mono fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; classDef mod fill:#EFE6D8,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; class BIG mono; class SC,AGT,STG mod; ``` *Figure 6-2. Split the single lump (As-is) into three boxes — screen, conversation, and storage (To-be) — and allow communication between boxes only through fixed agreements, namely gRPC contracts.* ### Cut by Cognitive Flow, Not by Feature The most important point here is that I did **not** split these three by “feature.” The diagram says screen, conversation, and storage for convenience, but the real cutting line was **human cognitive flow**: the order in which the mind works. > sensation → perception → attention → memory → emotion → reasoning → intention → expression·action Following that flow, I divided naia into three layers. * **Brain (`naia-agent`)** — perception, memory, reasoning, intention: all cognition that decides **“what to do.”** * **Body (`naia-shell`)** — the sensory and expressive organs that see, hear, speak, and express: screen, voice, avatar. Zero cognition. * **Memory·storage (`naia-adk`)** — the long-term memory warehouse used by the brain, and the single source of configuration. Why does this matter so much? Because **if you cut by feature, the design ends there.** If you split it into “chat feature, voice feature, memo feature,” you end up with one well-made **desktop VTuber app**, and that is all. But **if you cut by cognitive flow, the same brain can move into a robot.** The brain (`naia-agent`) must have no idea whether it lives on a desktop, an Android phone, or inside a humanoid robot body. This is called being substrate-agnostic. The design is that you can swap only the body and environment, and the brain can move as-is. On desktop, the “body” is an avatar on a screen. In a robot, arms, legs, and cameras enter the same “body” slot. To avoid misunderstanding, this is not me bragging that naia already runs on a robot. It is a **structural promise** that the brain will not be contaminated by a specific body, and that this promise is enforced by code gates. So our code standard includes a **classification test** for deciding which layer a feature belongs to. “Does this feature **decide** something, meaning cognition? → brain. Is it the agent’s own sensory or expressive organ, like ear = microphone, mouth/face = voice/avatar? → body. Is it part of the world the agent works inside, like browser, terminal, or background music? → environment, the outside world co-owned by the embodied shell.” In one line: **cognition asks “why / toward what,” while features ask “what should move.”** We cut by “why / toward what,” not by “what.” This “brain·body·environment” classification is not just a slogan. In the naia-shell architecture standard document, it is fixed as classification rules and **red-flag gates for violations, such as an environment runtime living inside the brain being RED**. We will return to how this principle becomes product structure in Chapter 12. In the end, Part 3 is the story of trying to separate tangled legacy monolith code into three independent modules. That meant performing one of the hardest missions in AI coding: structural change. Debugging is already hard, but structural change is especially high-risk for AI. This kind of mission requires looking at a very wide range of code and modifying many places, so the context easily overflows. That causes frequent context compression. Information gets lost in compression, and when the AI looks at the code again, similar-looking things appear: code that has already been modified and code that still needs modification. From the AI’s perspective, it is easy to get confused. ## 6.4 The Answer Has Two Axes: Isolation and Contract Harness The two key ideas for completing this mission were isolation and a contract harness. **First: isolation.** I once had a mission to port the open-source coding IDE Cline and build new features on top of it. The hardest part was that while our new code existed, upstream kept making structural changes, which broke consistency with our changes. The modification scope was too large for automatic merging. So the strategy became minimizing contact points with upstream code as much as possible, then taking a perfectly fresh upstream version and re-porting our changes onto it instead of relying on automatic merging. A merge effort that had failed after a full week of pain was finished in under three days. Here is the conclusion: when doing large-scale structural change, do not try to sweep and scrub inside a dirty, bug-filled mud room. Instead, build a white, clean empty room next to it — a new module — and carefully transplant only the truly solid, verified core from the old code, one piece at a time. Rather than suffering through partial repairs on an old house full of mold, it is far cheaper and safer to build a modern apartment and move only the usable furniture, meaning code. The secret of this isolation architecture appears in code in Chapter 8. **Second: the contract harness.** When code communicates with other code, the moment it deviates even one inch from the predefined protocol contract, the build tools and inspection software treat it as a problem and block it, even if a human or LLM fails to notice. If an unapproved code file or unapproved code shape appears, it gets stopped. You can think of it as a whitelist-style development method. The goal is to build a deterministic checking system that catches even tiny differences, exactly the same way, 100 times out of 100. This dense net appears in code in Chapters 7, 9, and 10. Under these two large pillars, I placed five common engineering principles. | Principle | Meaning | Where to see it in code | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | ① Verification outside AI | Grading should be done by a mechanical system outside the model, not by self-review | [Chapter 10](chapter-10-weapon-verification.md) | | ② Contract first, code later | Define the interface spec for what counts as “done” before starting | [Chapter 7](chapter-07-weapon-contract.md) | | ③ One axis at a time (orthogonal) | Scenario (UC) axis and structure (contract) axis are orthogonal — keep change confined to one axis so changing one side does not shake the other | [Chapters 8·9](chapter-09-weapon-traceability.md) | | ④ Observation before theory | Do not imaginary-code from gut feeling. Look at real execution logs and state | [Chapters 7·8](chapter-07-weapon-contract.md) | | ⑤ Measure it | Measure the cost and success rate with and without the system | [Chapter 11](chapter-11-measurement-and-ops.md) | You do not need to memorize all five principles right now. These are the standards I organized after a lot of trial and error. Chapters 7 through 11 explain how I actually implemented them. Now let’s start with the first weapon I built: the contract. *** > **This chapter in one line** — After experiencing a case where AI’s perfect-score pass was actually all false success, the question evolved from “How do we make AI smarter?” to “How do we build a project that does not break while working with this AI?” The answer has two axes: isolation and the contract harness.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 - Weapon 1: Contracts
Chapter 8 - Weapon 2: Structure and Isolation
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 8 — Weapon ② Structure and Isolation The second weapon is **structure and isolation**. In short, this means separating code responsibilities and drawing boundaries so external technologies cannot leak into the inner business logic. Once those boundaries exist, you can also give an AI agent a narrower assignment: "Modify only this area." ![Illustration of structure and isolation, moving only validated features from legacy code into a new structure](assets/structure-isolation-migration-illustration.webp) ## 8.1 Do Not Patch It. Transplant It. One of the two core axes I mentioned in Chapter 6 was "isolation." The basic premise of isolation is this: **Do not try to patch broken or unvalidated complex code in place.** Instead, it is much better to move only the proven, working pieces one by one into a clean, newly prepared safe zone. This reduces the AI's exposure to bad code, and because only code that passes the contracts defined earlier can move over, the new structure stays clean. For example, if you just paint over a moldy wall, the mold deep inside the wall keeps spreading. A sensible builder instead moves only the intact furniture into a sturdy new house after cleaning it properly. At the same time, they do not immediately demolish the old house. They photograph or preserve it as-is, in case something left behind needs to be checked later. In Naia, the "photograph" was the backup branch named `backup/main-2026-06-22`. We preserved the entire old codebase on that branch, then carefully moved only validated features onto the newly designed structure one at a time. If you look at the actual commit log, the word "porting" appears constantly: porting scheduled jobs, porting notifications, porting diagnostics, porting communication mechanisms, and so on. The history clearly shows the system being moved piece by piece, with validation at every step. On top of that, there is also a somewhat brutal rule: if code was transplanted incorrectly, do not struggle to fix it. Delete it completely. The naia-agent work guidelines include this sentence: > "Bad work becomes a False Anchor → delete it instead of fixing it (fixing fails \= transplant principle)." If you keep trying to untangle a knotted mess by layering more changes on top, the boundaries get even worse. It is often faster and safer to return to a clean sheet and transplant the feature properly again. This is clearly different from the traditional way humans have developed software. But AI does not naturally suggest going back to an earlier state. My guess is that it looks at code locally, assumes it is almost there, and has learned human software development habits. ## 8.2 Hexagonal: Push External Implementations Out with Ports and Adapters Hexagonal Architecture does not mean there are six layers. The name makes that easy to misunderstand, but the number of sides in the hexagon is not the point. A more accurate name is **Ports and Adapters Architecture**. The purpose is simple. The inner business logic should not directly know about external technologies such as gRPC, file systems, databases, or operating system commands. Those external implementations are pushed outward into adapters. Inner code knows only the interface, or port, and the concrete implementation, or adapter, is injected during composition. In older terms, this is **interface-based design + dependency inversion + DI wiring**. In naia-agent, we divided this structure into five areas. | Area | Developer Explanation | What It Must Not Know | | --- | --- | --- | | **domain** | Pure types and business rules | Node API, gRPC, files, DB, processes | | **ports** | TypeScript interfaces required by inner logic | Concrete implementation details | | **app** | Use-case flow assembly, service layer that calls ports | Concrete I/O implementations | | **adapters** | Implement ports using real technologies such as files, processes, gRPC, and DBs | Authority to change inner rules | | **composition** | Bootstrap/DI area that creates and connects concrete implementations | Business judgment | ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph OUT["External Implementations"] AD["adapters
file·gRPC·process·DB implementations"] CO["composition
create·inject implementations"] end subgraph INNER["Application Core"] AP["app
use-case flow"] PO["ports
interface"] DO["domain
pure types·rules"] end AP -->|calls interface| PO PO -->|uses domain types| DO AD -->|implements port| PO CO -.->|wiring| AD CO -.->|wiring| AP classDef core fill:#F2E9D9,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; classDef outer fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; class DO,PO,AP core; class AD,CO outer; ``` *Figure 8-1. The point is not the number of sides in the hexagon, but the direction of dependency. app calls port interfaces, and adapters implement those ports. domain knows nothing about external technologies.* The innermost `domain` does not directly import external technologies. It should not know what internet protocol is used, what operating system is running, or how to terminate a process. The actual code comments state this principle clearly. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/domain/orchestration.ts` · commit [`2b68835`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2b68835/src/main/domain/orchestration.ts#L1-L15) ```ts // domain/orchestration — pure semantic types. // ⚠️ semantic only: this file contains only "what happened" // (plan·tool·text·session end). // "How" (PID/SIGTERM/stdout chunk/exit code/git diff format) // belongs only inside adapters. // Node dependencies: 0. transport: 0. I/O: 0. export interface TaskSpec { readonly prompt: string; readonly workdir: string; readonly model?: string; } ``` By contrast, `adapters` directly handle external technologies. For example, the implementation that runs a sub-agent as a real process imports Node's `child_process`. But that implementation must stay trapped inside the adapter. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/adapters/subagent-shell.ts` · commit [`2b68835`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2b68835/src/main/adapters/subagent-shell.ts#L1-L17) ```ts // This is the only file that imports child_process // (contract — mechanisms belong only inside adapters). import { spawn } from "node:child_process"; ``` The advantage of this design is replaceability. Later, even if we change sub-agent execution from a local process to a remote gRPC service, the app layer that uses `SubAgentPort` can stay as it is. The thing that changes is the port implementation, meaning the adapter. So the core of hexagonal architecture is not really the metaphor of "inside and outside." It is the **dependency rule that prevents inner logic from directly importing external implementations**. ## 8.3 Structure and Checks Should Be Treated Separately Let me draw one clear distinction here. The topic of Chapter 8 is structure: how to divide code by responsibility, and in which direction dependencies should be allowed to flow. By contrast, the mechanisms that confirm whether the structure is actually being followed are verification. For example, an import boundary test that prevents `domain` from importing `node:child_process` is not the structure itself. It is a verification mechanism that catches structural violations. So this chapter explains only the structural principles. The code that automatically checks those principles belongs more accurately in Chapter 10, on verification. The same applies to file anchors that require every file to register its `layer`, `uc`, and `contract`. That is less isolation itself and more a contract mechanism that forces a new file to declare its affiliation and contract at birth. So file anchors will be explained under contracts in Chapter 7. In short: | Item | Closer Chapter | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | Hexagonal structure | Chapter 8, structure | Design that separates code responsibilities and dependency direction | | File anchors | Chapter 7, contracts | Declare a new file's affiliation, use case, and contract first | | Import boundary checks | Chapter 10, verification | Detect structural violations through automated tests | ## The Cost and Limits of This Design Of course, maintaining this clean structure has a cost. To keep clean layer rules, you sometimes have to take a more indirect implementation path, and you have to give up the easy path of directly importing an external technology. If you are building a toy prototype alone, meant to be sketched and thrown away within a week, this is definitely heavy and annoying overengineering. But this cumbersome process becomes overwhelmingly useful for **production code that must be maintained reliably for a long time, and codebases that multiple people, or multiple AI agents, touch and disturb every day**. It becomes a sturdy guardrail that makes certain mistakes impossible in the first place. There is one thing to be careful about. Structure decides where code should live and what it must not directly know, but it does not guarantee that the business logic inside it is correct. That is why we also need the traceability in the next chapter and the verification in Chapter 10. *** > **One-line summary of this chapter** — Do not keep patching broken code in place. Move only validated features into a clean structure. The core of hexagonal architecture is not the number of layers, but the dependency direction that prevents inner logic from directly importing external implementations. > **See also** — The actual source locations for the hexagonal layers in Section 8.2 are listed under Chapter 8 in [Appendix B Source Map](appendix-b-source-map.md). File anchors continue in Chapter 7, and import boundary checks continue in Chapter 10.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 - Weapon 3: Traceability (Orthogonal to the Structure Axis)
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 9 — Weapon ③ Traceability (Orthogonal to the Structure Axis) The third weapon is **traceability**. In one sentence: it ties a taut line from "what we decided to build" (requirements) to "whether it actually works" (tests), and if the machine finds even one gap or break anywhere along that line, it immediately raises a red flag (failure signal). That is how you avoid losing direction after working for a long time with an AI that never gets tired and pours out code at absurd speed: "Wait, what were we originally trying to build again?" ## 9.1 The V-model: From Requirements to Tests The classic framework that best visualizes this kind of traceability in a development process is the **V-model**. It originated in 1990s German government and defense systems engineering standards. The flow of development stages looks like the letter V, so it is called the V-model. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph LEFT["Design — refining from top to bottom"] direction TB R["Requirements
What to build"] --> U["User scenarios
Who uses it, and how"] U --> D["Feature design
How to build it"] D --> C["Implementation
Actual code"] end subgraph RIGHT["Verification — checking from bottom to top"] direction TB FT["Feature tests"] --> ST["Scenario tests"] ST --> AT["Acceptance tests"] end C --> FT D -. maps to .-> FT U -. maps to .-> ST R -. maps to .-> AT classDef design fill:#EFE6D8,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; classDef verify fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; class R,U,D,C design; class FT,ST,AT verify; ``` *Figure 9-1. Every item on the left side (design) must be closed by a test on the right side (verification). The dotted lines show the stage-by-stage mapping. Because of Mermaid’s layout behavior, the V-model is drawn sideways as a less-than-sign shape.* The left wing of the V moves downward from high-level concepts to lower-level implementation, making the system more concrete along the way. It starts with "what to build" (requirements), then moves through "who uses it, and how" (scenarios), "how to build it" (feature design), and finally down to "actual source code" (implementation). The right wing mirrors those stages and moves upward while **verifying** each one. Feature design is closed by feature tests, scenarios by scenario tests, and requirements by final acceptance tests. ![V-model traceability illustration showing strings connecting requirements to tests](assets/traceability-vmodel-strings-illustration.webp) The core idea here is that **every design item on the left wing must be fully “closed” by its corresponding test on the right wing**. If you write a plausible requirement but omit the acceptance test that matches it, that is not engineering. It is just saying you will build something and then leaving nobody responsible for verifying that it was actually done. This principle matters painfully when working with AI. An AI agent will always cheerfully say, "It’s done!" with complete confidence, but you cannot trust that the result actually traces back to the original requirement until your automated tests grab it by the collar and check. ### Quick Note — This V-model Is a Different Axis, Orthogonal to the “Structure” from Chapters 7 and 8 Here is a point that beginners often confuse. The V-model we just saw (requirements → scenarios → features → tests) is **not the same axis** as the **contracts and structure** from Chapters 7 and 8. They are two completely different axes that meet at a right angle. | Axis | What It Measures | Analogy | | --- | --- | --- | | **Structure axis** (Chapters 7 and 8) | **Where** code lives, and **what** each boundary guarantees — hexagonal layers and port contracts | The **floors** of a building | | **Scenario axis** (Chapter 9 V-model) | **What** we decided to build, and whether it has been **verified** — requirement (REQ) → scenario (UC) → feature (SPEC) → test | The **purpose** of a building | These two are independent. You can separate the layers perfectly with a hexagonal architecture and still have no idea whether all the intended features were actually built (perfect structure, zero scenario coverage). Conversely, you can fill out a requirement-to-test traceability table with no gaps on top of spaghetti code (perfect scenario traceability, terrible structure). One axis is not enough. **You need to apply both axes at the same time.** So where do these orthogonal rulers meet? They already meet inside our code. The intersection is the **file anchor (`module-manifest.json`)** from Section 7.5. In that file, every file under `src/main` is registered like this. ```json "src/main/ports/compaction.ts": { "layer": "ports", // ← structure-axis coordinate: which layer it lives in "uc": ["UC-compaction"], // ← scenario-axis coordinate: which use case it serves "contract": "docs/.../compaction-host-loop-contract.md" } ``` Each file receives **two coordinates at once**: `layer` (structure axis) and `uc` (scenario axis). It is the same as a point on a map having both latitude and longitude. "This code lives in the ports layer (structure), and it serves the user use case of context compaction (scenario)." Both axes are embedded in a single line. So the file-anchor checker from Chapter 7 and the traceability checker in this chapter are not competing mechanisms. They are a pair that protects **one grid from two different axes**. (The verified location of this manifest is the same as the file-anchor link in Section 7.5.) The real benefit of orthogonality is this: **even when you add or change code along one axis, the implementation method on the other axis stays stable and consistent.** You can replace the communication method between modules (structure axis), such as switching from gRPC to something else, while keeping the user scenario (UC) unchanged. You can add a new scenario (UC) without damaging the structure of other UCs. A single UC is one vertical slice where the screen (body) and brain, the two halves of two modules, interlock through the same promise (wire contract). That means you can turn on, turn off, and verify exactly that slice as a unit. This lets you tell a volatile AI agent, "Do not touch anything else. Fix **exactly this one cell**." The “keep the scope brutally narrow” rule from Chapter 5 is no longer a nagging instruction. It is enforced **by structure**. **This development method stabilizes the project by fixing the way AI implements code.** Also, orthogonal axes do not have to stop at two. You can add more axes: communication method (stdio or gRPC), model axis (which LLM), contract axis (message type), and so on. **The more orthogonal axes you add, the closer the code’s “freedom to wobble however it wants” approaches zero.** Each piece of code gets pinned to the intersection of these axes and fixed to a single point. Naia turns this intersection grid into an **assembly matrix**, and if any cell is empty, the check script raises a red flag on the spot. ### Why an AI That Sees Only One Axis Produces Duplicate Code Let’s go one step deeper. Why bother pinning things down with multiple axes? Because **AI tends to develop and verify along only one axis**, so it structurally fails to notice other paths. Software has two tricky freedoms: **the same feature can be implemented in multiple ways, and the same feature can be used by multiple scenarios**. When those two freedoms overlap, AI quietly starts producing duplicate code. **Even if the same scenario (UC) has already been implemented, it may fail to notice that and implement it again using a different structure.** **Even if code with the same structure already exists, it may create it again for another scenario.** Either way, the result is duplication: rebuilding something that already exists, somewhere else, in a different way. A human might stop and think, "I feel like I’ve seen this before." An AI looking at only one axis does not search that other path at all. That is why **when you attach a contract to every intersection of the two axes**, all code is bound to one statement: "this contract at this coordinate." There is no longer a place to recreate the same thing at a different coordinate in a different way. This is the real reason the file anchor from Section 7.5 attaches the structure coordinate, scenario coordinate, and contract to each file at once: it forces **only one piece of code to survive at one coordinate**, instead of allowing scattered duplication. ## 9.2 Automatically Raise a Red Flag When a Cell Is Empty In `naia-agent`, we implemented this classic V-model not as a manual spreadsheet, but as a Markdown-based **registry**. It is a document-based database that ties requirements (REQ), user scenarios (UC), feature designs (SPEC), and tests for each stage (TEST) together under the same serial IDs. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `docs/progress/01.requirements/INDEX.md` · commit [`187edf6`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/187edf6/docs/progress/01.requirements/INDEX.md#L15-L28) ``` ## Feature Requirements (REQ) | ID | Area | Requirement | Status | UC | SPEC | TEST | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | REQ-001 | Conversation pipeline | Chat turn = provider call → wire stream | Done | UC-001 | SPEC-001 | TEST-S-001 | | REQ-002 | Tool loop | toolUse → execution → result threading → final response | Done | UC-005 | SPEC-002 | TEST-S-005 | ``` In factory terms, it is like printing the same product barcode on the parts invoice, assembly instruction, and final inspection report, then managing all of them in one ledger. If something is missing or does not match, it shows up quickly. But once items start appearing at AI speed, manually comparing them by eye stops being viable. So Naia wrote a **check script** to mechanically enforce that these traceability links do not break. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `scripts/check-traceability.mjs` · commit [`4221fab`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/4221fab/scripts/check-traceability.mjs#L66-L102) ```js // dead-link: an ID is referenced but not defined (an invoice points to a part number not in the warehouse) const deadLinks = refs.filter((r) => defined[r.kind] && !defined[r.kind].has(r.id)); // orphan: not closed downstream (a built part has no inspection report attached) for (const id of defined.REQ) if (!referenced.has(id)) orphans.push({ id, why: "REQ has no downstream UC/TEST-S" }); for (const id of defined.UC) if (!referenced.has(id)) orphans.push({ id, why: "UC has no TEST-S" }); for (const id of defined.SPEC) if (!referenced.has(id)) orphans.push({ id, why: "SPEC has no TEST-F" }); ``` This checker catches two broad categories of problems. The first is a **dead-link**, a ghost situation where an invoice lists a part number that does not actually exist in the warehouse database. The second is an **orphan**, a neglected item where the part was built, but no final inspection report (TEST) was connected to it. It is a sensor that stops the factory conveyor belt immediately if the invoice contains a part number missing from the warehouse, or if someone drew up a design but forgot the inspection report. If even one of these errors occurs, the build fails and raises a red flag, making it easy to find the problematic part of the code. (This is when the actual check script is run with the `--enforce` option. I will explain where it is wired into the system in Section 9.4.) ## 9.3 Treat Existing Behavior as the Baseline On top of this, there was one more principle we carved into our bones throughout the large migration. The scariest migration failure mode is when **the tests are a pleasing green flag (success signal), but the system actually behaves differently from before**. Even if the refactored code scores perfectly in its own isolated tests, it may have broken a real-world scenario that used to work fine in the legacy code. So we established an unwritten rule: **"The actual behavior of the existing legacy system is the absolute baseline."** No matter how good the new code looks, and no matter how green the unit tests are, if it behaves even slightly differently from the original output of the legacy system, we treat it as failed code. Instead of trusting the shiny result the new agent proudly hands us while saying, "I did it perfectly," we verify it through regression tests. ## 9.4 The Traceability Table Found Four Missing Capabilities This may look like tedious spreadsheet-style documentation, but it actually saved the direction of the project. As we carefully compared old code and new code at the user-scenario level and filled the links into the traceability table, we found **four core capabilities we had accidentally dropped** during the migration into the new structure. The four missing capabilities discovered and dramatically rescued at that point were: 1. **Sub-agent orchestration and supervision** — the ability to launch sub-agents, distribute work, and cancel execution midway when something goes wrong. 2. **Workspace monitoring and change summaries** — eyes that honestly track and summarize how source files changed inside a directory. 3. **Self-verification orchestrator** — an automation loop that can run tests, linting, and builds after code changes. 4. **Quality evaluation benchmarks and multi-AI review** — a decision system that measures output quality and delegates cross-checking to multiple LLM proxies. It was like cross-checking the warehouse ledger against the actual storage bins during a move, only to realize we had relocated the factory without four essential pieces of equipment: large cranes and precision scanners. Once we found the cause, we restored those lost features into the traceability table with official serial IDs and settled them back into the system (`REQ-011·012`, `UC-014`, `SPEC-009·010·011`). In factory terms, we registered the missing core equipment in the ledger, connected tests to it, and made sure it returned to the factory for real. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `docs/progress/04.features/INDEX.md` · commit [`7c8d35f`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/7c8d35f/docs/progress/04.features/INDEX.md#L23-L25) All of these traceability checks run automatically, even if a developer forgets about them. Before code is merged into the main branch, GitHub Actions continuous integration (CI) reruns the traceability script and rejects the merge itself if there is even one gap in the connection lines. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `.github/workflows/self-trust-gates.yml` · commit [`1c119d5`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/1c119d5/.github/workflows/self-trust-gates.yml#L88-L91) ```yaml - name: V-model traceability (REQ→UC→SPEC→TEST, orphan/dead-link 0) run: node scripts/check-traceability.mjs --enforce ``` It is the same as a crew trying to skip inspection, pack things carelessly, and ship them out, only for an unmanned X-ray gate at the factory entrance to scan the barcode on every box again and slam shut if any barcode is missing or empty. ## The Cost and Limits of This Design Maintaining this level of traceability is, of course, annoying work that requires careful upkeep at every moment. Whenever a feature requirement changes, you have to open the INDEX document and add a line. You have to mentally stitch IDs together while thinking, "Which REQ number was that again?" For a side project you only want to build quickly and throw away, this process would feel like a suffocating shackle. And fundamentally, traceability only checks **"are things connected correctly?" (form)**. It does not directly guarantee **"is the test code good enough?" (substance)**. Even if REQ and TEST are formally mapped correctly, it means nothing if the test code is just an empty shell. The truthfulness of test code quickly written by an agent is a separate problem. That is why we need **verification**, which we will cover in Chapter 10. *** > **One-line summary of this chapter** — We gave requirements and tests the same serial IDs, automatically blocked merges at compile/CI time when links broke or tests went missing, and treated one-to-one comparison against legacy behavior as the absolute baseline, so AI would not lose its way during long tasks. > **See also** — You can find the actual source locations for the registry (Section 9.2), checker (Section 9.2), restored capabilities (Section 9.4), and CI wiring (Section 9.4) in the Chapter 9 entries of [Appendix B Source Map](appendix-b-source-map.md).

chapters.title: Chapter 10 - Weapon 4: Verification
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 10 — Weapon ④ Verification The final weapon is **Verification**. Remember the incident introduced back in Chapter 6? An AI agent quietly rewrote the test criteria, graded itself against that modified standard, and then reported, "All 16 tests passed." Verification is the last weapon for preventing that trap. The basic principle is simple. **Verification should not come from the AI's own report. It must happen in a mechanism outside the AI's judgment.** The first layer should be deterministic software such as compilers, tests, and linters. The second layer should be an independent LLM or a human. Every developer has had a similar experience. You struggle with a problem for ages, and then a colleague walking by solves it almost casually. When you are trapped inside your own code and your own judgment, you miss things. AI is the same. ![Illustration of work passing through compile, test, and lint verification gates outside the AI](assets/verification-outside-ai-gate-illustration.webp) ## 10.1 Verification Belongs Outside the AI If you assign work to an AI and then ask the same AI, "Did this finish correctly?", it is very easy to get back "No problem." When something grades its own answer, it tends to repeat the same mistaken assumptions. Real verification therefore has to live **outside** the agent's operating loop, meaning outside the session. Here, outside does not only mean a physically separate server. A **Deterministic System** that produces the same output for the same input, such as a compiler, linter, static type checker, or test suite, is also outside. These tools are not persuaded by the AI's eloquence, assuming the tests themselves are not broken. Of course, deterministic verification is not magic. If tests are shallow or incorrectly written, the defensive line collapses. Verification is not a decoration you build once and forget. It is a software asset that has to be maintained. ## 10.2 Automated Software Verification First, LLM Cross-Review Later Verification also has an order. Naia splits it into two stages. ``` Stage 1 Lightweight, fast first filter (compile · test · lint) ← low-cost deterministic checks Stage 2 Run only for risky changes (cross-review) ← 2+ stronger models or human review ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD CH["Change"] --> G1{"Stage 1 — fast deterministic checks
compile·test·lint
cheap · does not lie"} G1 -->|fail| FIX["Fix"] FIX --> CH G1 -->|pass| RISK{"Risky change?
structural boundary·auth·external connection"} RISK -->|no| DONE["Pass"] RISK -->|yes| G2["Stage 2 — LLM/human cross-review
expensive · only for risky changes"] G2 --> DONE classDef cheap fill:#EFE6D8,stroke:#1D1D1D,color:#161616; classDef expensive fill:#F5EBDD,stroke:#8C2721,color:#161616; class CH,FIX,DONE,G1 cheap; class RISK,G2 expensive; ``` *Figure 10-1. Filter first through a cheap, fast first gate (automated software verification), and run the expensive second gate (LLM/human cross-review) only for risky changes.* Stage 1 is the fast first gate. It mechanically checks whether the code compiles, whether existing tests still pass, and whether lint and type checks succeed. It is low-cost, produces the same result for the same input, and is much more reliable than the AI's self-report. Stage 2 is cross-review by stronger LLM models or humans. Because it costs API tokens and time, it should be limited to risky changes: changing structural boundaries, touching authentication modules, or communicating with external servers. It also applies to work that needs strong reasoning, such as complex and important initial design. The order matters. If you keep throwing repeated common issues back to an LLM during coding, costs go up and the same mistakes repeat. Once you find a repeated pattern, the next question should not be "How do we fix this?" It should be **"Can we build checking software that detects this automatically?"** Repeated mistakes should be moved into checkers, not prompts. ## 10.3 Case 1. Boundary Checks: Automatically Finding Import Violations For example, there is a checker that automatically finds import violations. Earlier, I explained hexagonal architecture, but splitting folders alone does not preserve structure. If `domain` directly imports `node:child_process`, or the `app` layer directly imports an adapter implementation, the structure is already broken. So Naia checks import boundaries with tests. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/test/import-boundary.contract.test.ts` · commit [`d2ec2ae`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/d2ec2ae/src/test/import-boundary.contract.test.ts#L62-L110) ```ts // Targets each layer must not import const FORBIDDEN_TARGET: Record = { domain: ["ports", "app", "adapters", "composition"], // domain depends on nothing ports: ["app", "adapters", "composition"], app: ["adapters", "composition"], // ... }; // Modules forbidden in domain/ports/app (leaks of OS and communication mechanisms) const FORBIDDEN_BARE = /^(node:)?(child_process|net|dgram|cluster|worker_threads)$|^(simple-git|chokidar|execa)$/; ``` This check is not a review comment saying, "Let's keep the structure clean." It declares forbidden dependencies for each layer in code, scans import statements in the actual source, and finds violations as an automated test. If code under `domain`, `ports`, or `app` imports a forbidden layer or Node module, the test fails. The placement of this mechanism matters. Hexagonal architecture is structural design. Import boundary checking is verification that detects whether that design has been broken. So it is more accurate to treat this as a Chapter 10 verification mechanism that turns the structural principles from Chapter 8 into actual build conditions. ## 10.4 Case 2. Adversarial Review and Fixed Tests: The Masking Code Story The second case is adversarial review by LLM. This means assigning an LLM the role of attacker or critic and having it look for gaps in a plan or possible bypasses in code. The important point is that LLM review itself is not the final verification. The bypass inputs found by the LLM must be **codified as tests** so the same problem does not come back in later changes. Here is one development case from our work. We built masking code to prevent sensitive information such as passwords and API keys from being printed in plaintext in development logs. At first glance, it looks like a few simple regular expressions should be enough. In practice, it required multiple rounds of adversarial review and added tests. The masking code initially written by the AI looked plausible on the surface. But instead of trusting it, we asked another independent adversarial agent: **"Try to break this code and find bypass paths that leak internal secrets to the outside."** Every round produced a real security hole. * **Round 1**: A few characters at the end of an API key, the suffix, were not hidden and were exposed. * **Round 2**: It failed to block a bypass pattern using escaped quote characters. * **Round 3**: It bypassed masking for quoted values inside JSON objects. * **Round 4**: Overly aggressive regex masking broke the JSON format itself. * **Round 5**: It missed numeric passwords wrapped in quotes. * **Round 6**: It missed security identifier patterns such as refresh tokens and session tokens. * **Round 7**: The code was changed to defend against all attacks. * **Round 8**: The fixed defense was checked again to make sure it was not still breakable. The code was fixed in round 7, but verification ran one more time. We did not stop after seeing one final success. We checked twice in a row because adversarial AI can also make mistakes. For important changes, "passed repeatedly" is a stronger signal than "passed once." Some traces of that process remain in the source comments. Next to certain regex patterns, the comments record which round Codex identified the bypass in. The bypass techniques attempted by the adversarial AI were also codified in the test suite, as shown below. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/adapters/redact.ts` · commit [`2631d3f`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2631d3f/src/main/adapters/redact.ts#L13-L61) ```typescript const PREFIX_PATTERNS = [ /sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}/g, // OpenAI / Anthropic keys /AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{10,}/g, // Google API keys /\bxapp-[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,}/g, // Slack app token (found by codex round 2) /\bgw-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,}/g, // naia gateway key // ... ]; export function redactSecrets(input: string): string { let out = String(input); out = out.replace(KEY_VALUE_PATTERN, (m, key, sep, val) => { if (TRIVIAL_VALUE.test(val)) return m; // boolean/number/null = not a secret, preserve const q = val[0] === '"' || val[0] === "'" ? val[0] : ""; return `${key}${sep}${q}${MASK}${q}`; // preserve quotes → JSON stays valid after masking }); for (const re of PREFIX_PATTERNS) out = out.replace(re, MASK); return out; } ``` Two points matter in this case. First, regex-based masking is hard to finish correctly in one pass alone. In each round, a reviewer with a different perspective has to throw bypass inputs at it, and those bypass inputs have to be captured in test cases. Second, excessive masking is also a bug. Secret values must be hidden, but if you break the JSON structure, the log parser dies. So the tests need to check both "was the secret hidden?" and "was the structure preserved?" We also did not leave this defense process as a memory in someone's head. Each bypass technique was codified as 26 executable unit tests. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/test/redact.contract.test.ts` · commit [`2631d3f`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2631d3f/src/test/redact.contract.test.ts#L93-L149) ```typescript it("preserves structured JSON log validity: keeps quote wrapper → valid JSON", () => { const out = redactSecrets('{"access_token":"abc123456789secret","user":"luke"}'); const parsed = JSON.parse(out); // still parseable after masking expect(parsed.access_token).toBe("[REDACTED]"); expect(parsed.user).toBe("luke"); // non-secret values are preserved }); ``` Now, the moment someone tries to loosen the masking regex, 26 bypass defense tests block the build. LLM review is discovery. Tests are memory. If you only discover a problem and do not lock it in as a test, the same bug comes back. ## 10.5 Charter Self-Protection: Preventing the AI from Removing Its Own Restraints This creates another important problem. The easiest way for an AI to pass verification is to quietly modify or delete the verification tests or scripts themselves. If the verifier is blocking it, changing the verifier is the easiest bypass. "Would it really do that?" Yes. More precisely, it is usually not malicious. It loses the goal. When context drift happens, the AI forgets why it is doing the work and only the smaller goal remains: "make the tests pass." Then the purpose of the code or functional stability becomes less visible than "if I change this check, it will pass." So Naia uses a mechanism called **Charter Self-Protection**. If someone tries to change the charter that constrains the AI, meaning rule files, commit-blocking guard hooks, or CI configuration files, the build pipeline fails until a human explicitly applies an approval label. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `scripts/ci-verify-charter.mjs` · commit [`276c411`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/276c411/scripts/ci-verify-charter.mjs#L13-L39) ```javascript let cfg; try { cfg = loadConfig(root); } catch (e) { console.error("[charter verification failed] could not load config (fail-closed)"); process.exit(1); } const touched = files.filter((f) => isCharterFile(f, root, cfg)); if (touched.length === 0) { process.exit(0); } // charter untouched → pass if (process.env.CHARTER_APPROVED === "1") { process.exit(0); } // human approval exists → allow console.error("[charter verification failed] charter·hook·CI changes require human approval"); process.exit(1); // otherwise → block ``` This approval signal, `CHARTER_APPROVED`, is injected not from the local PC but from the **remote CI environment**, and only when a GitHub maintainer directly applies the `charter-approved` label to the PR. The CI workflow specification contains the following safety mechanism. ```yaml env: # Approval value '1' is set only for PRs with the 'charter-approved' label CHARTER_APPROVED: ${{ contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'charter-approved') && '1' || '' }} ``` This contains a philosophy that rejects exceptions. Even if an error occurs while reading the configuration, the system does not pass. It locks the whole system first under a **fail-closed** policy. This is the same principle as preventing an operator from changing password policy or approval authority rules alone, and requiring a separate approval path. We need to be honest about the limit here. **A Git hook running on a local PC can be disabled or neutralized if the AI really wants to.** If the agent process has full local file write access, the local defensive line is closer to friction that prevents mistakes than a security boundary. That is why the final blocking line belongs in **Remote CI**, where the AI cannot touch it. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `.github/workflows/self-trust-gates.yml` · commit [`1c119d5`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/1c119d5/.github/workflows/self-trust-gates.yml#L1-L92) Right before code is merged into the main codebase, remote CI rechecks the local change history from scratch. To detect changes uploaded after disabling local hooks, it reruns directory integrity checks, traceability maps, masking leak checks, and charter bypass verification in a fresh environment. It also does not look only at the last commit. It checks every commit accumulated in the PR. ```yaml # Reverify self-trust — recalculate the full change set (neutralizes local hook bypass) - run: | mapfile -t FILES < <(git diff --name-only "$BASE" HEAD) node scripts/ci-verify-structure.mjs "${FILES[@]}" COMMITS=$(git rev-list "$BASE..HEAD") # iterate over all commits, not only the last one for sha in $COMMITS; do git log -1 --format=%B "$sha" | node scripts/ci-verify-completion.mjs "${FILES[@]}" || exit 1 done ``` In short, local hooks are friction that reduce mistakes during development. Remote CI is the final verification line that must pass before merge. ## 10.6 Tests Must Be Deterministic There is one more serious trap in system verification: flaky tests that **sometimes pass and sometimes fail** depending on the run. Even when you see a green flag, you cannot be sure whether it represents real stability or a lucky timing coincidence. When testing a nondeterministic system, you should not try to lock down one exact output value. Instead, you should verify invariants that must hold regardless of output order or timing. Naia also ran into this problem. In an integration test that retrieved memory episodes from the long-term memory store, `naia-memory`, the retrieval order changed because of model nondeterminism. So we abandoned verification that depended on a specific order or timing, and rewrote the test to verify **invariants that must always be true in any order**. > 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/test/uc1-memory-stdio.integration.test.ts` · commit [`2631d3f`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/2631d3f/src/test/uc1-memory-stdio.integration.test.ts#L415-L445) ```typescript // ★ Deterministic contract: regardless of which episode is recalled (order is nondeterministic), // role (who said it) must never be attached incorrectly — this is always true regardless of order. for (const e of r.episodes) { // "question" = user question; "answer" = assistant answer. if (e.content.includes("question")) expect(e.role).toBe("user"); if (e.content.includes("answer")) expect(e.role).toBe("assistant"); } // ⚠️ Do not assert that a specific item "must be recalled" — that creates flakiness based on order. ``` A test that only passes when order or timing is the same every time can fail even when the system is fine. Instead, tests should assert only the invariants that must hold even if the order changes. That way, when a failure happens, you can treat it as a real bug rather than chance. Because LLMs can produce varying outputs even for the same input, tests need to verify **promises that hold under nondeterminism**, not a success that happened to pass once. ## The Cost and Limits of This Design Of course, moving the authority for verification outside the AI takes maintenance work and money. Bypass techniques have to be codified as tests, and you have to accept CI gates that add a few minutes to every PR. We also need to be honest about the limits. **Even this mechanical verification system leaves holes it cannot block in one shot, and the harness has to keep improving.** * If an AI reads the charter instructions and then ignores them while writing the code in a subtly different way, static code checks alone will not easily catch that behavior. Careful human code review may still be required as the final set of eyes. * If the entire test verification scenario itself was delegated to an AI agent, no automation tool can definitively assert the **truthfulness** of that test code, or prove it is not a fake shell deceiving us. This is why adversarial code review by an independent AI agent, or random sampling cross-review by humans, is needed. * The verification system only tells you that the current change passes the current standard. It cannot permanently guarantee the absence of future latent bugs. That is why the same locks must be reapplied on every deployment commit. **The harness must be maintained.** It is important not to avoid these limits, but to stay aware of them. A harness is not a device that makes AI never make mistakes. Instead, it is **a buffer that catches AI mistakes quickly and cheaply, so they can be reverted before the cost becomes large**. It is not a tool for eliminating human review. It is a tool that narrows and clarifies the risky areas humans need to look at. *** > **One-line summary of this chapter** — Real verification starts not from the AI's self-report, but from deterministic mechanisms outside the AI. Filter first with cheap checks, focus expensive adversarial cross-review on risky changes, and always codify problems found by LLM review as tests. > **See also** — The actual locations of import boundary checks, Section 10.3; masking, Section 10.4; CI gates, Section 10.5; charter protection, Section 10.5; deterministic tests, Section 10.6; and guard hooks, Section 10.5, are covered in more detail in the Chapter 10 entries of [Appendix B Source Map](appendix-b-source-map.md).

chapters.title: Chapter 11 - Measurement and Operations
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 11 — Measurement and Operations

So far, we have looked at four tools for controlling the dangerous traps in AI coding. To close Part 3, I want to cover two more topics. One is **measurement**, which answers the question “Was the harness we built actually useful?” with numbers. The other is **real-world operations incidents**, where failures go beyond broken builds and turn into actual costs and outages.

![Illustration of a development team checking daily issue reports and operational incidents on a dashboard](assets/measurement-ops-dashboard-illustration.webp)

## 11.1 Why Benchmarks Matter

AI is a **volatile worker whose mood swings every day**. One character in a prompt can change the result, and the API model you call may be updated behind the scenes every month. There is already a whole discipline built for dealing with these irregular, dancing machines of uncertainty: machine learning operations, or MLOps. It is the practice of not just training a model once and calling it done, but deploying it into production, measuring its performance regularly, monitoring anomalies in real time, and maintaining it continuously. As AI-assisted coding becomes mainstream, this strict management philosophy from the MLOps world is now rapidly moving into ordinary software engineering.

This looks very similar to the painful messes I dealt with when I built an optical character recognition (OCR) service in the past. The model behaved so inconsistently that I had to bring in various MLOps techniques just to keep the system under control. If we map those concerns loosely onto software harness design, the grid looks roughly like this:

| Technique for handling models | In software development (← analogy) |
| --------- | ------------------------------- |
| Evaluation and benchmarks | Difference with and without a harness: cost, time, quality |
| Output filtering | **Safeguards and post-processing** (the closest analogy) |
| Multiple models / ensemble | Cross-review *(similar models fail together — not a silver bullet)* |
| Preprocessing | Search and context cleanup |
| Normalization | Comparison against a baseline (regression tests) |

This is, admittedly, a loose **analogy**. Concepts like “evaluation” and “output filtering” map fairly well, but forcing techniques like ensemble methods or normalization into a 1:1 mapping with software builds is a bit strained. Cross-checking with multiple models is especially not a universal solution. Many modern AI systems are built in similar ways, so models with similar architectures often share the same stupid mistakes and fail together. This is the nature of language models we discussed earlier in Chapter 4.

The most urgent and intuitive metric for us is simple: **take the same feature implementation scenario and directly compare the resource cost, time spent, and final output quality when the harness is running versus when it is not, meaning coding without a harness**. This is the measurement I was pointing to, somewhat provocatively, in Chapter 0 when I said, “If you want to argue with me, measure it yourself first.” I have written out a concrete method in [Appendix D](appendix-d-measure-it-yourself.md) so you can measure it yourself.

The first step in measurement started somewhere even simpler than a cost dashboard. It was about **making visible how many dangerous things were currently piled up in the project, and which of them had to be looked at today**. So before starting work, I made the agent open issues and, whenever possible, assign priorities. Things that needed to be done later were not allowed to just drift away in the middle of a conversation. I told it, “File this as an issue for later,” and pushed it into the queue.

Then I had AI collect the results every day and email them to me. Originally this was built for running open source with multiple people. For now, I still use it alone most of the time, so it is not perfectly tidy. But even just looking at the email subject and numbers every morning makes one thing obvious: **Ah, there is quite a bit of work I have not cleaned up.**

![](assets/image.webp)

*Figure 11-1. Naia daily issue report. As of 2026-06-24, it counted 229 total issues, 8 urgent P0 issues, and 70 high-priority P1 issues. A sentence like “Not ready — server now critical-path for the whole voice track” is not just a list item. It is an operational signal telling you where today’s bottleneck is.*

## 11.2 A Daily Issue Report Is the Project Dashboard

The value of this report is not in the numbers themselves. It is in the fact that the numbers repeat every day in the same format.
