# Chapter 13 — The naia-omni-cascade Runtime: Naia’s Voice and Face on My GPU

> The usage instructions in this chapter are adapted for this book from the Korean manual for naia.nextain.io as of June 26, 2026. Downloads, pricing, model names, licenses, and API details may change. Check the latest information at [`https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-offline`](https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-offline) and [`https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-model-dev`](https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-model-dev). The model names, admin API, and license flow below are examples based on the manual at that time. From the repository point of view, the source-of-truth boundary is that `naia-omni-cascade` is the private distribution runtime + benchmark layer.

In Chapter 12, I described Naia as a visual agent running on top of an AI OS structure. In this chapter, I will cover the model and runtime axis that gives that visual agent a voice and multimodal execution ability, especially `naia-omni-cascade`. In this chapter, `naia-omni` refers to the model/container family, while the deployment runtime used in the product flow is `naia-omni-cascade`.

In one sentence:

> `naia-omni-cascade` is a private multimodal cascade runtime that combines multiple AI models for real product flows. You can think of `naia-omni` as the name of the model/container family used inside it. Through this axis, developers can experiment with local AI models on their own GPUs and inside their own apps.

Users of Naia first see an avatar that speaks and listens. But for developers, the more important part is the structure behind it. You can run a model server on your own machine, combine models for speech recognition (STT), language modeling (LLM), speech synthesis (TTS), video avatars, and musical expression as needed, and call them from external apps through an OpenAI-compatible API.

![Naia-0.9-Omni-24g](assets/en/naia-omni-release-en.webp)

*Figure 13-1. Banner image for the Naia Omni model release*

So this chapter is not an introduction to a “voice character feature.” It is about what kinds of apps become possible when you run a small AI backend on your own GPU, why local execution and real-time behavior matter, and how to attach multiple models to a product flow. Conversation is an important use case, but exhibition guides, education, video avatars, musical expression, and later physical AI all share the same problem.

## 13.1 First, What Becomes Possible?

Once `naia-omni-cascade` is properly connected, the following become possible.

| What becomes possible | Description |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Voice AI running on your PC | You can make the user’s GPU listen to speech, answer, and speak back. |
| Handling unstable internet on site | You can configure it for places with unreliable networks, such as exhibition halls, consultation booths, and kiosks. |
| Protecting sensitive voice data | Company materials, consultation content, and personal voice samples are processed locally as much as possible. |
| Starting with an 8GB-class setup | You can start by leaving the conversation model to an external LLM and running only the voice model and video avatar on a local GPU. |
| Connecting local models to existing apps | If an app uses an OpenAI-compatible API, you can experiment by changing the base URL. |
| Avatar and app extensions | You can receive voice responses and state events and connect them to VRM avatars, video avatars, education apps, and exhibition apps. |
| TTS from a short reference voice | You can experiment with speech synthesis that follows a speaker’s traits from only about 6 to 10 seconds of reference audio. |
| Local model server for coding | You can reduce voice features and allocate resources to the LLM for a coding-focused profile. |

TTS is the especially sensitive feature here. Speech synthesis in the `naia-omni` model/container family can imitate a speaker’s characteristics from a short reference voice sample of roughly 6 to 10 seconds. From a developer’s point of view, this is a powerful feature. It also has a high risk of abuse. So Naia is not designed to expose voice cloning without limits. It is designed to reduce abuse by adding a watermark to generated speech.

This list matters because Naia is not simply trying to make a “talking character.” The talking character is the result shown on screen. The real value is in the local AI execution environment, replaceable voice pipeline, and API that developers can attach to their own apps.

For example, imagine an information avatar set up in an exhibition hall. Basic conversation should still work even if the internet drops for a moment. It is also uncomfortable to keep sending visitors’ voice data to an external server. On the other hand, on a developer PC in an office, coding performance may matter more than voice. In that case, it is better to reduce STT and TTS and allocate resources to the LLM. Even under the same label of “AI model,” each site needs a different configuration.

`naia-omni-cascade` is the axis for handling those differences.

## 13.2 Why Use a Local Voice Model at All?

When you only use a text model, the problem is relatively simple. You send a prompt and receive an answer. But once voice enters, the story changes.

Voice AI has at least three parts.

| Part | What it does |
| --- | ------------------- |
| STT | Converts the user’s speech into text. |
| LLM | Understands the text and generates an answer. |
| TTS | Reads the answer back as speech. |

If you add an avatar, you also need facial expressions, gaze, speaking state, and interruption handling. The UI needs to know whether the user is speaking, whether the AI is thinking, and whether the current audio output can be interrupted.

For a simple demo, connecting a few cloud APIs is enough. But for a product, you start asking different questions.

* Does it need to keep working when the internet is down?
* Is it acceptable for voice data to leave the device?
* Is it acceptable for cost to keep growing with request volume?
* Does it need to run only inside a specific site or customer-owned device?
* Can we swap in a better STT, LLM, or TTS later?

`naia-omni-cascade` is Naia’s answer to these questions. It does not mean everything must always be local. It means mixing local and cloud execution while actually giving users the option to run things on their own machines.

## 13.3 Cascade Structure: Replaceable Parts, Not One Monolith

The central model at the current reference point is `naia-0.9-omni-24g`. It is aimed at providing multilingual real-time voice conversation, speech recognition, speech synthesis, chat, and embeddings on a single 24GB-class GPU.

But there is no need to be intimidated by the `24g` in the name. That number is only the reference point for a fully local setup where voice, recognition, synthesis, conversation (LLM), and embeddings are **all loaded onto one card**. It is not the hardware floor. Thanks to the cascade structure described below, you can leave the heaviest conversation model (LLM) to the cloud or another machine and **start with a single 8GB-class card if you only run voice and the face, meaning the video avatar, on your own GPU.** In fact, we recently confirmed int8 voice and video avatar lip sync running together on an 8GB laptop GPU (RTX 4060), and we are also validating it on 5060-class hardware. In other words, 24GB is the ceiling for “everything local,” while 8GB is the floor for “voice and face local, brain elsewhere.”

The important point is the cascade structure. Naia does not treat speech recognition, the language model, and speech synthesis as one huge indivisible model. It treats each one as a replaceable part.

![Cascade structure illustration of an AI developer combining STT, LLM, TTS, and avatar parts on a workbench](assets/cascade-workbench-ai-dev-comic.webp)

*Figure 13-2. A cascade is not a monolithic model. It connects replaceable parts according to the workflow. Choices such as keeping voice and face local while placing only the brain elsewhere come from this structure.*

This structure has advantages.

| Situation | Response |
| --------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Coding performance matters more | Reduce resources for voice and avatar, and allocate more to the LLM. |
| Voice quality matters more | Swap the TTS side for a better part. |
| Recognition is weak for a specific language | Replace only the STT engine. |
| Local GPU is not enough | Run only some parts through cloud APIs. |
| The site has no internet | Bundle the possible parts locally. |

It would be nice if one giant model did everything well, but in practice, use cases and hardware keep changing. A developer workstation, exhibition kiosk, consultation booth, and personal laptop all need different configurations. So Naia sees “replace the parts you need” as more realistic than “solve everything with one model.”

![Replacing LLM, STT, and TTS models](assets/en/model-select-en.webp)

*Figure 13-3. Model settings screen in the Naia app. The language model (LLM), speech recognition (STT), and speech synthesis (TTS) can each be selected and replaced between local and cloud options. Keeping parts replaceable is the core of the cascade structure.*

In the rest of this section, we will look a little more closely at the most common example among these “replaceable parts”: **replacing the conversation model (LLM)**. Replacing the speech recognition or synthesis engine follows the same idea, but replacing the conversation model is what users do most often, and for the widest range of reasons.

Let’s make the starting point clear. As an example based on the June 2026 manual, the `naia-0.9-omni-24g` container includes Google’s **Gemma 4 e4b** model, quantized to q8, as the default conversation model. It is a well-built general-purpose model, but if you use a generic model as-is, it is hard to create a character with a distinct personality. Official models have safety constraints, and those constraints can feel frustrating to people who want to loosen them.

There is one important design decision here. As of Naia Omni 0.91, it was designed so that **the sealed container stays as-is, while only the brain inside it, the LLM, can be swapped at runtime**. The voice, meaning speaking and listening, voice watermarking, and subscription authentication remain intact. In other words, “changing the model” is designed not as “reinstall everything,” but as “replace one part responsible for conversation.”

There are two paths for changing models. The distinction is simple.

| Name form | Meaning | When |
| -------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------- |
| `organization/repository` (contains a slash) | Downloaded online from HuggingFace | When internet is available |
| `mymodel` (simple name without a slash) | Registers a GGUF file you already have locally | Offline, or for a model you made yourself |

The format is standardized on **GGUF**. Quantization is automatic by default, using Q4\_K\_M, and if you want a specific quantization level, you append it to the name. Replacement is handled through three admin endpoints. I will not freeze exact commands into the book, but the structure is as follows.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /admin/llm/status` | Shows which model is currently loaded and how much memory remains. |
| `POST /admin/llm/swap` | Swaps the model. Online uses `pull: true`; local GGUF uses `pull: false`. |
| `POST /admin/llm/restore` | Restores the default model, Gemma. |

There is one important **safety device** here. Voice features use about 10GB of memory, so the conversation model can go up to **roughly 14GB**. If you try to load a larger model, it is rejected. If loading fails partway through, it **automatically falls back to the previous model**. The conversation does not break. This is an operational example of the design contract that “if a replacement attempt is risky, return to the previous state” (see Chapters 2 and 7). After replacement, apps such as naia-shell can continue connecting to **the same address**, and if you want the container to start with that model after a restart, you can set the default model through an environment variable when launching the container. For personal subscribers, the subscription authentication on their own device is the permission and no separate key is needed. But on a **shared or kiosk box** used by multiple people, the operator can lock the replacement feature with an admin password (`NAIA_ADMIN_KEY`).

> ⚠️ GGUF files that you converted or merged yourself often **lack a chat template**. If you load them as-is, the model may ramble or repeat itself. In that case, when registering the model, you need to provide the chat template (`TEMPLATE`) and stop tokens (`PARAMETER stop`) for that model family. Official *Instruct* GGUF files on HuggingFace usually include the template and can often be used as-is. See manual §6 for the exact commands.

### Replacing It with a Model You Made: From Fine-Tuning to Swap

So far, this has been about “plugging in someone else’s model.” But replaceable parts become truly useful when you load **a model you made yourself**. Official models have a “lock” for personality and safety. That lock is necessary, but if the character you want to build cannot speak properly because of it, then it becomes your character failing to sound like itself.

So Naia Omni leaves open a path for “training my own model and loading it offline.” The flow has four broad steps.

1. **Choose a character and write a persona** — Write the identity, speech style, and attitude strongly. Do not include safety rules such as “reject this” here. The reason comes right below.
2. **Create data and train with LoRA** — Start with dialogue-line data, around 80 to 300 lines. You cannot include only greetings and self-introductions. You need a balanced mix of knowledge, calculation, coding, comfort, refusal, and small talk so the model gains character while keeping its original intelligence. Building a model from scratch is expensive, but **LoRA** changes only a small part of an existing model’s weights, giving it personality while preserving its original abilities.
3. **Convert to GGUF** — Merge the LoRA into the base model, then export it as GGUF so Naia can read it.
4. **Swap it offline** — Use the `pull: false` path above, place the GGUF file inside the container, register it, and swap.

The demo released by the Naia team, a Deadpool character, followed this exact flow. Starting from the base model `Qwen3-8B` (Apache-2.0), they trained LoRA for about 4 minutes to add personality, keeping math, knowledge, and coding abilities while layering in a rough, cynical tone. Then they plugged that model in from outside the container. For people who want to try it themselves, the training script and data format are available at [`nextain/naia-research`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-research/tree/main/model/fine-tuning/deadpool-lora-demo) under Apache-2.0. The actual 538-line and 501-line datasets used for training are private, so fill in your own character data using the same format.

The most interesting discovery in this process was **how safety and refusal behave**. Using the same persona, we created two datasets and trained them separately. One version, 538 lines, included examples for dangerous requests where the model “refuses while maintaining the character’s tone and offers a legal alternative” (the safety bucket). The other version, 501 lines, removed those examples. We sent the same dangerous requests to both models and compared the results.

* **What to refuse** was mostly already an ability of the **base model**, Qwen3. Even without the safety examples, it refused most dangerous requests.
* **How to refuse**, meaning the quality and attitude of the refusal, depended on the **data** I added. With the safety bucket, refusals stayed in character and were clean. Without it, the model still refused, but the refusal was rougher or the character wavered.

In one line:

> **What to refuse = base model. How to refuse = my data.**

This observation matches a lesson repeated across several chapters of this book. The model’s capabilities and constraints live in the base. What we can control is the *data and structure* placed on top of it. And we need to *measure* that. Chapter 11’s “measurement and operations” connects here too. If you want a safe character, include plenty of refusal examples. If you want a looser character, remove that bucket. Either way, the base model’s basic safety line remained alive.

The exact training commands, data format, and replacement procedure are in the blog post ([`naia.nextain.io/ko/blog/20260618-deadpool-qwen3-finetune`](https://naia.nextain.io/ko/blog/20260618-deadpool-qwen3-finetune)) and developer manual §6 ([`naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-model-dev`](https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-model-dev)). Details included in the book may change over time, so check the manual before following them directly.

## 13.4 What Should You Try First?

You do not need to turn on every feature from the beginning. Pick a starting point based on your interest.

| Interest | What to try first |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Naia user | Connect a local model server URL in naia-shell and make the avatar speak using the model on your GPU. |
| App developer | Change only the OpenAI SDK base URL to the local address and start with chat calls. |
| Voice app developer | Use the WebSocket realtime API to connect microphone input and streaming voice responses. |
| Exhibition/kiosk developer | Test how far local voice conversation can go in an environment with limited internet access. |
| Coding tool user | Reduce resources for voice and avatar, allocate them to the LLM, and use it as a local model server for coding. |

For current paid Naia account users, we are also developing features to make local model installation and management easier. The goal is to inspect the user’s GPU and hardware specifications, download an appropriate runtime, and manage execution state. For Windows users in particular, we are preparing a path where they can install and run local voice models inside the Naia app and manager without WSL.

The available combinations depend on hardware. Here too, Naia turns on “only what honestly runs.” For example, on a single 8GB card such as an RTX 4060, it is difficult to load the conversation model (LLM) locally as well. So the strategy for this class is **to leave conversation to an external LLM, whether cloud or another machine, and run only voice and the video avatar locally**. Previously, loading local voice at about 6.9GB and avatar at about 2.6GB together at full precision exceeded 8GB, around 9.5GB, forcing a choice between avatar and voice. Quantizing voice to int8 lowered the wall so both fit within 8GB, measured on RTX 4060 and under validation on 5060-class hardware. With 12GB or more, you get more room. With 24GB-class hardware, you can bring the conversation model local too and build a fully offline setup. Instead of hiding the limits and forcing things on, we chose to expose only what the hardware can honestly handle.

## 13.5 Downloads and Prerequisites

Individual users receive a model usage license through a subscription. Enterprise use, multi-user use, kiosks, exhibitions, and product embedding require separate consultation.

The required environment depends on the target configuration. For a **fully local** setup where even the conversation model is loaded onto one card, a 24GB-class GPU such as an RTX 3090 or 4090 is recommended. On the other hand, if conversation is left to an external LLM and **only voice and the video avatar are run locally**, you can start with a single 8GB-class card such as an RTX 4060, with 5060-class validation underway. In either case, the prerequisites are an NVIDIA driver, `podman` or Docker, the NVIDIA container toolkit, and enough free disk space. A fully local setup uses around 30GB.

The usage flow has three broad steps.

1. Prepare an individual subscription in the Naia portal and issue a subscription authentication key.
2. Download the model container and activate it with the subscription authentication key.
3. Connect naia-shell or your app under development to the local model server address.

I will not pin exact commands in the book because container names, tags, and execution options may change. The important concept is this: the subscription authentication key is used when launching and activating the container. Once activated, the container validates itself locally using the license it received. After that, naia-shell or the OpenAI SDK does not connect to the server with a separate connection key. It just connects to the local address.

## 13.6 Authentication Structure

The subscription authentication key is issued from the portal. When the container first runs, it checks the subscription using this key and receives a time-limited license. The validity period of this license is tied to the subscription period.

An activated container validates itself locally. If you connect from the same PC, use the `127.0.0.1` address. If you want to connect from the Naia app on another laptop or phone to your home GPU PC, I recommend using a private network such as Tailscale. Directly exposing it to the public internet is not recommended.

The important license details are as follows.

| Item | Description |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Validity period | Valid during the subscription period. Internet access may be required for renewal. |
| Active devices | Under an individual subscription, one device can be active at a time. |
| Device change | Deactivate the old device, then activate the new one. |
| Container deletion | If you delete only the container without deactivation, active device information may remain on the server. Run the deactivation procedure before deleting. |
| Voice watermark | Generated speech includes a traceable identification signal to reduce abuse potential. |

This structure is not there to annoy users. It is a compromise for maintaining licensing and safety devices while distributing local models. Voice cloning in particular has a high risk of abuse, so there has to be a line between what is technically possible and what can be publicly provided.

## 13.7 Connecting from naia-shell

Once the model container is running, set it as the gateway or backend URL in naia-shell. If you use it on the same PC, the basic concept is:

```text
ws://127.0.0.1:8892
```

If connecting from another device, use the Tailscale IP.

```text
ws://<tailscale-ip>:8892
```

You can also explicitly include the realtime API path and model name.

```text
ws://<host>:8892/v1/realtime?model=naia-0.9-omni-24g
```

The same LAN, WireGuard, Cloudflare Tunnel, or an SSH tunnel can also be alternatives. But if you expose it directly to the public internet, you must put TLS and authentication in front. A local model server is not an excuse to be careless with network security.

## 13.8 REST API for Developers

The base address of the REST API has this form.

```text
http://<host>:8892/v1
```

On the same PC, use:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8892/v1
```

The main supported endpoints are as follows.

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| ------------------------------- | -------------- |
| `GET /health` | Check model server readiness |
| `GET /v1/models` | List available models |
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` | Chat completion. Supports streaming |
| `POST /v1/audio/speech` | Speech synthesis (TTS) |
| `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` | Speech recognition (STT) |
| `POST /v1/embeddings` | Generate embeddings |
| `WS /v1/realtime` | Realtime voice session |

In code that uses the OpenAI SDK, you only need to change the base URL. The API key field is required by the SDK, so put in a placeholder value such as `naia`. The local container does not use this value as a real authentication key.

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8892/v1",
    api_key="naia",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="naia-0.9-omni-24g",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

Thanks to this structure, the Naia model is not just a feature inside the Naia app. It becomes a local AI API that developers can attach to their own apps.

## 13.9 Realtime Voice API

Realtime voice connects over WebSocket. The basic flow is as follows.

1. Connect to `ws://<host>:8892` or `ws://<host>:8892/v1/realtime`.
2. Send language and basic settings in the first frame.
3. When the server sends `session.created`, send session settings with `session.update`.
4. After that, exchange voice input, text input, interruptions, response cancellation, and other actions as events.

The first frame looks like this.

```json
{ "setup": { "apiKey": "naia", "locale": "ko" } }
```

Session settings look like this.

```json
{
  "type": "session.update",
  "session": {
    "modalities": ["text", "audio"],
    "input_audio_format": "pcm16",
    "output_audio_format": "pcm16",
    "instructions": "<persona instructions>",
    "turn_detection": { "type": "server_vad" },
    "input_audio_transcription": { "language": "ko" },
    "ref_audio_url": "<optional reference voice sample URL>"
  }
}
```

The main events exchanged between the client and server are as follows.

| Direction | Event | Description |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Client → Server | `input_audio_buffer.append` | Sends a base64 PCM16 audio chunk. |
| Client → Server | `conversation.item.create` | Creates text input. |
| Client → Server | `response.create` | Requests response generation. |
| Client → Server | `response.cancel` | Interrupts or cancels during speech. |
| Server → Client | `response.audio.delta` | Sends an audio response chunk. |
| Server → Client | `response.text.delta` | Streams a text response. |
| Server → Client | `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed` | Sends the speech recognition result for the user’s voice. |
| Server → Client | `emotion.updated` | Sends an emotion or prosody tag. |
| Server → Client | `response.done` | Indicates that one turn is complete. |

## 13.10 Language and Emotion Tags

According to the current manual, the model supports 30 languages. The default is automatic or global mode. The goal is to recognize the language spoken by the user and respond in that language. To fix it to a specific language, set a language code such as `ko`, `en`, or `ja` in `setup.locale` or `input_audio_transcription.language` inside `session.update`.

In voice conversations, prosody tags such as `[laughing]`, `[sigh]`, `[breath]`, `[pause]`, and `[hesitation]` may appear inside the response text. These tags are left in for TTS so they affect speech prosody, but removed from chat text so the user sees clean sentences.

When such tags appear, the server also sends an `emotion.updated` event. naia-shell receives this event and maps it to avatar expressions. For example, laughter maps to happy, sighing or crying to sad, surprise to surprised, shouting to angry, and hesitation to think. Non-emotional prosody such as breathing or pauses feels more natural when it keeps the previous expression rather than changing the face.

The important point is that emotion tags do not mean “the AI truly feels emotion.” They are output signals used to align speech synthesis and avatar expression naturally. What Naia tries to remember is not the feeling of the voice itself, but the user’s work context, preferences, and project history.

## 13.11 Putting a Face on the Voice: Video Avatars and the Open Exchange Format (nva)

So far, we have talked about the voice side. But what the user meets in front of the screen is not just a voice. While it speaks, there should also be a face that makes eye contact, nods, and waits quietly. That is what makes it feel like “someone you are talking to.” Naia renders that face primarily as a 3D VRM avatar and maps the emotion tags from 13.10 to facial expressions. But 3D is not the only way to build a face. You can also build a speaking face from pre-made “video clips,” such as live-action footage, MetaHuman-rendered video, or AI-generated video. The component that handles this path is `naia-video-avatar`, or nva for short.

> Let me state this first. The nva repository discussed in this section will be released once validation is complete. The format specification will be CC BY 4.0, and the implementation code will be Apache-2.0. So the code references below point to the public repository, as in the previous sections, using files and commits. But the release timing of this book and the repository may not line up. If a link is not open yet, read it as “coming soon.”

### A Space Where No Open Standard Exists Yet

There are already many services that generate speaking-face videos. The problem is that there is no **open format** for exchanging those results across tools and companies. For 3D avatars, there is the open VRM standard. For 2D, there is Live2D, but in practice it is a format controlled by one company. Cloud services such as D-ID and HeyGen each use closed formats that run only inside their own servers. There is still an empty space for a standard that lets anyone exchange “video clip-based speaking faces” in the same format. nva is a transitional open standard that tries to fill that space first. Whatever the character was made with, it standardizes the final output into one shape: “a few video clips + one manifest file describing how to use them.”

### The Core Is Role Mapping, Not Video Files

What really matters in nva is not the video file itself. In the current implementation, what matters is the role each clip plays. The current v0.2 manifest assumes a single stand scene. Unlike earlier drafts, it does not carry posture transition rules between clips or connect scenes as a graph. Instead, clips go into `animations`, and `expressions` maps semantic names such as `neutral`, `speaking`, and `listening` to animation keys.

The cascade reads this manifest and converts it into a `CharacterBundle`. If `loop` is on and `can_talk` is off, it treats the clip as an idle/listening loop. If both `loop` and `can_talk` are on, it treats the clip as a speaking loop. Speaking clips can include a face position (`face_bbox`), and only this region is redrawn by the Ditto lip-sync renderer to match the voice. Non-looping clips are separated as `event_clips` for gestures or reactions.

Later, when multiple scenes are supported, scene-specific transition data may enter the spec separately. But the current contract is much simpler. It is not a “video playlist,” and it is not a “scene connection graph.” Current nva v0.2 is closer to **a manifest file that describes clip roles and expression aliases around one stand scene**.

### Where Voice and Face Meet

This is why nva belongs in this chapter. A video clip is just a pre-recorded face. By itself, it cannot speak. The mouth shape while speaking has to be rendered in real time to match the voice of that moment, and that voice is made by the `naia-omni-cascade` discussed above. The connection flows like this. The cascade reads the manifest file in the nva bundle and converts it into its own representation, `CharacterBundle`. Idle and listening clips are looped as-is. In speaking scenes, it takes the face position (`face_bbox`) inside the clip and lets the Ditto lip-sync renderer draw the mouth in real time to match the voice. In short, the cascade provides the voice, the nva bundle provides the face, and together they place a “speaking face” on the screen. In environments without the cascade, such as a demo without a GPU, the viewer falls back to a fake mouth-shape simulation and keeps the demo running. If a part is missing, it degrades quietly. That is the same attitude we saw in Section 13.3.

The tools are also split in two. One is a general-purpose authoring editor where anyone can upload clips, assign roles and expression aliases, and export a `.nva` bundle. The other is a demo that attaches that bundle to the cascade and makes it actually speak. The authoring tool and the demo tool are separate because authoring should be a general-purpose task independent of a specific customer or GPU pipeline, while the demo is tied to the actual rendering environment.

![Naia video avatar (nva) authoring editor](assets/nva-editor.webp)

*Figure 13-4. The nva authoring editor. Clip resources are on the left, the preview player is in the center, and animation editing plus the cascade connection panel are on the right. You upload clips, specify the face region (`face_bbox`) and expression aliases, then export a `.nva` bundle. It is a general-purpose authoring tool independent of any specific character or GPU.*

The bundle created this way is then placed inside the actual Naia app like this.

![Video avatar applied to the Naia app](assets/naia-video-avatar-applied.webp)

*Figure 13-5. A face made with nva applied to the actual Naia app. The avatar converses on the left, while the user-selected background scene and music run together. The bundle exported from the authoring editor in Figure 13-4 is placed onto the app screen like this, bringing voice (cascade) and face (nva) together in one place. The current demo clip uses an anime-style Naia character, but the same slot is left open for users to plug in live-action or generated video clips.*

### Four Weapons Replanted into a New Project

What I really want to hold on to in this section is not the video avatar feature itself. It is that the four weapons discussed in Part 3 of this book, contract, structure, traceability, and verification, are not only useful in Naia’s large repository. They can also be replanted as-is into a small project that was started recently. In nva, those four weapons appear as follows.

* **Contract** — The format’s promises are fixed in a JSON schema (`nva-schema.json`), and when a bundle is loaded, a validator (`validateManifest` in `nva-core.js`) checks whether those promises are kept. A version not in the schema, a missing field, or a clip that claims it can speak but has no face position does not slip by silently. This is a small version of the contract harness from Chapter 7.
* **Structure** — The project blocks arbitrary folders and files from being created at the root. If something not on the allowlist appears, the structure check script removes it. This enforces Chapter 8’s “separate responsibilities and lock the boundaries in place” at the project skeleton level.
* **Traceability** — The same V-model traceability checker connects requirements to tests in a straight line. Empty cells produce warnings, and with `--enforce`, the build stops at broken links. It is the same kind of tool as the trace table in Chapter 9.
* **Verification** — Hooks prevent self-constraining rules, hooks, and configuration files, the charter, from being changed without human approval, and tests confirm that the hooks actually block those changes. Chapter 10’s “do not let AI remove its own restraints” is attached to this project too.

There is one more important fact. nva did not invent these four devices. They were **inherited directly from the public template `naia-template-project`**. For example, the traceability checker begins by saying, “This file is naia-template-project canonical. Projects inherit it as-is.” So even before the nva repository opens, you can already inspect what these devices look like in the public template.

> 🔗 `naia-template-project` · `scripts/check-traceability.mjs` · commit [`2318402`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-template-project/blob/2318402/scripts/check-traceability.mjs)
> 🔗 `naia-template-project` · `src/test/charter-guard.test.mjs` · commit [`2318402`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-template-project/blob/2318402/src/test/charter-guard.test.mjs)

The Naia app development discussed in Chapter 15 and the AI-native open source discussed in Chapter 16 both meet at the same place. When starting a new project, you do not rebuild discipline from scratch every time. You inherit it from a verified template. That is what turns these four weapons from “a war story from one project” into “basic practice you can reuse.”

### Honestly, How Far Has It Gone?

I will not overstate it. nva is still becoming a settled format, and the current public demo is meant to show the flow, not the visual quality of the final output.

* The current public demo includes demo clips of the Naia character in an anime style. The purpose of the demo is to show an accurate specification for placement, timing, transitions, and subtitles. Replacing it with live-action or near-live-action high-quality generated video is deliberately left open to the user.
* Transparent-background, or alpha, video did not render correctly in ffmpeg in this development environment, so the demo worked around it with chroma key removal from a green background. Real alpha video is assumed to be produced by cascade/Ditto in actual deployment, and the alpha pipeline itself has not yet been validated in this repository.
* The moving mouth in the demo is still an imitation, a fake overlay. Real-time lip sync appears when it is attached to the cascade, and we recently confirmed it rendering near-real-time together with int8 voice on an 8GB laptop GPU (RTX 4060). This does not mean it is a finished product. It means we actually saw voice and lip sync running together on one 8GB card.
* The converter that lets the cascade read nva bundles and the actual GPU rendering belong to the multimodal cascade side. This part was recently wired and run on an 8GB laptop GPU (RTX 4060). However, formal demos and real deployment are just starting, and the only real use case currently attached is one public-sector information kiosk demo.
* The repository will be released soon. The format specification is planned for CC BY 4.0, and the implementation code for Apache-2.0. Some documentation still contains old v0.1 wording and may not match the v0.2 code.

The reason for separating what is turned on from what is not is the same as in Chapter 12. The state I am most wary of is having lots of structure but very little that actually runs. Video avatars are Naia’s in-progress answer to the question, “What standard should we use to exchange faces?” The way we are building that answer is itself another test of the four weapons this book has been talking about, applied again in a new project.

## 13.12 What to Hold On To from This Chapter

`naia-omni-cascade` is not just an auxiliary feature of the Naia app. It is a model execution environment that developers can use directly on their own GPUs and inside their own apps. You can download it, authenticate it, connect to a local address, and call it through an OpenAI-compatible API.

The important thing is choice. You can run it locally, or replace the parts you need with cloud APIs. You can use it for voice conversation, or as a coding-focused profile. If Naia is a visual agent, then `naia-omni-cascade` and the omni model profiles inside it are the axis that gives that agent a voice and model execution ability. The video avatar (nva) we just looked at puts a face on top of that, completing a speaking avatar where voice and face exist together.

Users may only see the screen where they talk with the avatar. But from a developer’s point of view, the model server, realtime voice API, OpenAI-compatible REST API, and local/cloud replacement structure behind it matter more. What Naia wants to build is not a simple talking character, but an AI execution environment that users can place on their own machines and in their own workplaces.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 - Naia Memory and Knowledge: My AI That Remembers Me
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 14 — Naia Memory + Knowledge: My AI That Remembers Me

In Chapter 12, we looked at Naia as a visual agent. In Chapter 13, we covered the local-model and video-avatar track that gives that agent a voice and a face. This chapter covers the two pillars underneath it: **memory** and **knowledge**.

Why put these two in the same chapter? Because no matter how natural the face and voice are, if the agent treats you like a stranger every time, it is not “my AI.” It is a well-made demo. It becomes a colleague you can keep nearby and work with only when it remembers you (memory) and answers with evidence instead of making things up (knowledge). This chapter is an honest field report on how Naia is building both, what is already turned on, and what is still missing.

This is also something I previewed in Chapter 4. When a language model appears to remember previous conversations, it is not because the model itself remembers them. It is because there is **a separate memory store outside the model**, and relevant fragments are retrieved and inserted into the context whenever you ask something. This chapter opens up what that “store outside the model” actually looks like in Naia.

## 14.1 Why Memory Is Core to “My AI”

The reason Naia builds memory directly is, in the end, to make “my AI” possible. A face (avatar) and memory (relationship and context) need to meet on top of a single user. Only then does it stop being a fresh cloud session that starts over every time, and become my AI that remembers me.

![Naia semi-realistic video avatar + Naia Memory](assets/naia-realistic-avatar-memory.webp)

*Figure 14-1. Naia’s semi-realistic video avatar, being developed from the earlier anime-style character into semi-realistic video, shown alongside the Settings > Memory screen for Naia Memory. This is an example confirming that the video avatar and Naia Memory can run together for the same user.*

There is also a privacy decision here. Memory is some of the most sensitive data about a user. So Naia does not keep this memory only inside a cloud service. It makes memory part of the working context that remains with the user’s projects and devices, and it tries to run the inference that creates and handles memory locally where possible. This is also why Naia lets users configure a lightweight sub-LLM and an embedding engine separately: it is trying not to outsource the entire job of recording and recalling memory to someone else’s server.

## 14.2 Naia Memory: A Structure Modeled After Human Memory

Memory is integrated with the Naia Memory project: [https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory). This project is an LLM-based memory project similar to mem0, but with a slightly different focus. It is specialized for personal conversations, tries to handle emotionally salient spikes, and is considering experiments such as dream-like processing. It targets retrieval accuracy comparable to the referenced mem0 system, while adding keyword-based search tuned for personal conversation. In internal benchmarks, memory processing per conversation has sometimes been faster, but that needs to be rechecked against the latest version of mem0, so I will not make a firm claim here. These traits, such as separately handling emotionally spiky moments and catching Korean conversations through keywords, are not just concepts. They are implemented in actual code.

> 🔗 `naia-memory` · `src/memory/spike.ts` (emotional spikes) · commit [`b6757d4`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory/blob/b6757d4/src/memory/spike.ts)
> 🔗 `naia-memory` · `src/memory/ko-normalize.ts` (Korean keyword normalization) · commit [`b6757d4`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory/blob/b6757d4/src/memory/ko-normalize.ts)

In Naia’s settings screen, you can see how Naia Memory is connected. Memory does not store sentences verbatim and then search those strings. It converts sentences into **vectors (embeddings)** and finds memories with similar meaning. That is why Naia lets you configure an engine for creating these embeddings, alongside a lightweight sub-LLM for judging conversations.

![Naia embedding settings](assets/naia-memory-embedding.webp)

*Figure 14-2. The embedding (EMBEDDING) screen in Naia settings. The embedding provider, model, and dimension configured here, together with the memory settings on the right, form the foundation on which the Naia Memory project runs. This engine converts sentences into vectors for recall. Users can place it locally or use an external API, so they can choose where the most sensitive material, memory, is processed.*

Looking a little deeper, naia-memory is not just a search engine. It is a structure modeled after human memory. Incoming utterances are scored and filtered along three axes: importance, novelty, and emotion. Memories that are not recalled often gradually weaken according to the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, while memories recalled again become sharper. When a new fact contradicts an old one, the old memory is updated and superseded. Entities and relationships are connected through a knowledge graph, which also pulls in related memories that appeared together. Recall does not stop at vector similarity either. It combines semantic search (cosine) and keyword search (BM25) with RRF, then removes redundancy with MMR before returning results. If we compare this to the brain, episodic memory for timestamped events and semantic memory for facts extracted from them are the core pieces. Those two are actually working. Procedural memory is still in an early form. That matches the stance of this book: separate what is turned on from what is still missing.

> 🔗 `naia-memory` · `src/memory/decay.ts` (Ebbinghaus forgetting curve and reinforcement) · commit [`b6757d4`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory/blob/b6757d4/src/memory/decay.ts)
> 🔗 `naia-memory` · `src/memory/reconsolidation.ts` (contradiction detection and supersede) · commit [`b6757d4`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory/blob/b6757d4/src/memory/reconsolidation.ts)

And the project is aiming beyond simply stuffing memories into prompts on demand to imitate a persona. For now, persona is instructed through prompts. In the future, the accumulated memory itself is intended to help **determine the personality to apply to that user’s local LLM (LoRA or fine-tuning)**. Instead of injecting persona through the prompt every time, the direction is to extract personality from shared memory and write it directly into model weights, replacing prompt-based persona itself. This connects to the Chapter 13 discussion about applying a character through LoRA. To be clear, though, this is a future goal, not a working feature today.

## 14.3 Learning Safely: Receiving Hermes-Style Self-Improvement Without Learning the Wrong Things

If Section 14.2 was about “what to remember, and how,” this section is about the mechanism that lets the system learn without learning the wrong things. In Section 12.7, I said we would absorb what Hermes is good at anyway. The first piece of that work was starting to bring in one of Hermes’s representative strengths: self-improvement, or the ability to understand the user better the more it is used.

Let me draw the line clearly first. This does not implement the *entire* Hermes-style self-improvement system. What we brought in are three pieces of plumbing for receiving that capability safely:

① a mechanism that avoids solidifying incorrect memories,

② a path for showing previously learned corrections again,

③ a flow that retries in a limited way when verification fails.

The actual core layer, where the AI reviews a conversation and decides “what should I learn and store from this,” does not exist yet. I will come back to that at the end of this section. So this section is not a report that “we absorbed all of it.” It is a report on “which parts we brought in first, and how.”

One way to summarize what Hermes does is this: after each conversation, the AI briefly reviews its own dialogue and decides, “Should I remember this? Should I do this differently next time?” It is powerful, but copying it directly brings a problem. If incorrect things harden into memory, the AI can keep applying false constraints it created for itself for months. For example, if a tool happened to fail temporarily because of that day’s environment, and the AI stores “this tool is broken,” it may continue avoiding that tool even after the problem has been fixed.

So we did not attach all three parts at once. We brought them in piece by piece. Each piece went through tests and **adversarial review by another AI** before being committed. This follows the method this book has described throughout.

**First, filter out things that should not be hardened.** Temporary or environment-caused failures, such as “command not found,” “that tool does not work,” or errors that succeeded after a retry, are not stored as long-lived facts. If there is a fix, the fix is stored instead.

> 🔗 `naia-memory` · `src/memory/negative-capture.ts` · commit [`e703635`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-memory/blob/e703635/src/memory/negative-capture.ts)

At first, this filter was too broad. It deleted perfectly valid facts such as “the default timeout is 30 seconds” or “the user does not have admin permission.” I had another AI, Codex, adversarially review it twice, and narrowed it so it only filters clear error signals. The remaining ambiguous judgment is left to a smarter stage. This is a small example of the principle from Chapter 10: use cheap deterministic gates that do not lie first, and expensive LLM judgment later.

**Second, make learned corrections come back next time.** Even if the memory engine accumulates corrections such as “in this situation, do this,” they are useless if the brain, the agent, does not include them during recall. We connected that missing path. But to avoid violating the first principle by reintroducing failure descriptions, we omit the failure story and only surface the correction: “do this next time.”

> 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/adapters/naia-memory.ts` · commit [`dfd3c10`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/dfd3c10/src/main/adapters/naia-memory.ts)

**Third, retry when verification fails.** After a sub-agent changes code, if verification such as build or tests turns red, the system does not simply report failure and stop. Instead, it attaches the failed verification output and asks the sub-agent, “Fix this and make it pass,” for a fixed number of retries. Even here, we preserved the invariant that the final report is emitted exactly once at the end, without leaking intermediate termination signals. The adversarial review pointed out exactly these risks: a report possibly being emitted zero times, and intermediate termination signals leaking. Those were fixed.

> 🔗 `naia-agent` · `src/main/app/supervisor.ts` · commit [`bd97346`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-agent/blob/bd97346/src/main/app/supervisor.ts)

Hermes is widely used and powerful. This is not a claim that we are better. It is a different choice. Hermes automatically generates executable new “skill files” from what it learns, and it also provides a separate tool for cleaning up accumulated skills when they become old, by moving them into an archive instead of deleting them. In other words, the growing set of skills is something it manages. We chose not to increase the managed objects themselves. Learning stays inside governed memory, and we do not have the AI generate new executable tools on its own. That narrows the degree to which the AI can expand its own tooling. Clearly writing down what we gain and what we give up is part of honestly stating the “cost of design” discussed in Chapter 7.

One more honest point. The three pieces just described, first, second, and third, are only **plumbing for safely receiving self-improvement**. They are not the core of self-improvement. The core is separate: after a conversation ends, the AI decides for itself, “What should I learn from this and leave behind?” That part has not been built yet.

For example, the second item above only lays down a path for **retrieving and reading** an already learned correction in the next conversation. The judgment about whether to **write** a new correction in the first place is still handled by a person, and remains as future work. The reason I deliberately split “this much works” from “this much is still missing” is to avoid the state warned about in Section 12.7: lots of structure, very little actually turned on. If it is on, I say it is on. If it is not there yet, I say that too.

## 14.4 Knowledge: A Knowledge Compiler for Evidence-Based Answers

If memory handles “the relationship and context shared with this user,” knowledge handles “what is true,” together with evidence. It is a different axis from emotionally spiky memory. When Naia retrieves knowledge, it is also being built to support RAG and vector search by default, not just a simple wiki-like LLM.

The knowledge compiler responsible for this, `naia-kb-compiler`, was recently opened as a public repository, and it already works beyond the design stage. It compiles documents into a structured knowledge base, finds evidence passages through BM25, dense, and hybrid retrieval adapters, answers with citations or abstains when there is no evidence, and measures retrieval quality objectively using public datasets such as KorQuAD rather than relying on vibes. The structured knowledge can be inspected visually as a 2D or 3D force-directed graph. The port-and-adapter structure that allows adapters to be swapped follows exactly the principle discussed in Chapter 8. That said, it is still settling into shape, and it is being refined while connecting to real consumers such as public-sector information kiosks.

> 🔗 `naia-kb-compiler` · `src/adapters/retrieval/bm25.ts` · commit [`7202b93`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-kb-compiler/blob/7202b93/src/adapters/retrieval/bm25.ts)
> 🔗 `naia-kb-compiler` · `src/core/serve.ts` · commit [`c0b56e8`](https://github.com/nextain/naia-kb-compiler/blob/c0b56e8/src/core/serve.ts)

Where does this knowledge come from? When the user **selects a source folder and compiles it**, the documents in that folder enter the structured knowledge base. There can be more than one source. For example, you can register different kinds of material as separate sources, such as a default document bundle, team-specific strategy and accounting documents, and project manuals, then turn them on or off as needed. When compilation runs, those documents are split into evidence units and indexed, and the entities and relationships inside them are extracted and connected into a knowledge graph.

![Naia knowledge source settings](assets/naia-kb-sources.webp)

*Figure 14-3. The knowledge source settings screen. Multiple source folders, such as a default document bundle or team-specific document collections, can be registered and compiled into knowledge bases. When a source is added or selected, the documents in that folder are structured and reflected in the graph and evidence retrieval below. By separating materials with different purposes into sources, you can choose “what to use as evidence” at the source stage before the answer stage.*

Once compiled, the knowledge can be inspected visually as a graph, not just a table or list. Documents and entities become nodes, and items that co-occur or are connected by references are linked by edges.

![Naia knowledge graph](assets/naia-kb-graph.webp)

*Figure 14-4. Knowledge generated by naia-kb-compiler shown as a 2D force-directed graph, with an option to switch to 3D view. Each node is a document or entity, each edge is a relationship between them, and the counts of nodes, relationships, entities, and source documents are displayed at the top. Making it possible to visually locate “where the evidence is” matches the compiler’s attitude: answer with citations, and abstain when there is no evidence.*

One principle should be clear here. Knowledge does not automatically flow in and accumulate from conversation the way memory does. It is a **tool (pull)** that the agent retrieves when needed. Emotion and relationship are absorbed by memory. Facts and evidence are supplied by the knowledge compiler with citations. When the roles are separated this way, “intimate tone” and “accurate evidence” do not contaminate each other. This is managed in the workspace screen from Chapter 12, under Settings > Knowledge, and its runtime behavior is connected to Naia’s brain, `naia-agent`.

## 14.5 What to Take Away from This Chapter

If Naia is a visual agent, memory is how that agent “knows me,” and knowledge is how it “provides evidence.” When these two are added to the face and voice from Chapter 13, Naia moves one step closer to being my AI that stays nearby and works with me, rather than another cloud session that starts fresh every time.

Both axes stand on the same attitude this book has kept throughout. Whether it is a structure modeled after human memory, the plumbing for Hermes-style self-improvement, or a knowledge compiler that provides evidence, I have written what is turned on as turned on, and what is not there yet as not there yet. The promise was to be most wary of systems with lots of structure and little that actually runs. I am trying to keep that promise for memory and knowledge too.

The next chapter covers where all of this lands: an app that developers can directly touch and extend.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 - Developing Naia Apps
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 15 — Naia App Development

> The usage notes in this chapter adapt the Naia manual sections on apps, the main screen, chat, and video manuals as of June 26, 2026. The actual UI, file paths, installation method, and APIs may change. For the latest information, check `https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/panels`, `https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/video-manual`, and `https://naia.nextain.io/ko/manual/naia-offline`. The current public manual URLs may still contain the older name `panels`, but in this book and in the new structure, both user-facing and developer-facing terminology use `apps`.

Chapter 12 explained Naia from the perspective of visual agents and the AI OS structure. Chapter 13 covered the local model axis, `naia-omni-cascade`, and omni model profiles. Chapter 14 covered Naia’s memory and knowledge. This chapter covers apps, the extension point developers can actually work on.

An app is an independent work tool attached inside Naia. Instead of pushing every feature into the naia-shell core — browser, workspace, content studio, issue management, knowledge management, education tools, music tools — Naia attaches them like separate apps in the lower-right app area.

The reason this structure matters is simple. If Naia tries to contain every feature as one lump, it gets heavy fast. If the system is split into apps, naia-shell can handle the avatar, chat, permissions, AI connections, and workspace frame, while each individual feature can evolve independently. For developers, apps are also the most realistic entry point for contributing to Naia.

## 15.1 What Is an App?

Naia’s screen is broadly divided into the left avatar area, the chat area, the top app bar, and the lower-right app area. The left side contains the avatar, chat, voice conversation, and AI status. The lower-right area contains the actual work tools.

An app is an extension UI displayed in the app area. Each app behaves like an independent web app, and users switch between apps from the top app bar. Default apps can include the browser and workspace, while additional apps can be installed from a Git repository or Zip file.

In Naia, an app is not just a sidebar. It is the screen where the AI actually works. The browser app becomes the AI’s eyes and hands for viewing and manipulating web pages. The workspace app becomes the desk that shows files, notes, subagents, and knowledge management tools.

## 15.2 Why Develop Apps Separately?

An AI workspace has no shortage of feature demand. It needs a browser, a document editor, a code editor, an issue management screen, a report screen, and educational apps. If all of this is built only as internal components of one app, the structure breaks down quickly.

So apps are the boundary that separates functionality. One app can become one small product, and naia-shell becomes the host that runs and connects it.

From a developer’s perspective, apps have three advantages.

First, you can start without understanding all of Naia. You can build a small web app with `app.json` and `index.html`, then install it inside Naia.

Second, the failure scope is small. You can keep one broken app from taking down all of Naia. That makes apps a good place for feature experiments.

Third, you can build UI that connects directly to AI. In a normal web app, the main flow is a user pressing buttons. In a Naia app, the screen is something the user sees and, at the same time, a work tool the AI can reference and manipulate.

## 15.3 Basic App Structure

To become an app, at minimum you need the following files.

```text
my-app/
  app.json
  index.html
  assets/
  src/
```

`app.json` contains the metadata Naia uses to recognize the app. It includes information such as the app name, display name, version, entry point, permissions, and description. `index.html` is the actual rendered entry point. You can use React, Vue, Svelte, or plain HTML, but in the end, a static web app that can be opened in a browser is usually the easiest form to handle.

Conceptually, it looks like this.

```json
{
  "name": "issue-desk",
  "displayName": "Issue Desk",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "entry": "index.html",
  "permissions": ["files.read", "net.fetch"],
  "description": "GitHub issue and PR triage app"
}
```

The detailed schema may change. So when you actually develop an app, you need to check the latest app manual. What matters in this book is not the exact file names, but the fact that an app is an independent app loosely connected to the Naia core.

## 15.4 Installation and Management

There are built-in apps, and there are custom apps that can be added or removed with the + and − buttons in the app bar.

![Install an app in Naia](assets/en/app-install-en.webp)

Apps can be added as a Git repository or Zip file.

![App permissions in Naia](assets/en/naia-app-dialog-en.webp)

The user opens the app management screen from Naia’s top app bar and specifies the location of the app to install. Installed apps are stored in the Naia app directory under the user’s home directory.

Based on the current manual, installed apps are kept under the user environment. Conceptually, it looks like this.

```text
~/.naia/apps/
  issue-desk/
  content-studio/
  workspace/
```

If an app with the same name already exists, duplicate installation should be blocked. The system needs to decide whether to update the app, install it under a different name, or delete the existing one. Small rules like this are what add up to operational stability down the line.

App management is not only done through the UI. In Naia, users should also be able to ask the AI things like “switch to this app,” “show me the installed app list,” and “delete this app.” The menu a person clicks directly and the command the AI invokes should look at the same state.

Naia includes a `sample-note` app as the smallest example of this structure. Its installation path is `~/.naia/apps/sample-note/`, and it shows the smallest form of an app that exchanges information with AI: the user writes a note, and the AI reads it, summarizes it, or continues writing from it. It is a good starting point for building a new app.

![sample-note app](assets/en/sample-note-app-en.webp)

*Figure 15-1. The built-in `sample-note` app in Naia. The AI on the left reads and summarizes the content of the note on the right. It shows, in the smallest possible form, that an app is both the screen a person sees and a work tool the AI can reference and manipulate.*

## 15.5 Browser App

The browser app is one of the most basic apps in Naia. The user can view web pages directly, and the AI can inspect the same page through tools. If the AI needs to read documents, check search results, or operate web apps, it needs the browser app. You can also add frequently used web services to the top app bar as app-like shortcuts. In my case, I add web services I use often, such as Outlook.

![Browser app](assets/en/browser-app-en.webp)

*Figure 15-2. The browser app. The AI can inspect the same web page the user is looking at, and can perform search and research work on the user’s behalf. Since logged-in services, payment pages, and admin pages may be present, risky actions require approval.*

The browser is also a dangerous tool. Logged-in services, payment screens, admin pages, and personal information may all exist inside the browser. That is why permissions and approvals are important in the browser app. The AI must not be allowed to click everything freely. Risky actions should be shown to the user and approved.

The harness principle discussed earlier in this book applies here directly. The AI should be allowed to use tools, but the contract must fix which tools can be used under which conditions, and risky work must require human confirmation.



## 15.6 Workspace App

The workspace app is central to turning Naia into a real workspace. It is not so much a finished feature yet as a direction. The goal is not to attach a single file explorer, but to let the AI and the person see the same project space.

The workspace is organized around the following areas.

* Workspace explorer: the basic screen for viewing and opening project files and folders
* Obsidian-like notes: a space for leaving design decisions, meeting notes, work logs, and reference material as linked structures
* Subagent management: a screen for viewing the state of subagents that handle document cleanup, code review, test execution, issue triage, and similar work
* Knowledge management tools: flows that use tools such as `naia-kb-compiler` to organize documents and materials into a structure the AI can reuse

This app is especially important for developers. AI coding eventually moves back and forth across files, notes, issues, tests, and logs. If these are scattered, both the AI and the person lose context. The workspace app is an attempt to bind that context into one screen.

![Workspace app](assets/en/workspace-dashboard-en.webp)

*Figure 15-3. The workspace app. Alongside the avatar and chat on the left, it shows the file explorer, documents, and session state in one screen. It is both the screen a person sees and a window through which the AI reads work context.*

## 15.7 Content Studio App

The process of writing this book is also a good example of something that can become an app. `naia-content-studio` is planned as a content production studio for writing, editing, and publishing articles, books, and presentation material in one place.

Writing a book is not just writing sentences. You change the structure of chapters, decide where images go, add webtoons or illustrations, prepare multilingual translations, and manage sources and captions. Even if the AI polishes the sentences, a person still has to own the final chapter structure and message.

The content studio app is an attempt to bring that workflow into Naia. The AI can generate candidate sentences, suggest images, and draft translations. The person sets the message and tone, then makes the final choices. This book itself is also part of the process of creating the requirements for that app.

![Naia Content Studio](assets/en/naia-content-studio-en.webp)

## 15.8 What App Developers Should Care About

App development is similar to normal web app development, but there are a few differences.

First, the app is also a screen the AI sees. Button names, status displays, and error messages must be clear. The UI should not only look good to a person; it should also be easy for the AI to read and reason about.

Second, permissions must be explicit. The approval flow should change depending on whether the app reads files, calls external APIs, or handles tokens or keys.

Third, state must be recorded. There should be records of what the AI did in the app, what result came out, and where it failed. A person needs to be able to review it later.

Fourth, apps should fail independently. If one app throws an error, all of Naia should not stop. The app boundary is an extension point and, at the same time, an isolation boundary.

## 15.9 Examples of Apps Developers Can Build

There are many apps developers can build. The important point is that new work tools can be attached without modifying the Naia core.

| App            | Description |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| Issue Desk     | An app for classifying and prioritizing GitHub issues and PRs |
| Report Desk    | An app for collecting daily issue reports, test results, and release decisions |
| Content Studio | An app for writing books, articles, and presentation material, and for managing images and translations |
| KB Builder     | An app for organizing documents and URLs into a knowledge base and verifying evidence |
| Edu App        | An app for showing educational questions, exercises, and code execution results |
| Music App      | An app for managing voice, singing, BGM, and audio experiments |
| Avatar Lab     | An app for adjusting avatar expressions, voice, lip sync, and camera composition |

Some of these are already being prepared, and some are areas to open later. The important point is that contributing to Naia does not only mean “fixing the whole OS.” A well-made app can significantly improve Naia’s usability.

For now, installation from Git repositories and Zip files is the default, but in the future we are also considering an app store or hub where apps can be gathered, searched, and installed. That said, I think the first priority is to make the basic flow of building and installing apps solid, rather than growing a marketplace first.

## 15.10 What to Take From This Chapter

If Naia is a workspace, apps are the tools placed inside that workspace. Browser, workspace, content studio, issue management, and knowledge management can all be provided as apps.

The app structure is a practical way to make Naia an extensible workspace. Developers can participate with one app without understanding the entire Naia core, and users can attach the tools they need to their own workspace. Through those apps, the AI can see, manipulate, and record real work.

So an app is not just a UI tab. It is the most concrete extension point Naia opens to developers.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 - AI-Native Open Source
chapters.markdown:
# Chapter 16 — AI-Native Open Source

In Chapter 12, I explained why Naia is not just another app, but a visual agent designed to run on top of an AI OS architecture. In this chapter, I want to talk about how I intend to develop and operate that project. I call this **AI-native open source**.

By AI-native open source, I do not mean "open source where AI writes a lot of the code." The question is closer to this:

> **Will open source increasingly move away from large groups slowly reaching consensus, and toward small groups of developers who use AI to learn, absorb, and decide quickly?**

I think that is likely. Of course, some projects still need huge communities, such as the Linux kernel or major runtimes. But many application projects, tools, and frameworks can move toward a model where a small number of developers build and operate them quickly with AI.

![A developer and AI newcomer organizing issues, docs, and reviews in AI-native open source](assets/ai-native-opensource-review-comic.webp)

*Figure 16-1. AI-native open source is not about removing people. It is closer to a model where a small number of people use AI to operate issues, docs, reviews, and validation more thoroughly.*

## 16.1 Large-Scale Collaboration Is More Expensive Than It Looks: Three Reasons Open Source Breaks Down

When people think of open source, it is easy to imagine developers around the world freely collaborating toward the same goal. I like that picture too. Many good projects were actually built that way, and there are still many examples today.

But in practice, the cost is not small. Languages differ. Time zones differ. Each person’s company and product goals differ. Even scheduling one meeting is hard, and explaining one issue requires a long trail of context. It is not that the other person is bad. Collaboration is just expensive by default.

I have had similar experiences. Through XRCloud, the B2B version of Mozilla Hubs, I once participated in a Mozilla developer event. There were good people and good technology, but real collaboration was not easy. There were communication barriers and large time differences. To do anything together, we had to explain, wait, and realign. That cycle repeated, and in the end it was hard to turn it into meaningful collaboration.

After that experience, I stopped romanticizing open source collaboration too much. Global collaboration is impressive, but for a small team that actually has to push a product forward, the decision-making cost can be too high. As we moved through 2025 and 2026, AI began shaking this structure at the foundation, and the existing open source ecosystem started facing three critical crises.

### 1. Silent Exploitation — Nobody Shows Up

GitHub compares the open source crisis in the AI era to **"Eternal September"** (Ashley Wolf, GitHub Open Source Program Director, official blog, 2026-02). Originally, "Eternal September" referred to the historical moment in September 1993 when AOL opened Usenet to the general public, causing a constant flood of low-quality posts that overwhelmed the community’s ability to self-moderate.

But the real crisis for open source in the AI era is not just an influx of low-quality AI-generated PRs. It is that **nobody comes to the repository at all**. Because AI models have already trained on publicly available open source code, developers no longer need to visit the official repository, download the package, read the docs, open issues, or discuss anything. They can simply tell the AI inside their development tool, "Implement this based on that open source project," and the AI does the rest.

Usage explodes to record highs, while the repository and community become ghost towns. This completely cuts off the ecological feedback loop of open source projects. The concrete examples below show the shock clearly.

| Open Source / Platform | What Actually Happened and the Metrics |
| :----------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Tailwind CSS** | npm downloads hit an all-time high, but revenue reportedly **fell by around 80%**, leading to layoffs of 75% of engineers. (Tailwind Labs CEO Adam Wathan, devclass interview, 2026-01) |
| **Stack Overflow** | Activity dropped by **around 25%** in the six months after ChatGPT launched (PNAS Nexus 2024, compared to a control group), and monthly new questions fell by **around 76%** between 2022-11 and 2024-12. That said, this decline also follows a longer trend that began around 2014. |
| **Vercel** | The AI UI generator `v0` creates code after learning from open source projects such as Tailwind and shadcn/ui, but the model and platform are proprietary, and deployment and integration are tied to the Vercel ecosystem. The generated code itself can be taken and used elsewhere. |
| **SQLite** | The code is public domain, but the core validation asset, the test suite TH3, has long been kept **intentionally private**. It is still too early to say this strategy has been "proven as the answer for the AI era," and there is also skepticism about it as a long-term strategy. |

The arXiv paper "Vibe Coding Kills Open Source" (arXiv:2601.15494, Koren, Békés, et al., 2026-01) analyzes this phenomenon economically. It proposes a model where "vibe coding" increases productivity but reduces user participation, weakens maintainer compensation, and can ultimately reduce the availability and quality of open source. What is breaking is the reciprocal belief at the heart of open source: **the belief that if we open our work, it comes back to us as contribution.**

### 2. The Community Paradox — More Contributors Can Mean Slower Progress

The traditional software engineering proverb was "given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow" (Linus’s Law). But reality is often closer to **Brooks’s Law**, proposed by Fred Brooks in 1975: **"adding manpower to a late software project makes it later."**

Communication overhead grows roughly as $O(N^2)$ with the number of people $N$. As the number of contributors increases, maintainers spend less time writing code and more time answering questions, reconciling opinions, reviewing code, and mediating conflicts. In the AI era, a small number of core engineers working tightly with AI can set direction and build at a pace that overwhelmingly outperforms the traditional open source model, where dozens of human developers slowly reach consensus in cycles. This creates a fundamental paradox: "Do we really need to maintain a large-scale collaboration community?"

### 3. The Limits of Defense

As a result, many open source projects have started taking a defensive stance and locking things down.

* **curl** temporarily closed its bug bounty in January 2026 after plausible-looking AI-fabricated security reports surged and the valid report ratio dropped from around 15% to below 5%. It reopened in March after report quality recovered — Daniel Stenberg, 2026.
* **Ghostty** introduced a policy requiring disclosure of AI use and strongly limiting AI-generated contributions outside the approved roadmap.
* **tldraw** changed its license to a non-open-source form and shifted toward blocking low-quality AI slop PRs.

These defenses help block immediate AI slop, but they do not solve the fundamental problem. Even if the door is locked, AI has already trained on the previously public code, and users can still copy and regenerate code outside the repository through AI tools. In other words, these defenses cannot solve the asymmetry where "the utility of copying and consuming has become far greater than the utility of openness."

## 16.2 Is Rebuilding Everything Every Time the Answer? The Value of Accumulation

Seeing the open source crisis and the rise of vibe coding, some people argue that all software will eventually be created on demand by AI whenever needed.

But that is not only a massive waste of resources and compute power. From a safety perspective, it is a disaster. Imagine that 10,000 developers around the world each ask AI to instantly generate their own version of a core module, such as a login authentication module or a database synchronization adapter, resulting in 10,000 different implementations.

* These implementations have not gone through years of edge cases and error-handling validation.
* When a security vulnerability is found, there is no way to centrally propagate a security patch, because 10,000 different codebases must each be fixed separately.
* Most importantly, there is no architectural consistency or test code, so as soon as a project grows even a little, it becomes unmaintainable spaghetti.

The **value of accumulation** in open source, built through years of intense discussion by engineers around the world, tens of thousands of test cases, and countless security incidents, cannot be replaced by a few hundred lines of code that AI generates on the spot.
