The words appeared on the radio net, and a low vibration began at the rear of the landing zone. At first, Yujin thought the ground was shaking. Then the sound of rotors descended over his body. Two AH-64Fs rose into a low hover. The wind swept red dust from the top of the blast wall and pressed down on Yujin’s shoulders. The helicopters did not climb into the sky. They tilted toward the plain, roaring low—far too low.

The orc ranks wavered. Yujin could not know what they thought the helicopters were. But he could see them falter. The sound of the rotors drowned out both beasts and men. Beneath it, the 30-millimeter chain guns spat fire.

Another flare burst.

The red plain was filled with broken lines. Shields dropped, flags fell, bodies clambered over one another. The Earth forces were overwhelming them. So utterly overwhelming that Yujin could not call it victory. But the radio net was precise.

“Western approach blocked.”

“Southern formation collapsing.”

“Open ammunition crate three.”

“Medical team standing by.”

War lingered longer as orders than as screams.

Incendiary rockets struck the edge of the forest. The red branches blackened first, then white smoke rose. Several orcs burst out from that direction. Some were on fire. The displays marked them as heat signatures. They were so bright that their human shapes disappeared.

Akira vomited. The emergency absorbent lining inside his helmet activated at once. He started to swear, then swallowed his breath.

“Are you all right?” Yujin asked.

“What does ‘all right’ even mean?” Akira said.

The words did not go out over the radio net.

The battle did not last long. The orcs surged forward several more times and broke several more times. The final formation withdrew toward the walls. The Earth forces did not pursue. Hale conserved ammunition and fuel. The two Apaches returned to the landing zone and went straight under the maintenance canopy. The technicians checked the rotors and sensors, the temperature of the chain-gun barrels, and the remaining ammunition. Someone wiped the red dust clinging beneath a nose section, while someone else detached an empty ammunition box. The procedure was the same as always. That made it worse.

As dawn approached, Menon picked something up at the edge of the battlefield. It was a small metal tag. A fragment of red stone and a thin lock of hair were tied to it.

“An ornament?” Yujin asked.

Menon shook his head.

“Probably something tied to the dead.”

“Are you sure?”

“No.”

He carefully placed the tag in a specimen bag.

“But ornaments worn in battle don’t repeat like this.”

Dubois came closer and looked toward the bodies. She was wearing two pairs of gloves.

“Specimen collection will be limited. No contact with bodily fluids.”

Menon nodded.

A victory report appeared on the tactical network. Heavy enemy casualties. Three friendly personnel lightly wounded. Minor equipment damage. Landing zone successfully defended.

Something else remained on Yujin’s camera. Eyes shining white beneath the flares, a flag curling in the wind, a small metal tag half-buried in the earth.

And the ringing in his ears that continued long after the Apache rotors had stopped.

chapters.title: 07. What Was Left in the Forest
chapters.markdown:
# 07. What Was Left in the Forest

![Chapter 7 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-07.webp)


The day after the first battle, the forward reconnaissance unit entered the Red Forest south of the Citadel Belt.

Their mission was not pursuit. They were to determine where the orc formation that had collapsed under the flares the night before had retreated, find a route armored vehicles could use, and plant temporary relays along it. The signal poles they carried were stakes as tall as a person, fitted with folding antennas and position beacons. If communications failed inside the forest, the soldiers were to drive the poles into the ground, laying short bridges one by one between the drones and the landing zone.

The poles were the first things to disappear.

The feed from the forward reconnaissance unit did not cut out. If anything, it was too clear. The drone flew above the trees, while the soldiers’ helmet cameras transmitted red trunks, black leaves, and low mist in turn. Then one of the position markers at the bottom of the screen turned gray. The signal-strength indicator dropped from five bars to four, then from four to three.

Captain Han Doyun was watching those numbers. He was at the head of the forward maneuver company. His face was sun-darkened, and a thin old scar ran above his left eyebrow. He was a man of few words, but his eyes moved first. People always mentioned that he had served in South Korea’s 707th, but he never used it to introduce himself. When Yujin first asked him for an interview, his answer had been brief.

“I’m an officer in a contract unit now.”

“Does your military experience in Korea affect your operations here?”

“A rifle is heavy no matter where you fire it.”

That was all.

Hale ordered verification instead of pursuit. If the route was open, the engineers would install more relays, and armored vehicles would follow to widen the supply route.

It was a short distance on the map. In reality, the Red Forest folded and unfolded the road. The low gravity made each step light, but the view was heavy. The trees did not grow straight like trees on Earth. Their trunks twisted, and their black leaves drooped like cloth that had swallowed the light. When the drone rose above the canopy, it could see the road. When it descended, it lost the people.

“Setting up Relay Three.”

Han Doyun’s voice came over the radio.

A work robot advanced carrying a folded antenna. Two soldiers watched the perimeter while another drove the stake in without digging. Martian soil was soft until it suddenly hardened like stone. The robot spun uselessly three times.

“Do it manually,” Han Doyun said.

The soldier swore. Only static came over the radio net.

Yujin watched the feed from inside the landing zone control tent. Though he was not in the field, his shoulders ached as if his body were there. Beside him, Nowak calculated the supply route. He was watching the road rather than the reconnaissance unit.

“If just two kilometers of ground to the right of that point is open, the armored vehicles can get through.”

“And if they aren’t?”

Nowak did not answer. He selected another route. The screen turned red. Grade exceeded. High canopy density. Unstable communications.

An orc appeared on the reconnaissance feed for the first time. There were three of them. They wore no armor and carried no weapons. They were dragging something along the roadside. It looked like a cart, but one wheel was broken. One of the soldiers raised his sights.

“Do not engage,” Han Doyun said.

“Presumed civilians.” For a moment, the word silenced the radio net. Civilian had not yet officially entered the operational documents. Han Doyun had used it, then immediately added another order.

“Do not make contact. Go around.”

The soldiers went around them. The orcs beside the cart saw the Earth forces. They did not flee. Instead, they gripped the cloth covering the cart more tightly. Yujin could not see what lay beneath it.

The signal dropped to two bars.

“Send up the aerial drone.”

The drone rose above the canopy. The view widened. Another wall of the citadel, a red waterway, a small bridge, and moving dots appeared in the distance. Farther still, something gleamed deep inside the forest. Metal.

“Possible ambush,” the tactical AI said.

At the same moment, the signal dropped to one bar.

Someone inside the landing zone control tent drew a breath. Hale did not take his eyes off the screen.

“Reconnaissance unit, return.”

The order went out.

Han Doyun answered at once.

“Returning.”

He did not hesitate. But returning was harder than advancing. The route the drone had seen was not a route people and armored vehicles could use. Relay Three, installed only moments before, blinked green and then turned yellow. The feed from the returning work robot shook violently.

“Relay Three signal unstable.”

“Cause?”

“Physical movement. Or external impact.”

A horn sounded inside the forest. It was close. This was not the long note they had heard from the citadel walls. Short, low blasts overlapped from several directions.

Han Doyun’s feed cut out once, then returned. He did not run. He was a man who knew that running would break the formation.

“Slowly. Don’t look back. Drone to the left canopy.”

“Do we shoot?” one of the soldiers asked.

“If you see it.”

“See what?”

Han Doyun did not answer for a moment.

“A weapon.”

The forest showed nothing clearly. Red leaves stirred, and shadows passed between black trunks. The reconnaissance unit returned to the landing zone, but not by the same route they had taken out. Relay Three was left behind. So was one work robot. One drone landed inside the forest when its battery ran low.

Inside the control tent, Nowak added the losses to the list.

One relay. One work robot. One reconnaissance drone. Four hours, twenty minutes.

Hale studied the report, then replayed the final footage from Han Doyun’s feed. It showed the orcs beside the cart gripping the cloth.

“You said presumed civilians?” he asked.

“That’s what they looked like,” Han Doyun replied.

“From now on, write ‘local noncombatant entities’ in the report.”

“Civilians is more accurate.”

There was a brief silence.

Hale did not get angry.

“We haven’t approved that word yet.”

Yujin wrote down the sentence. Inside the landing zone, everyone was relieved to see the reconnaissance unit return. But the relay, the robot, and the drone remained in the forest. And perhaps the cloth-covered cart remained there as well.

chapters.title: 08. Friday Night at the Landing Zone
chapters.markdown:
# 08. Friday Night at the Landing Zone

![Chapter 8 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-08.webp)


What came after the shooting lasted longer than the shooting itself.

Sergeant Nakamura Kenji removed the bolt from his M4A2 and wiped away the red dust. The cloth quickly grew filthy. He did not take out a fresh one. He knew it would soon be just as dirty. He checked the inside of the barrel, applied the barest trace of lubricant, and wiped it again. Beside him, another soldier had opened the knee joint of his powered suit and was picking out the red particles that had worked their way in like sand.

There was no victory music at the landing zone. Instead, there was the hum of generators, the whir of fans at the drone charging stations, the pressure controls in the medical tent, and, in the distance, the clatter of tools from the Apache maintenance shelter. It was the night of their first victory. No one celebrated. There was too much to do.

Seo Yujin walked among the soldiers cleaning their weapons. One had taken off his gloves and was rubbing his fingers. Blisters had formed inside them. The powered suit could carry his load, but it could not use his fingers for him. The hand that pulled the trigger, the hand that changed magazines, the hands that dug earth and gripped a stretcher were still human hands.

“You just finished a battle, and you do this right away?” Yujin asked.

Kenji did not look up.

“If we don’t, it won’t go out next time.”

“The rifle?”

“The rifle. Us too.”

He slid the bolt back into place.

“Guns are heavy and dirty. Movies rarely show that.”

Another soldier beside him gave a short laugh.

“Reporter, do you know what matters most right now, after we just defeated a medieval alien army?”

“What?”

“Drying our socks.”

He was holding up a pair of socks. Red mud stained them to the ankles. Yujin could not laugh. The soldier did not laugh for long either.

Major Tomasz Nowak was recounting the inventory in the supply shelter. The screen listed combat rations, ammunition, aviation fuel, filters, drone batteries, water-purification membranes, spare joints, and medical blood substitutes. There were many numbers, but they all moved in one direction.

“We won, but you don’t look happy,” Yujin said.

Nowak turned the screen toward him. Aviation fuel consumption was eighteen percent above plan. Filters were being replaced at twice the expected rate. Drone battery use had exceeded projections.

“Even a battle you win consumes supplies.”

“You didn’t expect this?”

“I did. The problem is that it consumes a little more than expected. War always consumes a little more.”

He pointed to the time remaining until the next supply window. The number was mercilessly calm.

26 months.

That did not mean nothing would arrive before then. Small emergency shipments could come through. Medicine, electronic components, data, vaccine candidates. But the windows for bringing in enough food and aviation fuel for a battalion, armored-vehicle parts, and ammunition were fixed. There were no roads in space. No trucks waiting to come when called.

In the medical tent, Major Sara Ben Youssef was attending to three wounded soldiers. She was small, but her voice was low, and when she examined a patient, she watched their breathing before looking at their face. All three were their own. One had broken an arm in a fall, another had taken shrapnel from a fire pot in the thigh, and the third had caught his fingers in the door of his own armored vehicle. Some wounds had been inflicted by equipment rather than combat.

“Have you checked for local casualties?” Yujin asked.

Ben Youssef paused for a moment.

“There must be some.”

“Are you documenting them?”

“We’re preserving battlefield footage and thermal records.”

She tightened the wounded man’s bandage. He clenched his teeth.

“The medical unit isn’t going in. We have no orders and no quarantine protocol.”

It was cruel, but it was not a lie. The medical tent had been erected to save Earth’s soldiers, and for that reason it filled all the faster.

Dr. Claire Dubois was inspecting the waste bins outside the quarantine shelter. Gloves, filters, soil samples, and bloodstained cloth collected after the battle had been placed in separate color-coded bags. When a soldier tried to put his gloves in the general waste, she caught him by the wrist.

“Red bin.”

“There’s no blood on them.”

“Just because you can’t see it doesn’t mean it isn’t there.”

The soldier did not complain. He put the gloves in the red bin and used hand sanitizer. Its smell sharpened briefly in the air.

As the night deepened, a low sound came from beyond the landing zone. At first, it sounded like the wind. Soon they realized it was a horn. One from the direction of the walls, one from the southern woods, another from the distant coast. They sounded as though answering one another.

The soldiers stopped what they were doing.

Lieutenant Colonel Marcus Hale’s voice came over the radio net.

“Maintain perimeter watch. Continue maintenance.”

Continue maintenance.

The words set the landing zone in motion again. Rifles were wiped clean, drones charged, and helicopter mechanics ducked beneath the rotors. Yujin raised his camera and photographed those hands. The hands of a victorious army were not clean.

Just before dawn, Kenji rested the rifle he had finished cleaning across his knees and closed his eyes for a moment. Beside him lay three magazines still waiting to be cleaned.

The horns from the walls did not stop.

chapters.title: 09. The Fighting Begins
chapters.markdown:
# 09. The Fighting Begins

![Chapter 9 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-09.webp)

A low rumble spread through the entire Red Forest.

First came the horns. Then a sound like drums joined them, and finally came the footsteps. Earth's screens tried to separate the trembling leaves from the heat signatures, one by one. People, beasts, carts, fire. The squad support AI put up too many markers. The display was more confusing than helpful.

“Cut down the markers,” Captain Han Doyun said.

Half the icons vanished from the screen. The forest became a forest again. That made it more frightening.

This time, the orcs did not strike directly at the landing zone. They advanced along several routes. Some emerged from near the walls carrying shields, while others entered the southern woods. There were groups pulling carts as well. At first, the Earth forces classified them as supply units. Soon they saw that the carts were loaded with jars of incendiary liquid.

Hale divided the defensive line.

“Armored vehicles to the west. Mortars to the south. Heliborne units on standby. Launch Apache One only.”

“What about Two?”

“Under maintenance.”

That brief answer explained the entire landing zone. They had weapons, but not all of them were ready to use.

The first group of orcs approached from the west with overlapping shields. The shields could not stop bullets. When the M250s opened up, the shields split and bodies fell. But while they were falling, another group drew closer through the southern woods. The number on the tactical network kept rising. 300, 500, 700. A small label said estimate, but the soldiers saw the number.

“I thought they were medieval,” someone spoke.

“There were plenty of people in the Middle Ages too,” Captain Han Doyun replied.

He was not angry. Nor was he trying to erase their fear. It was simply a fact.

Apache One lifted off and stayed low. Its rotors drove dust across the landing zone. The pilot acquired the carts laden with incendiary jars gathered at the forest's edge. A Hellfire streaked toward them. The explosion was brief; what followed lasted longer. Something like burning oil spilled across the red grass. Two carts burst at once, scattering the orcs around them.

But another cart had come closer. It was concealed behind a group carrying shields. The thermal displays of the Earth forces separated bodies, fire, and metal, but detected the ceramic jars behind the shields too late.

“Southern barrier!” Captain Han Doyun shouted.

An incendiary jar came flying. Yujin could not tell whether it had been launched from a catapult or thrown by hand. It failed to clear the barrier and fell outside. But the fire that spilled from the shattered jar caught the edge of a solar canopy. The canopy was more fragile than bullets. The white membrane shriveled black, and sparks flew from the connected power cables.

“Cut Power Two!”

“Move the drone charging station!”

“Where's the fire-suppression robot?”

“South!”

Commands overlapped. The inside of the landing zone suddenly became a battlefield. No one had been shot, but six drones stopped charging, one relay went down, and the medical refrigerator switched to backup power. The orcs' incendiary jars could not penetrate a tank. They did not need to.

Yujin filmed the fire-suppression robot running toward the flames. The small four-legged robot carried a tank of suppressant on its back. It paused for a moment before the fire, then sprayed. At that instant, another incendiary jar landed nearby. The robot toppled onto its side, one leg still turning uselessly.

Akira raised his camera and started to run, but Yujin caught him.

“Don't go.”

“We have to get that.”

“You have to be alive to film it.”

Yujin was briefly startled to hear those words come from his own mouth.

The battle raged both outside and inside the landing zone. To the west, machine guns cut bodies down; to the south, combat engineers dragged burning equipment away. Each mortar round that struck the edge of the forest sent blackened red leaves surging into the air. Incendiary rounds burned out the ambush positions, and the fire spread beyond them into what looked like farmland.

Menon watched from behind the barrier.

“That's their watercourse,” he said.

No one heard him. Or they heard him and could not answer.

The Martian forces eventually withdrew. The Earth forces had won again. But this victory left a long list behind it. Two solar canopies damaged. One relay lost. One drone charging station destroyed by fire. Medical refrigeration unit switched to backup power. One fire-suppression robot written off. Heat damage to the outer skin of an aviation-fuel bladder.

Nowak studied the list and remained silent for a long time.

Hale asked, “Can we defend it?”

“The landing zone, yes.”

“The front?”

Nowak changed the display. The route between the southern woods and the gorge turned yellow.

“I can't say that yet.”

From near the walls, horns sounded again. This time, no one could tell whether they signaled victory or retreat. The Earth forces could not interpret them, and what they could not interpret was classified as a threat.

Yujin watched the last glow of the flares that had burned all night fade away. When darkness returned, the fallen bodies disappeared from sight. But the smell of the burned solar canopies remained.

chapters.title: 10. Storm and Incendiaries
chapters.markdown:
# 10. Storm and Incendiaries

![Chapter 10 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-10.webp)

The rain did not fall only from above.

Inside the Red Forest, it came from the side as well. Heavy drops struck trunks and leaves and burst apart, and the low wind drove the spray into people’s faces. Water and mud smeared helmet visors in turns. The filters kept running, but the soldiers were constantly clearing their throats. Martian rain smelled different from rain on Earth.

Captain Han Doyun stood beside the armored vehicle, looking toward the southern route. The tactical map showed three roads, but not one was visible before him. There were only red trunks and black leaves, low-lying mist, and channels running with water.

“Launching the drone,” the squad leader spoke.

“Keep it above the canopy. Don’t bring it down.”

“We need to see below to find the road.”

“If you bring it down, it won’t come back.”

That had already been proven twice. One drone had caught in the branches, and another had lost its signal and struck a rock while attempting an autonomous return. The third flew higher. Its view was broader but less useful. They could see the road, but not the rocks on it.

At the landing zone, the engineers were pushing the Green Corridor forward. Irrigation pipes were buried in the red soil, and a thin membrane held the water in place. Green moss and lichen were laid over it. The colors of Earth grew more vivid in the rain. The engineers called it stabilization.

Dr. Ravi Menon used another word.

“Less water is reaching the farmland over there.”

The engineering officer looked at the screen. At the edge of the red marsh, several orcs were pulling up something like roots and loading them onto a cart. They did not look toward the Earth forces. They merely walked for a long while along the route the water had once taken, then rubbed the blackened grass between their fingers.

“It’s inside the zone we occupy,” the engineering officer spoke.

Dr. Ravi Menon did not answer. The word occupation applied to water as well.

By afternoon, the storm arrived. The Martian sky abruptly darkened, and dust and rain flew together. The helicopters could not take off. Apache One was secured beneath the maintenance canopy, and the two Black Hawks had their rotor restraints checked again. The wind shook the solar membranes and lifted and dropped the ends of irrigation pipes that had not yet been fully anchored.

The orcs came in the confusion.

They did not form ranks. They appeared and vanished in small groups among the trees, rain, and dust. Few carried shields. Instead, there were canisters strapped to their backs, wet cloth, and short spears. Rain blurred the Earth forces’ screens, and thermal imaging rendered the entire sodden forest in muddied colors.

“Watch for fire canisters,” Captain Han Doyun spoke.

The first canister landed beside a relay. The flames did not go out even in the rain. Liquid ran down, burning through the cable insulation. Relay Five turned yellow, then went black.

“Five is down.”

“Set up the spare.”

“The spare is three hundred meters back.”

“Bring it.”

Two soldiers and a quadruped robot moved out. The robot carried the spare relay on its back. As it crossed a narrow channel, one of its front legs sank in. A soldier pulled at it, but the robot sounded an alarm. Joint overload. Manual release required.

Meanwhile, the second fire canister flew toward the solar membrane. Once again, the membrane proved more vulnerable than the bullets. When it caught fire, the power line shut down automatically, and the drone charging station went dark. Four reconnaissance drones that had been charging lay still, like dead insects.

Lieutenant Colonel Marcus Hale spoke briefly over the landing zone radio network.

“Incendiaries authorized.”

Captain Han Doyun looked toward the edge of the forest. Orcs were inside it. Beyond them lay the watercourse and the fields of red roots.

“Narrowing the strike zone.”

“Authorized.”

The incendiary rockets were calibrated to burn only the forest’s edge. But fire did not read maps. The wet leaves caught slowly, but once they did, they gave off black smoke. Several orcs ran out screaming. Behind them, the fields of red roots slowly turned black.

Seo Yujin watched the feed from the landing zone control tent. Li Wei’s Earth channel was open beside him.

“The official term is a supply-route stabilization operation,” Li Wei spoke.

“And the use of incendiaries?”

“Clearing ambush sites.”

“What about the farmland?”

The channel fell silent for a moment.

“An area of native vegetation.”

Seo Yujin wrote the phrase down. An area of native vegetation. It was easier to burn if you did not call it farmland.

The storm passed near sunset. A black line appeared along the southern route. On the map, the supply route had grown a little clearer. In reality, smoke rose from both sides of the line, and red water had pooled black.

Major Tomasz Nowak updated the damage report.

Relay Five lost. One solar membrane destroyed by fire. One drone charging station inoperable. One quadruped robot with joint damage. Two irrigation pipes ruptured. Reserve aviation-fuel bladder requires relocation.

“Is the supply route open?” Lieutenant Colonel Marcus Hale asked.

Major Tomasz Nowak hesitated for a moment.

“On the map, yes.”

“And in reality?”

“We’ll have to look again tomorrow.”

Captain Han Doyun looked at the forest after the rain. The orcs had withdrawn, but they had not disappeared. Even if they could not block the road, they were raising its price. One relay, one solar membrane, several drones, one robot, two irrigation pipes. And a field of red roots that did not appear on the map.

When night fell, no sound came from the forest. The silence lingered longer than victory.

chapters.title: 11. The City Beyond the Window
chapters.markdown:
# 11. The City Beyond the Window

![Chapter 11 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-11.webp)


The orbiter’s screens were too clear.

Seo Yujin had boarded the orbiter not because of the fighting. He was there to back up his original ground footage in the orbital archive and submit the Earth-bound edit for security review. The official explanation was data synchronization and a public-affairs briefing. In practice, it was also a way to remove a reporter who had filmed too much on the ground from the landing zone for a while. Yujin knew this and pretended not to.

The recovery craft had lifted off from the landing zone the night before. He had been strapped into a windowless seat, and his body had grown light again. Muscles that had barely begun to adjust to the surface were pulled in another direction. Hours later, when he stepped into the orbiter’s corridor, there was no red soil under his shoes. Strangely, that made him more uncomfortable.

Colonel Elena Vosrov was watching the dots moving toward the coast. The screen could magnify the ruts left by cartwheels, the sails of small boats, even the bodies gathered at the water’s edge. But on the operational map, they were all dots of the same color. Yellow. Potential threat movement.

The observation room was dimly lit. Unlike the surface, there was no dust here, no smell of blood. The air circulated at a constant temperature, and the floor did not shake. On the screen, the red wetlands were dying black, while inside the observation room someone’s coffee substitute was going cold. Yujin hated the difference. From far enough away, everything could be explained.

He stood at the rear of the observation room. The surface was beautiful from Martian orbit. That made it worse. The red Inland Sea gleamed like dark glass, and the walls of the Citadel Belt were visible only as shadows. Forests and wetlands divided into layers of red. The Green Corridor traced a thin line between them. Earth’s colors stood out even from this distance. They looked like a wound, and on Earth’s military maps, like a supply line.

“Is that spreading?” Yujin asked.

Vosrov enlarged the image. The red wetlands around the green line running from the landing zone toward the gorge to the south were turning black. Small bodies had gathered at the edge of the blackened area. They carried no weapons. They held tools like hooks and were scraping the bottom of the waterway.

“It’s a stabilization zone.”

“It’s dying black.”

“That’s a soil reaction.”

“Isn’t it damage, not a reaction?”

Yujin’s voice came out louder than he intended. One of the officers in the observation room turned to look at him. Yujin pointed at the screen. Small bodies had gathered along the edge of the blackened wetlands, and the hooks in their hands were no longer moving.

“We still don’t know what they were scraping up. Whether it’s food, medicine, a crop, or something used in funerals. But we’re destroying something we don’t understand.”

Vosrov did not change her answer.

“It’s a soil reaction.”

“Is that truly how you see it, Colonel?” Yujin asked.

Vosrov’s hand stopped over the screen. She did not answer at once. In the observation room’s dim light, her face looked harder.

“That is how I have to report it.”

“Does that answer the question?”

“Mr. Seo.”

Vosrov’s voice grew clipped.

“This is an observation room. Not a debating chamber.”

At her words, the officer at the rear of the room turned away. Yujin knew he had crossed a line. But as he watched the small bodies standing motionless at the edge of the blackened wetlands, he could think of nothing to say by way of retreat.

Vosrov looked at him slowly.

“Do you think I can’t see what’s on that screen?”

Her voice was not loud, but it had an edge.

“I see it every orbit. I see those wetlands, the dots moving toward the coast, the lights on the walls. But I’ve seen Earth too. Flooded cities, water-ration lines, old people killed by heat waves, families denied migration permits. We did not come here as tourists. We came with a mission.”

She paused to catch her breath.

“My orders are to maintain the orbiter, observe, communicate, and enforce quarantine. In this operation, the orbiter is positioned to eliminate even the slightest possibility of failure before it happens. If one communications link goes down, one supply line falls out of alignment, one quarantine door closes too late, it isn’t only the people down there who are put at risk. This ship is put at risk, and Earth’s next launch window closes with it.”

“So we’re not allowed to say anything?”

“You’re allowed to speak. But if you shout, I’ll have you removed.”

Vosrov turned her gaze back to the screen.

“And my feelings do not go into the operational log.”

She did not seem to be lying. Those appeared to be the only words she had for what was changing on the screen. Soil reaction. Stabilization zone. Planned settlement site. Give the same scene a different name, and it became a different event.

Dr. Ravi Menon entered the observation room. He looked as though he had barely slept. His pad displayed the photographs of symbols collected through the previous day. Funerary tablets, carts, evacuation boats, banners on the walls, irrigation channels in farmland. Red soil had dried around the edge of the screen protector. He was the only person aboard the orbiter who carried dirt with him.

“Please enlarge the coast.”

Without looking at him, Vosrov moved her fingers. The boats along the coast grew larger. There were orcs beside them who wore no armor. Small bodies moved among the adults, and the carts were loaded with boxes and cloth. Some carts were so heavy that two bodies pushed from behind while one pulled from the front. When they reached the water, the loads were transferred to the boats. They were hurrying, but there was an order to it. The small bodies first, then the things covered in cloth, and the water containers last.

“That’s an evacuation,” Menon said.

“It’s a possibility,” Vosrov said.

“If the possibility is strong enough, it needs to factor into operational decisions.”

“It does. Possible civilian movement.”

She opened a small entry at one side of the screen. Possible civilian movement was on the third line. The first was enemy force redeployment. The second was reinforcement of coastal defenses.

Menon looked at the order.

“Why is it third?”

“Risk assessment.”

“Risk to whom?” Yujin had asked the same question before. Once again, Vosrov did not take long to answer.

“Us.”

The observation room fell silent. Only the hum of the orbiter’s air circulation could be heard. There was no wind here, no smell. The wetlands dying on the surface were a change in color, and the people heading toward the coast were dots. Zoom out, and everything became an operation.

Vosrov analyzed the routes around the city. Red dots moved from the citadels to the coast, from the farmland to the Inland Sea, from the forest’s edge to the cart tracks. She divided them by category. Presumed armed. Presumed unarmed. Large carrier. Vessel. Unidentified heat source. Each time the classification was completed, the screen grew a little tidier. The tidier it became, the more the city’s noise disappeared.

Yujin enlarged one area. A child following behind a cart fell. An adult turned back and helped the child up. The child clutched one knee and cried for a moment. The screen had no sound. The adult did not pick the child up. With one hand, the adult pulled the child to their feet; with the other, they pushed the cart. The scene lasted only a few seconds. When Yujin zoomed out again, the child became a dot.

“Can I broadcast this?” Yujin asked.

This time, Vosrov looked at him.

“The original footage must undergo security review.”

“Why?”

“It contains operational intelligence.”

“The child too?”

Vosrov did not answer.

A new alert appeared at the bottom of the screen. Green Corridor irrigation pipe 3: pressure stable. Target soil moisture: 72 percent. The engineers were reporting success. At the same time, beyond the corridor, several orcs discarded blackened aquatic plants instead of loading them onto their carts. They picked up the discarded roots again, smelled them, and threw them far away. When a small body tried to retrieve one, an adult caught it by the wrist.

Menon spoke quietly.

“If that’s food, then what we’re taking from them isn’t just a road. It’s their food.”

“That has not been confirmed,” Vosrov said.

“Do we continue until it is?”

“There are no orders to stop.”

“Then submit the request now.”

For the first time, Menon’s voice was sharp.

Vosrov looked at him.

“What request?”

“A request to suspend work temporarily on Section 3 of the Green Corridor. Possible local reliance on native vegetation for subsistence. Simultaneous observation of evacuation movement and loss of farmland. Potential damage to the living territory of a sapient species.”

He held up his pad. His fingers were trembling slightly.

“You said it factors into operational decisions. Then put it in the main report. Not on the third line.”

The air in the observation room seemed to grow colder. Vosrov did not answer immediately. She looked at the screen, and Yujin saw her gaze briefly settle not on the corridor, but on the people.

“I’ll record the request.”

“Will you transmit it?”

“I’ll send it through the review channel.”

Menon did not smile.

“That means it will be delayed.”

“It means there is a procedure.”

“Procedure can make slow violence look lawful,” Menon spoke not like a scholar this time, but like a man who had not slept, a man who had held his anger in for too long.

Vosrov’s eyebrows shifted by the slightest degree. Irritation reached her face before fatigue did.

“Do you think I built that corridor, Doctor?”

“No.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

“Because you are watching.”

Vosrov looked at him for a long time.

“That is why I report it. Why I record it. Why I send it up the chain of command. If you demand more than that in this room right now, I will have to remove you from the observation room.”

Menon’s lips tightened. Yujin thought he would say more. But Menon remained silent. His anger had not vanished. It had simply lost any place to go aboard a military vessel.

No one spoke immediately after her answer. The responsibility of the person watching. The responsibility of the person giving orders. The responsibility of the person keeping the record. The three were not the same, but neither were they wholly separate.

Her answer took its place beside words they had heard too often. Without orders, we continue. With orders, we act. By the time the orders arrived, the work was already done.

Menon entered a brief note on his pad. Coastal evacuation. Family groups. Carts. Vessels. Possible loss of farmland. His writing hand stopped, and he looked at the screen again.

“They don’t understand us,” Yujin said.

“We don’t understand them either,” Menon said.

“But not understanding does not mean there is nothing there.” Vosrov moved to the next screen. South of the landing zone, the Green Corridor had grown a little more vivid. The engineers reported it as a success. Future agricultural land for Earth. Soil moisture stable. Irrigation pipes functioning normally.

At the bottom of the same screen, the orcs who had been loading red roots onto their carts stood beside the blackened wetlands. They did nothing. They simply stood there. The Earth forces’ display marked their stillness as no movement.

Yujin recorded the scene.

At the top of the screen, a caption read “Environmental Improvement Zone.” Beyond the observation room window, Mars turned slowly. With each orbit, the Earth forces saw more. And the more they saw, the clearer it became that they knew more and continued anyway.

chapters.title: 12. The Inland Sea from Orbit
chapters.markdown:
# 12. The Inland Sea from Orbit

![Chapter 12 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-12.webp)

The sails on the Inland Sea were all facing the same direction.

They were small boats. Some had a single sail; others had oars. A few rode low in the water, while others were so heavily laden they sat deep. The Earth forces’ observation display marked them as a vessel concentration. The term vessel concentration contained no children, no elderly, no carts. All that remained were the number of vessels, their direction, and their speed.

Vosrov drew a coastal blockade line. A white line appeared across the narrow neck of the red Inland Sea. On the display, the line was clean. A line without currents, wind, or people aboard the boats. Lines on maps were always that clean.

“Two landing craft can block the passage,” the operations officer spoke.

“Are those vessels armed?”

Hale’s voice came in from the surface. Static threaded the command-post transmission, caused by the Citadel Belt’s thick walls and the temporary repeaters.

“Structures believed to be catapults on some larger vessels. They may be carrying incendiary barrels.”

“They could be escort vessels,” Menon spoke. He was connected to the conference channel, but had been pushed into a small tile on the screen. The name of his data file appeared larger than his face.

“Escorting evacuation boats.”

“Evidence,” Hale said.

“Unarmed individuals, carts, juveniles, a coastal gathering, movement from inland citadels toward the coast. And the larger vessels are positioned outside the smaller boats. It resembles a protective screen more than an attack formation.”

“The enemy may be using civilians as shields,” someone said.

It was an old sentence on Earth. So old that no one asked where it had come from. A sentence used in colonies, on borders, in urban warfare, before columns of refugees. A sentence that had followed them all the way to an alien planet.

Menon drew a slow breath.

“I do not rule out that possibility. But based on the data we currently have, a mass evacuation is more—”

“We plan for the operational worst case,” Hale said.

That was the phrase that ended the discussion. The worst case always meant the worst case for our side. The worst case for theirs never entered the calculations.

From the back of the conference room, Yujin photographed the display. He had no right to speak. A war correspondent could ask questions, but he could not press the button that stopped an operation. The small boats on the screen kept moving. One had a torn sail; another was towing a lagging boat under oar. When one slow boat drifted sideways in the channel, two orcs aboard the boat beside it threw something like a rope. The Earth forces’ display marked it as an inter-vessel connection.

“Blockade order approved,” Vosrov said.

Her finger touched the screen. The white line grew thicker. The routes of two landing craft descended toward the Inland Sea. The orbital ship did not fire its guns directly. Not because it could not, but because this operation was being handled under surface and maritime control procedures. Violence looked less like violence when it came with procedures.

The landing craft were transported from the landing zone to the coast, then lowered into the water. They were small by the standards of Earth’s naval vessels, but among the Martian boats they looked like walls of iron. Composite armor, automatic stabilization, 30-millimeter remote turrets, missile pods, thermal sensors. Medieval oars and sails were no match for them.

Nowak was reviewing the coastal supply manifest. Landing-craft fuel, shells, missiles, recovery equipment, medical kits, spare communications buoys. Everything was a number. The numbers looked sufficient, but sufficiency always had limits.

“How much fuel do the landing craft have?” Yujin asked.

“Enough,” he answered, then added at once.

“For this operation.”

By now, Yujin knew the phrase well. There was always a condition after the word enough. For this operation. At this distance. In this weather. If no one was hurt. If the enemy moved as expected.

On the coastal feed, orcs were pushing boats into the water. Their feet sank into the mud at the water’s edge, and some fell. On one boat lay long objects covered in cloth. They might have been bodies. They might have been cargo. The Earth forces’ display marked them as freight.

Menon spoke quietly.

“The funeral procession and the evacuation are moving together.”

“Will you put that in the report?” Yujin asked.

“I will.”

“Will anyone read it?”

Menon looked at the screen.

“It will make it into the appendix.”

The landing craft’s engines started. The water of the Inland Sea churned. The small boats began to scatter. Some rowed faster; others stayed where they were. The boats that remained were either too heavy or waiting for someone.

The pilot feed from Landing Craft One was shared. The view sat low over the water. The Martian Inland Sea looked darker and thicker than Earth’s oceans. A thin film of red dust floated on the surface. Up close, the small boats looked smaller still. Wood grain, scraps of cloth, hand-mended sails, bowls used to bail water.

“Broadcast the warning.”

English went out first. Then Hindi, Chinese, and Arabic. The sound broke apart over the water. A few small boats changed course. Probably not because they understood the broadcast, but because of the landing craft’s size and noise. The other boats did not stop. If they stopped, the boats behind them would collide.

A Black Ship appeared to the south along the coast. It was larger than the other boats and rode low in the water. One mast was already broken, and its remaining sail was torn. Rows of oars moved along its sides. It did not head where the evacuation boats were going. Slowly, too slowly, it turned toward the landing craft.

“One large vessel changing course,” the operations officer spoke.

“High probability it is armed.” Menon said nothing. Yujin saw his hand pressing hard against the edge of his pad.

The Black Ship was still far away. But its course was clear. It was heading not for the route the evacuation boats were taking, but for the route of the approaching landing craft. While the Black Ship placed itself between the landing craft and the small boats, the small boats moved farther toward the coast. The operations display classified the action as interference with the landing.

Vosrov opened the rules of engagement. On the surface, Hale waited to authorize. The landing craft’s turret tracked the Black Ship.

Several small boats slipped through the space between them.

chapters.title: 13. With the Anthropologist
chapters.markdown:
# 13. With the Anthropologist

![Chapter 13 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-13.webp)


The shard of red stone was smaller than a fingernail.

Ravi Menon did not take it out of the specimen pouch. He examined it only through the transparent film. A fine strand of hair had been tied around the stone, twisted three times. Knots tied the same way had been found at several places across the battlefield: around the necks of dead orcs, inside shields, beneath broken spear shafts, and along the road leading back to the walls.

Yujin studied the tiny object for a long time. At first, he thought it was an ornament. Then he wondered if it might be a unit insignia. But after hearing that the knot appeared only near the dead, he adjusted the camera’s focus. On the screen, the stone was quieter than a weapon, yet it seemed likely to outlast one.

“Do you think it’s a funerary marker?” Yujin asked.

“We can’t call it that yet.”

Menon wrote a different phrase on his pad.

Recurring marker associated with the deceased.

“Why not?”

“If we call it funerary, someone will ask us to prove it. If we call it a recurring marker, they can’t erase it.”

He smiled wearily. In the space of a few days, his face seemed to have grown visibly thinner. It had always been lean, but now the hollows beneath his eyes were deeper, and dust clung to his jawline.

“In a report, you need words that survive more than you need certainty.”

The two of them emerged onto the edge of the Green Corridor south of the landing zone. Two sentries accompanied them, and a Black Hornet reconnaissance drone circled low overhead. Yujin had struggled to secure permission to walk with Menon. Officially, he was there to document the local social structure. In practice, he was there to make sure Menon did not wander off alone and get shot.

Daylight on Mars was different from daylight on Earth. Shadows were longer, colors thinner. Yet the Green Corridor was strangely vivid. Moss and cyanobacterial culture film brought from Earth spread across the red soil like a wet wound. The engineers called it an ecological starter. The manual listed local atmospheric stabilization and oxygen supplementation, soil binding, and dust suppression among its effects.

Seen up close, none of those claims were false. Water pooled beneath the thin film, with moss clinging to its surface. Every stake driven by the engineers bore a number, and irrigation lines had been buried underground at regular intervals. Where the soil processor had passed, the ground lost its red hue and turned dark with moisture. Earth’s machines were skilled at changing the land. The problem was that the land already belonged to someone.

Outside the corridor, several orcs were pulling up roots. They wore no armor. They did not flee when they saw the Earth forces. They only worked faster. One orc rubbed a blackened root between his hands. He looked at what came off on his palm, then showed it to a smaller figure beside him. The smaller figure did not put the root in the cart. It threw it away, shaking its hands for a long time afterward.

“This is farmland,” Menon said.

One of the sentries replied.

“It’s a native vegetation zone.”

Menon did not look at him.

“It could be farmland.”

“Our term is native vegetation.”

“Then are those people native specimens?”

The sentry did not answer. He was not a bad man. He was a man who followed the terminology sheet. Yujin thought men like that were more frightening. Those who disobeyed orders stood out, but those who obeyed the terminology sheet vanished into the system.

Menon photographed the cart and the tools. The handles were worn, and the blades bore marks from repeated sharpening. These were not sticks picked up by chance. Someone had used them for a long time. The bent piece of metal had been curved to a particular angle, and the handle bore callus marks running in the same direction. Farming tools testified to life more clearly than instruments of war. A weapon could be seized and used, but the worn place on a sickle could not be made by taking it from someone.

“Agriculture, funerary practices, evacuation, walls, military organization,” he said.

“Isn’t that enough?” Yujin asked.

Menon shook his head.

“The side with power decides what is enough.”

They walked on. At the end of the corridor was a narrow watercourse. It would originally have flowed into the wetlands. Now a low embankment built by the engineers had diverted it. The water ran beneath the green film, while the red aquatic plants outside the corridor had dried out. The edges of the wetland were cracked, and small insectlike creatures lay dead on their backs. Yujin hesitated over whether to film them. A camera could always record enough, but what you chose to record would later choose your side for you.

An orc stood across the watercourse. He held a long pole but made no move to attack. A strip of red cloth was tied to its end. He looked at Menon and Yujin, then pointed to the dry aquatic plants at his feet. Then he pointed to the Green Corridor.

The sentry raised his rifle. The sound of the M4A2’s muzzle rising was faint, but the air around them changed at once. The joint motors of his powered suit hummed low, and the other soldier’s finger halted near the safety.

“Lower it,” Menon said.

“You have no command authority,” the sentry replied.

“Then I’m asking you. Lower it.”

The muzzle did not come all the way down. It only dipped a little.

The orc pointed again to the dry plants. This time, he struck his own chest. They could not hear his words. Even if they had, they would not have understood them. But Yujin felt he knew what the orc was trying to say. To feel that you knew was dangerous. When a reporter wrote such a thing, it became bias. When a soldier said it, it became hesitation. When command said it, operations were delayed.

So everyone said they did not know.

Menon took out a drawing board. Water, plants, people, stop. He pointed to the drawing of water, then to the corridor, and spread both hands. The orc watched him for a long time. Then he slowly stepped back. Even as he retreated, he kept looking at the watercourse. He looked at it longer than he looked at the ground beneath his own feet.

“Was that a success?” Yujin asked.

Menon shook his head.

“No. We simply didn’t shoot each other.”

Behind his words, the soil processor started moving again inside the corridor. Its iron wheels rolled over the wet ground. The machine knew nothing of what had just happened. There was no reason it should. It treated the assigned area, sprayed the culture film, and adjusted the pH. Earth’s future was precise in this way.

On the way back, the drone once again detected movement toward the coast. Carts and boats, armed and unarmed bodies, all traveled together. The display tried to classify them, but the real world was more complicated than its categories. An orc with a bow across his back carried a child, while an unarmored orc dragged a long sword. A figure who walked like an old man leaned on a spear shaft. The line between armed and unarmed was thick on the screen, but blurred on the ground.

When they reached the landing zone, Menon submitted his report. Its title was Local Social Structure and the Possibility of Civilian Evacuation. The attachments documented the funerary markers, farming tools, altered watercourse, and movement toward the coast. He revised the final sentence three times. There is a strong possibility that the native species is intelligent. The native species has a complex social structure. The current terminology classifying the native species as a non-sentient hazard increases operational risk.

He sent the last sentence.

The operations network replied automatically.

Received. Pending review.

“Pending review” moved more slowly than a bullet.

That evening, the coastal interdiction operation proceeded as scheduled.

chapters.title: 14. London on Earth
chapters.markdown:
# 14. London on Earth

![Chapter 14 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-14.webp)

The television in the Sriharikota waiting room was muted.

Only the captions rolled past. First Mars Landing Battalion successfully defends landing zone. Settlement-related stocks rise. Special issue of wartime bonds. Second-round migration eligibility screening rescheduled. In a smaller line at the bottom of the screen came news of evacuation orders in coastal exclusion zones and the reclassification of radiation exclusion zones. News on Earth always packed several disasters into a single line. The war on Mars, atmospheric pollution on Earth, currency stabilization, and riot suppression all passed at the same speed.

Li Wei drank his coffee as he watched the captions. It was not made from real coffee beans. It was bitter water brewed from a substitute crop. The public information office still called it coffee. Keeping the name mattered. As long as the name remained, it seemed as though a little of the world remained with it.

On the screen before him were the unedited videos Seo Yujin had sent. A white flag, flares, grave markers, the Green Corridor, carts heading for the coast. Li Wei marked several of them. Cleared for release. Hold. Operational security. Context required.

Context required usually meant do not release.

In the corridor outside the public information office were people whose migration applications had been rejected. They had not come to protest. The complaints desk was in another building. This was the desk for submitting corrections. Errors in family composition, appeals of medical classifications, proof of skilled-work experience, applications for exemptions based on residence in radiation-contaminated zones. People held papers and terminals. Those rejected by the automated screening waited for a human being to review their cases.

But human beings also judged by looking at screens.

A migration eligibility chart hung on one wall of the waiting room. Strategic technical personnel, military contractors, orbital infrastructure maintenance personnel, equity investors, accompanying family members, public safety personnel, temporary labor assignees. Beneath them, in small print, was a category called humanitarian exception review, but the people seated in the waiting room wore the faces of those who did not believe it. Exceptions were broad only on paper. At the desk, they always narrowed.

Different words circulated inside the conference room. Delegates from developed nations, corporate legal teams, insurance consortiums, military procurement officers, the Migration Rights Allocation Committee. They called the fighting on Mars by other names.

“The landing zone’s defensive capability has been confirmed.”

“Initial losses are lower than market projections.”

“How far has stabilization of the ecological starter progressed?”

“There have been localized reactions, but in the long term, the soil improvement effects—”

“What about the indigenous life-form issue?”

“It is being managed as a risk factor.”

Risk factor.

Li Wei wrote the phrase down. In conference rooms on Earth, anything that got in the way became a risk factor, human or otherwise. He had worked with such language for years. Peacekeepers became security assurance forces, bombing became threat reduction, and refugees became a mobile population. People said words did not kill, but he did not think that was true. Often, the name was changed first, before the killing began.

The Korean delegation was also in the conference room. They did not represent the largest source of capital, but theirs was a seat that could not be omitted. Orbital communications components, powered-suit joint modules, military advisers, veterans of conflict zones, media cooperation. Since the Korean Civil War, Korea had grown accustomed to calling itself a victim. At the same time, it had also grown accustomed to selling weapons, sending soldiers, and receiving priority power allocations for its data centers. Korea was not in the conference room because it was a good country. It was there because it was strong enough and rich enough.

One committee member said,

“The footage from the Korean war correspondent will help win public support at home. As long as it isn’t too graphic.”

Li Wei looked up.

“If we remove the graphic parts, the context disappears.”

“The public information office can provide the context.”

That sounded reasonable too. Which was why it was dangerous. Public information was not made from lies alone. It organized facts, changed their order, and removed what was unnecessary. Most lies were tidier than the truth.

A child cried in the waiting room outside. The sound did not reach the conference room. There were thick glass walls and soundproof barriers. The Sriharikota launch site was close to the sea, close to the data centers, and close to the refugee queues. A few years ago, they said, there had been fishing boats, villages, and tourists around here. Now there were coolant pipelines, launchpads, security fences, and transit camps. Before setting out for Mars, Earth had changed its own shores.

A stockpile chart from the lunar supply base appeared on the screen. Propellant feedstock, ammunition pellets, drone wings, powered-suit joints, medical kits, culture membranes, catalysts for soil treatment. Supplies for Mars could not be sent when people wanted. They had to be pushed through when the orbit allowed. The people in the conference room adjusted the figures as they watched the chart. Change one number, and a soldier on Mars could keep firing for one more day while an applicant on Earth had to wait another month.

Li Wei reopened one of Seo Yujin’s videos. A small body was visible atop the wall. He could not tell whether it was a child. Zooming in made it clear. The released footage would not zoom in. Without the close-up, the war was easier to bear.

He drafted the public statement.

The First Mars Landing Battalion secured the landing zone during initial contact with indigenous risk factors, and work to establish the settlement base is proceeding as scheduled.

The sentence was smooth. So smooth that it asked nothing.

He stopped typing. The cursor blinked at the end of the sentence. Inside the conference room, the legal team was discussing the scope of liability. The insurance consortium was asking about the possibility of indigenous infection, while the military procurement officer was trying to shift responsibility for delayed consumables shipments onto the spacecraft operator. No one spoke of the hands pulling up roots beyond the corridor.

Li Wei attached another file beneath the statement. Seo Yujin’s original footage. Security review required.

He knew it would not be released.

He attached it anyway. So there would at least be a record that he had. If someone asked one day, he could say, “I submitted it.” He did not yet know whether those words would be an excuse or evidence.

Outside, the next screening number was called. Someone stood, clutching their documents. The captions at the bottom of the screen kept rolling.

Second allocation of Mars settlement rights, priority consultation for advanced contributing nations.

Another sentence passed beneath it.

Migration petitions from low-income regions, review suspended.

Li Wei finished his coffee. Black sediment remained at the bottom of the cup. He threw it away and returned to the conference room. The air inside was cold and clean. On Earth, clean air already came at a price.

chapters.title: 15. What Happened in the Citadel Belt
chapters.markdown:
# 15. What Happened in the Citadel Belt

![Chapter 15 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-15.webp)


The gate on the outer wall of the citadel creaked before the explosion came.

The autocannons of the CV90 armored vehicles struck the towers on either side of the gate, and combat engineer charges pushed against its iron reinforcement. For a moment, wood and metal groaned under the strain. The sound went on strangely long, as though the entire citadel were drawing one last breath. When the gate finally collapsed inward, dust rose like a red mist.

The gate was open, but Earth’s forces did not enter at once. The ruined gate was both an entrance and a bottleneck, and none of the blind spots inside had yet been cleared. They sent in sensors before bullets, machines before people.

The drones went in first. A dark passage, abandoned carts, broken jars, cloth hanging on the walls, long drag marks across the floor. The drones searched for heat sources, and the tactical AI marked possible ambush sites. Nothing moved.

“It’s empty,” the squad leader spoke.

Hale did not answer. A cross-sectional map of the citadel interior, drone footage, ammunition levels, and troop positions overlapped on his helmet visor. The display showed too much. It made him more suspicious.

“Check again,” a second drone went in. This time it flew lower. There were small rooms at the end of the passage, and inside them were water jars, folded cloth, and something like a small shoe. Yujin stopped breathing as he watched the feed. It might not have been an object that could be called a shoe. But it looked like one. It had the shape of something worn and taken off; one side was turned inside out, and a leather strip resembling a lace had come undone.

“Signs of civilian habitation,” Menon spoke.

The tactical network displayed different words.

Possible noncombat facility.

Hale gave the order to enter. The soldiers moved in slowly. Their weapons were not lowered. Flashlights and thermal cameras entered each room before they did. A robotic arm pressed down the handle before anyone kicked in a door, and a mirror drone went ahead before they rounded a corner. Even so, the soldiers’ shoulders were rigid. Death did not arrive at medieval speed merely because the citadel was medieval. In a narrow passage, even a single spear could kill a man.

There were things like paintings on the walls. A ship drawn in red pigment, a beast with long horns, figures holding hands. When one soldier stared at them too long, the squad leader spoke curtly.

“Eyes forward.”

The soldier turned his head. His rifle was heavy, and though the powered suit reduced the weight, it did not eliminate it. His fingers were slick with sweat inside his gloves. Inside his helmet, the sound of his own breathing mingled with the fans and the brief commands on the tactical net. War did not come one scene at a time, as it did in films. It came as noise that never switched off.

There was a flagpole in the citadel’s inner courtyard. The flag had been lowered. The cloth stirred slightly even though the wind could not reach it. Yujin raised his camera in front of it. A request had come from Earth for footage of victory. The fallen gate, soldiers advancing, the secured courtyard. Good images.

He lowered the camera a little. The shoe-like object on the ground entered the bottom of the frame.

Nowak already had the logistics map open. He looked like an unsentimental man, but not because he had no feelings. He knew too well that if he failed to look at the numbers, his soldiers would die.

“Securing the western Citadel Belt shortens the supply route by 4.2 kilometers. Three relay stations, one temporary refueling point, one medical staging post.”

“The Green Corridor?” Hale asked.

“We can run it along the waterway south of the citadel. It’s the most stable terrain.”

Menon looked up.

“That waterway leads to farmland.”

Nowak looked at him.

“That’s why it’s a route.”

They were not hostile to each other. Both were trying to save lives. Menon saw the people who had lived here; Nowak saw his own soldiers who would pass through here in the days ahead. The same waterway meant something different to each of them. That was how good intentions collided in war. And usually, the good intentions with the heavier equipment won.

The combat engineers began work that afternoon. Irrigation pipes were buried along the waterway south of the citadel. The water was channeled beneath a green membrane, and the red marsh began to dry out little by little. The engineering report called it a successful stabilization. Menon’s report called it an alteration of local agricultural waterways.

Both reports were uploaded to the same server. One became the main document. The other became an attachment.

Inside the citadel, the soldiers cleared the rooms. Some contained spearheads and bows; others contained dried roots and thin tablets. The same shapes were repeated across the tablets. No one knew whether they were writing, accounts, or prayers. When one soldier reached to pick one up with his bare hand, Ben Youssef shouted.

“No bare hands. Put it in a bag.”

She was a medical officer, but lately she moved like an infection-control manager. Alien microorganisms were still filed under unknown, and unknown was the costliest kind of risk. The soldiers complained but changed their gloves. Even discarding a single glove went on the supply ledger. On Mars, hygiene was calculated like ammunition.

In the fields outside the citadel, the orcs watched from a distance. They did not attack. Some retreated with carts in tow, while others gathered up the fallen flag. One orc bowed toward the citadel. No one could tell whether it was prayer, farewell, or anger.

Earth’s forces’ displays labeled the gesture as not a threatening action.

Yujin looked at the words and thought: just because it was not a threat did not mean it had no meaning.

Toward sunset, Hale established a temporary command post outside the citadel. Two armored vehicles stood before the gate, and a relay unit was installed on top of a tower. An antenna from Earth folded and unfolded atop a Martian wall. When the satellite link connected, Earth time and Mars time appeared together on the same display. The time of two worlds was synchronized within a single command network.

“We are not using the word occupation.”

Li Wei’s voice came over the Earth channel.

“Then what do we call it?” Yujin asked.

“Securing a safe settlement zone.”

In one of the rooms inside the citadel, a small scrap of cloth fell without any wind. Yujin filmed it. It was a room where someone had lived. A room someone had left in haste. A room someone might never return to.

The word safe seemed to strike the walls and echo back.

chapters.title: 16. Those Who Went to the Coast
chapters.markdown:
# 16. Those Who Went to the Coast

![Chapter 16 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-16.webp)

The cartwheels cut deep into the wet red earth.

This was not orbital footage. Yujin watched the procession from a low ridge on the outskirts of the Citadel Belt. They were too far away for him to see their faces, but he could see how they moved. Bodies pushing carts, bodies with loads strapped to their backs, bodies walking with smaller bodies in their arms, bodies that kept looking behind them. On a screen, they were a group on the move. Seen with his own eyes, they were refugees.

The tactical network marked the procession as a group moving southwest. Small triangles and dots moved across the map. Presumed armed. Presumed unarmed. Large cargo. Unidentified heat source. Yujin read the words, then looked again at the road below the ridge. One cart was stuck in the mud, and three orcs were pushing it with their shoulders. Beside them, two small figures were pulling off the cargo. The tactical network marked each of them separately, but in reality they moved like a single family.

Menon did not lower his binoculars.

“They’re refugees.”

“You already reported that,” Yujin spoke.

“I did. It wasn’t accepted.”

On the road below, one orc stopped. He retied the cloth over the cart. The wind lifted it, revealing long shapes underneath. They might have been corpses. They might have been wounded. Yujin could not be sure. Not being sure was a comfort. But the truth did not disappear simply because uncertainty was comforting.

“They take their dead with them,” Menon spoke.

“Does that matter?” the sentry asked without malice. He had spent the entire night at his post, his wrist-joint brace kept malfunctioning, and for two days he had eaten his ration packs cold. He was not a man who wanted to hear philosophy just then.

Menon lowered his binoculars.

“There is no civilization that does not matter,” the sentry looked as though he did not understand. Still, he asked no more questions.

Boats were gathering along the coast. Small sails dotted the dark waters of the Inland Sea. Some boats had already departed; others were waiting for their loads. Children were pressed into the inner parts of the boats. Adults readied the oars, moved water jars, and covered things with cloth. Some boats were so heavily laden that the slightest rocking brought water over the sides. Still, no one got out. Smoke was rising from the Citadel.

Two Earth landing craft entered the water farther north. When their engines started, the waters of the Inland Sea churned. The landing craft were low and broad, their turrets moving quietly. Dust clung to their armor plating, and their sensor windows gleamed like black glass. Among the medieval boats, they belonged to an age too far removed. An engine among sails and oars was as unfair as a machine gun among spears and shields.

The engines could be heard even at a distance. A low vibration tore through water and wind. Drums and shouts came from the orc boats, but the engines of the landing craft ran beneath every other sound. The noise was like invisible armor. As it drew near, anyone would flinch before it.

Hale confirmed the interdiction order.

“We cannot allow armed groups escaping the Citadel to cross the Inland Sea.”

Menon cut into the channel.

“They’re not all armed groups.”

“I know,” Hale spoke.

“That’s why we issue a warning before interdiction.”

“They don’t understand the warning.”

“Then only the interdiction remains.”

That was the end of it. Hale’s voice was not cruel. That made it all the more unyielding. He did not want to lose his soldiers. He did not want to let archers and catapults that might be concealed among the refugee boats slip through. He did not want the front stretching out beyond the Citadel. Operationally, every one of those reasons was sound. When enough sound reasons came together, they made the wrong thing possible.

Yujin filmed the landing craft and the refugee boats in turn. When he zoomed in, he could see the small bodies inside the boats. When he zoomed out, they became a concentration of vessels. It seemed the lens determined the ethics.

Below the ridge, the soldiers were servicing their rifles. They checked magazines, brushed away dust, and cleaned the lenses of their optics. War was not merely a matter of pressing the fire button. Rifles were brutally heavy, dust was relentless, and the red particles of Mars clung to every lubricated gap. After a rifle was fired, it had to be cleaned. If it was not, the next shot might never come. Weapons were stronger than people, but demanded just as much care.

The Black Ship appeared south of the coast. It was larger than the other boats and rode low in the water. One mast was already broken, and the remaining sail was torn. Rows of oars moved along its sides. It did not follow the refugee boats. Slowly, far too slowly, it turned toward the landing craft.

“Large vessel altering course,” the radio network spoke.

“Possibly armed.”

Something moved near the Black Ship’s bow. It looked like a catapult. Small barrels were lashed beside it. They might have contained incendiaries. They were not enough to destroy a landing craft. But they could burn its sensors or exposed components. No—the more important thing lay elsewhere. The moment the Black Ship turned, the smaller boats behind it began scattering in every direction.

Menon spoke quietly.

“It’s buying time.”

“For whom?” Yujin asked.

He did not answer. The answer was on the screen. The small refugee boats were scattering behind the Black Ship.

The landing craft’s turret moved. A warning was broadcast. English, Hindi, Chinese, Arabic. The sound broke apart over the water. The Black Ship did not stop. The words did not carry, but the intent did. A great mass of metal was bearing down on the small wooden boats. The Black Ship moved between them.

Yujin held the camera steady.

Yujin remembered an illustration he had seen long ago in a printed book. An old warship charged toward a monstrous machine through black smoke and pillars of water. But the Earth forces on the screen thought of nothing at all. To them, the Black Ship was an enemy vessel.

And an enemy vessel had to be stopped.

chapters.title: 17. The Black Ship
chapters.markdown:
# 17. The Black Ship

![Chapter 17 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-17.webp)


The Black Ship turned to face the force it could not defeat.

That was clear even on the Earth forces’ screens. The hull was old, one mast was broken, and the pace of its oars could not match the landing craft’s engines. One catapult and a few fire barrels, a wet sail and a wooden hull. Against it were two armored landing craft, automated turrets, thermal sensors, and missiles.

Still, the Black Ship turned.

The pilot of Landing Craft One issued a warning. Stop. Change course. Do not approach. The same words scattered across the water in four languages. A different sound came from the Black Ship. It was a low beat, impossible to tell whether it came from drums or feet. The oars struck the water as one. The rhythm was steady. It did not quicken in fear or falter in despair.

“Range eight hundred.”

“Continuing approach.”

“Armed structure confirmed.”

Yujin watched the feed from atop the ridge. The actual Inland Sea was far away, but the images streaming into his helmet were too close. He could see an orc standing at the bow of the Black Ship. He wore armor and held the broken mast with one hand. He raised something toward the Earth forces. Yujin could not tell whether it was a flag or a weapon.

The tactical AI marked him as a possible command unit.

Menon said nothing. When he fell silent, the people around him grew uneasy. They could argue with a scholar when he spoke, but when he was silent, there was no sentence to argue against.

The first catapult shot missed. A round barrel fell into the water ahead of the landing craft and shattered. Fire spread briefly across the surface. The flames burning on the Martian Inland Sea resembled an oil fire on Earth, but the color was slightly different. Red smoke rose first, and within it, yellow tongues flickered. The landing craft altered course slightly. That small movement carried several refugee boats behind it out of view.

“Landing Craft One, minor evasive maneuver.”

Vosrov’s voice came down from orbit. The scene would have been cleaner in the orbiter’s command room. The noise stripped away, ranges and trajectories and threat levels reduced to numbers, human shouts lowered to background sound.

“Cleared to engage?” Hale asked.

Several seconds passed. In those seconds, the Black Ship drew closer. The second fire barrel landed near the side of the landing craft. The flames did not penetrate the armor, but one external sensor went black. One side of the feed shook briefly, and the voices inside the landing craft rose.

“Sensor Three down. External temperature rising.”

“Damage minor.”

“Don’t call it minor. I can’t see ahead.”

The command net soon reduced those words to: Damage minor. Operational.

“Cleared to engage,” Vosrov said.

The 30-millimeter cannon spoke first. The air above the Inland Sea tore apart. On the screen, it looked as though a dotted line stretched toward the Black Ship, but the real sound was filthy and heavy. Each round broke wood, bodies, and water in a different way. The front of the Black Ship was ripped away. Wood, cloth, and bodies flew together. The ship did not stop. Several oars were gone, but those that remained kept moving.

At first, Yujin thought it was inertia. He thought the ship was moving forward because it had already been in motion. But even after a moment, the oars kept striking the water. They scattered like broken threads, then found their rhythm again. Someone was still giving orders, or even without orders, they knew what they had to do.

Landing Craft Two swung around to the flank and acquired a missile lock.

“Hellfire away.”

The missile moved too fast. To say it flew did not seem right. It vanished from one side of the screen, and the next instant white fire erupted in the middle of the Black Ship. The sound came later. A low, dull blast struck the Inland Sea, the ridge, and the citadel walls and rolled back. The mast snapped and fell into the water, and the hull seemed to split in two. Pieces of burning cloth rose into the sky, then fell back onto the water.

But the bow was still afloat. The shattered forward section drifted a little farther toward the landing craft. The orc commander at the bow was gone. Black smoke, red fire, and white steam filled the screen instead. Several fire barrels burst belatedly, and flames spread low across the water.

Landing Craft One turned farther to avoid the drifting wreckage. The pilot swallowed a curse, but the internal microphone caught a short breath. In the meantime, the refugee boats slipped through the narrow mouth of the Inland Sea. Some lowered their sails; others moved under oars alone. Small dots disappearing at the edge of the screen. One by one, failed-tracking markers multiplied on the command net.

“We’re losing the refugee boats,” the operations officer said.

“Enemy vessels.”

Someone else corrected.
