“They require the same temperature,” the person in charge at the Earth laboratory spoke. On the screen, he wore a spotless lab coat. This was Earth. An Earth that had received only the data. The samples were in orbit, but the calculations, synthesis, and production planning were being done on Earth.

“They do not mean the same thing,” Dr. Claire Dubois spoke.

The man paused.

“Logistically, they are the same.”

That sentence explained everything. Logistically, they were the same. Vaccine and moss, antiserum and irrigation pipe, quarantine membrane and incendiary bomb. The same warehouse, the same launch site, the same specification sheet. A logistics manifest did not distinguish good from evil. It saw only temperature, mass, volume, hazard class, and launch priority.

The first diagnostic test for the Red Swelling was developed in orbit. The protein reactions from sealed samples, traces of antibodies in patients’ blood, and the onset timeline were matched. The candidate antiserum was administered to several survivors. Its efficacy was not complete, but it was sufficient. The word sufficient returned with conditions attached. Increased survival with early administration. Limited efficacy after the pulmonary stage. Possibility of reinfection unknown.

The vaccine candidate was designed on Earth. Genetic information and protein data were transmitted, and automated production facilities produced multiple formulations. Confirming safety took time. Establishing the duration of immunity took longer. Politicians wanted quick results. Medical researchers wanted more time. A timetable was drawn up between them.

Seventeen months.

For the victims’ families, that number was long. For the team preparing the follow-up expedition, it was short.

During those seventeen months, the news on Earth moved on to other disasters. A seawall collapsed in a coastal city. Suspicions of tactical nuclear weapons use resurfaced along a border. Disputes over power allocations to data centers destabilized the electrical grids of several countries. The memorial ceremony for the dead of the Mars expedition proceeded at the scheduled time. The official documentary spoke of courage and sacrifice. The white flag did not appear, and the Black Ship appeared for six seconds as a “large enemy vessel.”

Major Tomasz Nowak’s proposed improvements grew over the same period. Redundant relay systems, safeguards against tampering with landing markers, increased cargo-drone payloads, additional small orbital descent vehicles, double the forward food allocation, dispersed helicopter fuel caches, improved dust protection for quadruped robot joints, enhanced local mapping in tactical helmets.

And an expanded Green Corridor.

The engineering report stated the causes of failure clearly. The corridor was too narrow, forcing supply vehicles to take detours. The irrigation pipes lacked protection and were vulnerable to flame-canister attacks. Control of local waterways had been insufficient. The solutions were equally clear. A wider corridor, deeper irrigation pipes, stronger defenses, faster soil treatment.

Dr. Ravi Menon attached a dissenting opinion to the report.

Expanded destruction of local farmland and waterways. Increased displacement pressure. Potential escalation of hostilities.

His opinion went back into the appendix. This time, the automated classification was faster. Supplementary ecological and anthropological opinion. Not operationally essential.

Colonel Elena Vosrov viewed two progress charts side by side aboard the orbiter. Red Swelling vaccine development: 62 percent. Green Corridor second-phase equipment readiness: 64 percent. The effort to stop the disease and the effort to expand the invasion were advancing at the same pace. She had to treat the two figures as separate tasks. One belonged to medical operations, the other to engineering. One was survival, the other settlement. But on the screen, they stood side by side.

Seo Yujin could not photograph the screen. He lacked the necessary clearance. Instead, he interviewed Sergeant Nakamura Kenji. He was recovering, and the tremor in his hands had diminished but had not entirely disappeared. He sat beneath the bright lights of the maintenance training room. Behind him lay the dismantled joint of a quadruped robot.

“I heard you’re contributing to the training materials for the follow-up expedition.”

“Only the maintenance sections.”

“Why are you doing it?”

Sergeant Nakamura Kenji thought for a long time.

“Because if I don’t, they’ll die the same way we did.”

“And if you do?”

“They’ll die some other way.”

He did not smile.

“But they need to know the maintenance procedures. How the red soil gets into the robot joints, how the drone markers get pulled out, how often the barrels need replacing.”

“What if that helps the next invasion?”

Sergeant Nakamura Kenji looked at his hands.

“It does.”

He did not deny it.

“But if I don’t tell them, soldiers die. If I do tell them, more people go over there. Both are true.”

Whenever the cargo rail moved beyond the wall, the liquid inside the incubator trembled.

In the adjoining hangar, the green moss culture vats trembled to the same rhythm.

chapters.title: 30. The Next Window
chapters.markdown:
# 30. The Next Window

![Chapter 30 Illustration](resources/assets/chapter-30.webp)

The hangar doors at Sriharikota opened at four in the morning.

The sea was out of sight. The launch complex lay shrouded in fog and waste heat. Hot air from the data center’s cooling towers hung low, and the lights of the coastal exclusion zone glimmered faintly in the distance. A line had formed again in front of Migration Terminal 7. Water bottles, documents, access passes, arms holding children, packets of medicine wrapped in plastic. The people were quieter than before. The official documentary of the first expedition had been released. It was not the original footage.

A different picture filled the screens in the waiting area. Larger cargo ships, more landers, thicker quarantine barriers, broader Green Corridor modules, refrigerated vaccine containers. The caption was brief.

Second Mars Settlement Security Mission. Enhanced quarantine protocols in effect.

There was no mention of war.

Li Wei was holding another press statement. He was thinner than before. Yujin was in the same room with him, but this time he carried no camera. His war correspondent credentials had not been renewed. The notice cited both medical and security reasons. Neither was entirely false.

“Mr. Seo,” Li Wei spoke.

“We aren’t taking official questions today.”

“I didn’t ask one.”

“You looked as if you might.”

Yujin watched the screen. A vaccine container was moving past. Behind it stood rows of starter-culture tanks for the ecosystem. Green moss swayed behind transparent walls.

“Those two are going together.”

Li Wei did not look at the screen.

“We need both.”

“Who does?”

He did not answer.

At the same hour, the hangar at the lunar base opened. Cargo stood in rows across the gray floor. Propellant feedstock, spare engines, robot joints, relays, drone beacons, food, aviation fuel modules, quarantine barriers, vaccines, Green Corridor equipment. For twenty-six months, the Moon had waited, Earth had built, and the orbiter had endured. The Moon was not a rest stop. It was a warehouse. A quiet warehouse where supplies were stockpiled so humanity would not forget the next invasion.

Nowak signed the supply manifest for the follow-up contingent. He had survived. That fact did not lighten him. Most of his proposed improvements had been adopted. Food allocations had increased, the drones were larger, and the number of relays had doubled. The risk of forward units becoming isolated had fallen.

It had not disappeared entirely.

Vosrov checked the follow-up contingent’s route from the orbiter. Orbiter One had still not been able to return to Earth. Some sections were permanently sealed, while others had been bypassed with new equipment. She was looking at the same planet again. The Red Inland Sea, the Citadel Belt, the Green Corridor, the strait where the Black Ship had sunk, the gorge where the forward company had vanished.

Mars looked quiet.

No one called that quiet peace anymore.

Menon’s determination that the orcs were an intelligent species was under academic review. It had not been made public. Dubois’s quarantine warning had been placed on the first page of the training manual. That had been made public. People were quicker to accept that eating them would kill you than that you should not eat people.

Kenji’s maintenance videos became training material for the follow-up contingent. On camera, he disassembled robot joints and showed where the red dust lodged. His voice was dry.

“If it gets in here, it stops. Once it stops, it becomes cargo. Once it becomes cargo, someone has to drag it. When someone has to drag it, they fall behind.”

The video was followed by excerpts from Han Doyun’s final report. The section ordering restricted cooking had been removed. Only the supply coordinates and relay losses remained. Responsibility did not become training material. Only technique did.

Yujin switched off the edited version halfway through.

He reopened his private manuscript. The title was unchanged.

The Invasion of Mars.

More sentences had accumulated beneath it. The white flag, the Black Ship, the red swellings, the sealed originals, Korea’s stake, the capital of advanced nations, the lines of those shut out. He kept writing. He could not make it public, but he had not stopped.

An announcement sounded across the launch site.

“Cargo transport for the Second Mars Settlement Security Mission will now begin final securing procedures.”

The people watched the screen. Some applauded; others wept. Those outside the line could not enter. People wearing white access passes moved toward another door. There was more than guilt on their faces. There was hope as well. Hope always made people more complicated.

Inside the hangar, the refrigerated vaccine containers went in first. Then came food, ammunition, relays, drones, robot joints, quarantine barriers, and tanks of green moss culture. The order had changed, but the same things were being loaded again.

Li Wei read from the press statement.

“Humanity has learned from its first experience. We will move forward more safely, more cautiously, and more responsibly.”

Yujin listened. More safely. More cautiously. More responsibly. All good words. Good words always opened the next door.

On the screen, the cargo ship’s doors closed. The locks turned green one by one. Steam rose beneath the launchpad. The sea remained out of sight, and the sky was overcast. Its long wait over, the blue Earth launched another rocket toward the red planet. The next window was already open.

chapters.title: 01. Author’s Note
chapters.markdown:
# 01. Author’s Note

The idea of humans invading Mars is the device that sets the story in motion, while reversing the events of *The War of the Worlds* provides its structure. What I wanted to portray throughout this novel was the horror and indifference of war, which cannot be reduced to a struggle between good and evil, and the process by which increasingly complex systems—and the survival needs and desires of groups—erode our humanity.

## The Horror and Indifference of War

The invasion in this story does not begin with the malice of any one person. The collective imperative to save more people on a devastated Earth, the desire to secure limited migration rights, capital’s hunger for new markets and resources, the military’s need to complete its mission, and scientific organizations’ pursuit of research findings all interlock. Survival and desire are not the same, but within a complex system they are gathered under the same phrase: “the future of humanity.”

This premise is also present in the source novel. The Martians in *The War of the Worlds* do not invade Earth simply because they are evil. Their world is cooling and the conditions for survival are deteriorating, while Earth abounds in water, vegetation, and life. For the Martians, invading Earth is a choice made so their declining species can survive. This work reverses that premise. Now it is humanity, struggling to survive on an Earth it has ruined, that looks toward a Mars with a red ecosystem and a civilization of its own. To the source novel’s motive of collective survival, I added modern systems of state power, capital, the military, science, and migration, expanding on how survival as a justification merges with desire and diffuses responsibility.

The more complex a system becomes, the more finely responsibility is divided. One person calculates only transport capacity, another assigns only quarantine classifications, another translates warning broadcasts, and another attacks the targets they have been ordered to strike. On each person’s screen, they see not the invasion as a whole, but only the ordinary task they are expected to complete. Everyone feels as though no one person chose the entire war, yet the war continues because each person diligently does their part. Humanity is not eroded only by exceptionally cruel people. It is worn away through routine procedures that turn people into entries such as targets, risk factors, transport mass, and quarantine subjects.

I did not want to make Earth’s forces simple villains. Among them are scientists who recognize that the orcs are a sapient species, journalists who document the evacuation of civilians, and soldiers who oppose their orders. Commanders try to keep their troops alive, medical officers try to save their patients, and logistics officers try to keep food and ammunition flowing. Yet the rational decisions each of them makes within their own sphere operate inside the larger machinery of invasion. Good intentions and diligent work do not necessarily stop a war. They may instead allow it to continue longer.

Nor did I want to make the inhabitants of Mars flawless symbols of goodness. They too have armies, citadels, power, and violence. But that does not change the fact that, in this war, they are the ones being invaded and driven from their homes. The fact that no society is perfect can never justify invading it.

War is indifferent to individual circumstances. Bullets do not distinguish between good people and bad, and disease does not ask whether someone supported or opposed an order. Equipment breaks down even after moments of heroism, the wounded become numbers on supply manifests, and corpses are recategorized as quarantine subjects or potential food. Even Earth’s forces, despite their overwhelming firepower, feel fear when confronted with endless enemy numbers and severed supply lines. That fear and anger keep them from seeing the other side as people, and the decisions made in that state produce still more fear.

I believe guns and armies should exist not to be used, but to protect. People are issued weapons and given military training not so they can use violence lightly, but so they possess the strength to protect without using it—and can take responsibility at the final moment if they must. Yet the Earth forces in this story destroy the people and homes of another world in the name of “protecting humanity.” The moment they narrow what must be protected to humanity alone, their instruments of protection become instruments of invasion. Because of this contradiction, I did not portray Earth’s weapons as glamorous spectacles to be enjoyed lightly.

I wrote the story so that readers would follow those decisions one by one through the eyes of Earth’s forces. Viewed only in the immediate circumstances, each choice is rational and sometimes appears necessary to save lives. But when those choices have accumulated, readers find themselves confronting the discomforting realization that they have been following the logic not of the victims, but of the invaders and perpetrators.

If perpetrators are portrayed from the outset as incomprehensible villains, readers can easily separate themselves from them. At that distance, violence can be consumed lightly as someone else’s cruelty. But if readers instead follow choices they can understand and judgments they themselves might have made, the discomfort they feel at the end allows that violence to reach them and acquire weight. This is also why the story is written entirely from the human perspective.

Even after the advance force succumbs to disease, the war does not end in reflection. Human deaths are reduced to failure reports and improvement plans, becoming data that will make the next invasion safer. I wanted to end the story at precisely that indifferent transition.

## Why This Novel Is Titled *The Invasion of Mars*

As a child, I read H. G. Wells’s original novel, *The War of the Worlds*. Around the same time, I also read a magazine article about Orson Welles’s radio drama. It told how the Martian invasion had been broadcast like breaking news and how people had mistaken it for a real event. The article was accompanied by illustrations of the invasion. I think my memories of the source novel and of the incident and illustrations I encountered in that magazine overlapped for years until they became one.

That is why I remembered Wells’s work under the title *The Invasion of Mars*. Later, when I saw Tim Burton’s film *Mars Attacks!*, I expected a film adaptation of the Wells novel I had read and was puzzled to find something entirely different. That does not mean I disliked the film. Quite apart from Wells’s original, I enjoyed Tim Burton’s distinctive humor and extravagant world. When I later watched Spielberg’s *War of the Worlds*, the story felt familiar, but the title struck me as strange. It was less a matter of misremembering a single translated title than of my reading of the original novel, the article about the radio drama, the magazine illustrations, and the Korean titles of the two films merging in my memory.

## Did the Original Story Really End There?

As a child, I felt relief at the ending in which Earth’s pathogens brought down the Martians. But as an adult, after completing my military service, I revisited the original story and found myself asking a different question. Would the Martians truly have given up after the annihilation of their first invasion force?

The Martians in the source novel have a clear motive for invading Earth. Their planet is cooling, and the environments in which they can survive are diminishing. Earth, by contrast, abounds in water, vegetation, and life. It seemed unlikely that a civilization with both the technology to send an expedition to another planet and a desperate motive for survival would abandon Earth after a single failure. If the first invasion force had fallen to Earth’s microorganisms, the next might investigate the cause, prepare quarantine and disease-control measures, and return. The pathogens might not be an absolute deliverance that ended the invasion, but merely the first cause of failure the invaders would have to overcome next time.

This work began by placing that question on the other side. Humanity, having ruined Earth by its own hand, also needs a new place to survive. Humans possess not only the technology to invade Mars, but also the motive to justify their choices in the language of survival. Even if the advance force is destroyed by a local disease, the needs and desires of Earth as a whole do not disappear. The orbiter and Earth analyze the infection data, improve quarantine, vaccines, and supply systems, and then set out again.

So when I thought carefully about the ending of *The War of the Worlds*, I found that the story did not end in complete happiness. Nor does this novel end with the death of the advance force. Only by continuing to the moment when the follow-up force, having learned from the failure, sets out could I answer the question I had carried with me for so long.

This work began anew from the title and images preserved in an old memory. In the original, Mars invades Earth; here, humans invade Mars. *The Invasion of Mars* can be read as either “an invasion originating from Mars” or “an invasion directed at Mars.” The cover and interior illustrations were also designed to revive the impression of the classic invasion art I saw in magazines as a child, while placing Earth’s forces in the role of the invaders.

That is why I wrote this novel. In the production notes that follow, I will explain how I planned, expanded, and reviewed this work with AI, along with the actual process and the problems I discovered along the way.

chapters.title: 02. Writing Fiction with AI
chapters.markdown:
# 02. Writing Fiction with AI

This document is not an appendix that retells the setting of *The Invasion of Mars*. It is a working index designed to show the sequence in which I created the novel with AI, what failed at each stage, and how I corrected it. The specific settings and review results can be found through the “Deliverables” links for each stage.

## 1. Where the Work Began

This novel began with the idea of reversing *The War of the Worlds*, in which Martians invade Earth, so that humans invade a Mars inhabited by a medieval fantasy civilization. I did not hand the entire novel over to AI from the outset. I continually supplied the work’s purpose, the scenes that had stayed with me, sensory details drawn from military experience, the technologies I would allow, and the clichés that naturally accompany the genre but that I wanted to avoid in this particular work. For example, when orcs and a medieval fantasy civilization appear, elements such as magic, sorcery, and monsters may naturally follow. In this work, however, fantasy lies in the appearance of the Martian ecosystem and civilization, while the rules of war remain grounded in realistic military practice and biology to the end. I also wanted to avoid using Earth’s near-future setting as an excuse to introduce superscience weapons such as lasers and giant robots, placing Korean characters in the role of virtuous observers to absolve Korea, or having a superintelligent AI solve every problem. I did not reject clichés unconditionally. Rather, I sought to prevent such elements from pulling the work away from its central themes of colonial invasion and war. The AI organized these conditions into structures and documents and reflected them in the manuscript. When I found a problem on rereading, I did not stop at revising a single sentence; I also revised the setting and the review criteria.

## 2. Actual Workflow and Deliverables

| Stage | What I Decided or Provided | Work Performed with AI | Problems Found and Corrections Made | Deliverables |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Fixing the Creative Intent | I established the invader’s perspective, a Mars of medieval fantasy, the horror and indifference of war rather than a struggle between good and evil, and an ending in which happiness was impossible. | We structured the idea into a one-sentence premise and an overall direction for the ending. | Writing the story immediately would have destabilized the setting and its homage to the source, so we decided to build the structure first. | [Canonical 30-Chapter Structure](thirty-chapter-structure.md) · [Source-Novel Mapping](war-of-the-worlds-correspondence.md) |
| 2. Breaking Down Events from the Source Novel | I selected the white flag, overwhelming weapons, evacuation, Thunder Child, and the pathogen ending as the key scenes. | We divided the source novel’s chapters by scene function: first contact, firepower, evacuation, sacrifice, isolation, and disease. | Rather than copying sentences or names, we transformed them into self-contained events that readers unfamiliar with the source novel could understand. | [Source-Novel Mapping](war-of-the-worlds-correspondence.md) · [Scene Design](scene-design.md) |
| 3. Limiting the World and Technology | I set Earth’s technology roughly thirty years ahead of the present and restricted ground weapons to next-generation versions of existing equipment. | We integrated a lunar stockpile base, low-Earth-orbit refueling, a Mars orbiter, landing battalion, armor, helicopters, drones, and robots into a single operational system. | To prevent every piece of equipment from becoming a superscience weapon simply because spacecraft existed, we imposed constraints involving supply, maintenance, and fuel. | [World and Force Settings](world-and-force.md) · [Military and Logistics Review](military-logistics-adversarial-review.md) |
| 4. Designing a Multinational Cast | I established the relative shares of capital and space infrastructure contributed by developed nations, the countries excluded from the venture, and a structure that did not absolve Korea. | We created a character table specifying nationality, role, political position, and memorable identifiers for readers. | The early draft contained too many characters of Korean descent, so we retained only Seo Yujin and Han Doyun and rebuilt the multinational cast. | [Character Table](characters.md) |
| 5. Designing the Causal Chain of Infection and Survival | I decided that isolated soldiers would eat orc meat and contract red swelling, and that the orbiter would also be affected. | We connected, in chronological order, the observation of animals eating it first, the order to cook it under limited conditions, incubation, orbital transmission, quarantine, and vaccine development. | If everyone who ate the meat died, the decision would amount to a meaningless mistake, so some characters survived because of that order. | [Continuity and Plausibility Table](continuity-matrix.md) · [Setting Review](setting-adversarial-review.md) |
| 6. The Flawed 18-Chapter Draft | I tried to contain both the source novel’s events and the additional ending within a single narrative flow. | At first, we structured the entire work in eighteen chapters. | Too many events were packed into each chapter, making the novel read like a plot summary. Instead of simply increasing the word count, we redesigned the scenes from the ground up. | [Canonical 30-Chapter Structure](thirty-chapter-structure.md) |
| 7. Redesigning the Work into 30 Chapters | I separated the framework of the source novel’s twenty-seven chapters from the later-wave ending that followed. | We first defined each chapter’s central scene, viewpoint character, military conditions, emotional shift, and next question, then restructured the work into thirty chapters. | The chapters became more self-contained, but characters and locations still appeared without explanation, so we strengthened the rules governing transitions and connections. | [Scene Design](scene-design.md) · [Continuity and Plausibility Table](continuity-matrix.md) |
| 8. Expanding the Chapter Drafts | I asked for the weight of weapons and equipment, maintenance and waiting, the noise and rotor wash of helicopters, and the fear produced by the enemy’s sheer numbers. | We expanded each chapter’s central scene through noise, dust, injuries, supplies, action, and dialogue. | The AI repeated across several chapters feedback that had been emphasized once, such as cleaning weapons. We distributed the same meaning across different actions and objects. | [Novel, Chapter 1](chapter-01.md) · [Novel, Chapter 30](chapter-30.md) · [Style Guide](style-guide.md) |
| 9. Creating Illustrations and Maps | I requested a documentary illustration style reminiscent of the source novel’s artwork, one illustration per chapter, a cover, and maps. | We converted the scenes from each chapter into image prompts and produced thirty illustrations and an operational map. | Some images looked atmospheric but conflicted with the manuscript in the scale of tanks and people, the size of ships, the number of flags, the period of the vehicles, and the directions of attack and evacuation. In the end, I had to compare all thirty images with the manuscript individually and regenerate them. | [Art Direction](art-direction.md) · [Design for 30 Chapter Illustrations](art-prompts-30.md) · [Mars Operations Map](mars-theater-map.md) |
| 10. Adversarial Reviews by Discipline | I called for aggressive scrutiny not only of the setting but also of military realism and literary quality. | We separated the reviews into setting, military and logistics, and style and literary quality. | We discovered the AI’s tendency to explain the creative intent directly in the manuscript using words such as “the reader,” “the source novel,” and “this story,” so we added this to the prohibited list. | [Review Criteria](adversarial-review-criteria.md) · [Setting Review](setting-adversarial-review.md) · [Military Review](military-logistics-adversarial-review.md) · [Style Review](style-literary-adversarial-review.md) |
| 11. Reading the Entire Work and Revising It Sentence by Sentence | I read from Chapter 1 onward at a reader’s pace, identifying problems with language, movement, dialogue, equipment, characters, and the causal chain of infection. | The AI searched other chapters for errors of the same kind, and I reread the revisions. In the process, we corrected the manuscript, setting, and review criteria together. | We found characters who appeared only briefly and left behind nothing but a name, abrupt transitions among the surface, orbit, and Earth, and the mechanical transplantation of a reference style. | [Character Table and Memorable Identifiers](characters.md) · [Style Guide](style-guide.md) · [Continuity Table](continuity-matrix.md) |
| 12. Recording the Production Method | I decided that Part Two of the book would contain not only the completed manuscript but also the method of creating it with AI and the failures along the way. | We recorded the workflow in this document and created an index linking to each deliverable. | Simply listing the resulting materials would not show when or why they were created, so we also recorded the actual workflow and the reasons for each revision. | This document and all linked documents above |

## 3. The Method Confirmed Through This Work

When creating a long novel with AI, it proved more reliable to fix the structure from the top down and then build out the scenes than to ask for the entire work to be written in one pass.

1. First, I define the work’s purpose and its boundaries.
2. I break down the source novel or idea by scene function rather than by sentence.
3. I establish the world, characters, timeline, and central scene of each chapter.
4. I expand each chapter into a self-contained fictional scene.
5. I divide adversarial reviews according to criteria suited to the work, such as setting, military realism, and style.
6. I read at the pace of an actual reader and identify what the AI has repeated excessively or omitted.
7. When correcting an error in one sentence, I also check whether the same error appears in the setting or other chapters.
8. Finally, I connect the resulting documents to the stages of the workflow so they can be reused in future creative projects.

The AI did not produce the right answer from the beginning. I narrowed the criteria for judgment, the AI propagated those criteria across multiple chapters and documents, and I reread the results to identify failures. The work’s quality came less from the first generation than from this iterative process.

## 4. Recurring Problems with AI Found During the Work

* It tends to repeat across multiple chapters an expression the user emphasized once. Cleaning weapons and maintaining equipment were representative examples.
* It tends to place the author’s explanation of the creative intent directly into the manuscript instead of conveying it through scenes. Words such as “the reader,” “the source novel,” and “this story” entered the prose.
* When adopting the style of another work, it first generalizes conspicuous surface rules rather than the conditions that made the style effective in that work. As a stylistic reference, I provided the AI with the manuscript of *The Legend of Dragonia*, an unfinished original novel I had worked on in the past. The AI generalized that manuscript’s practice of opening with physical objects in the immediate setting into a mandatory form for every chapter. As a result, scenes in *The Invasion of Mars* began before establishing enough about their time and place, disrupting the flow.
* It tries to solve functional problems by adding characters, which increases the number of named individuals and makes them difficult for readers to remember when they reappear after long absences.
* Image-generation AI can convincingly reproduce a scene’s atmosphere and visual style while getting relationships essential to the narrative wrong. An Apache faced friendly forces, refugees walked toward the invasion force’s landing craft, a carrier-sized ship impossible to transport through space appeared in the Inland Sea, and a tank was depicted like a toy car only slightly larger than a person. Conditions explicitly stated in the manuscript—the number and positions of white flags, the number of people in the Green Corridor, and the period of the vehicles—were not automatically preserved either.

### Every Image Also Required Human Review, Chapter by Chapter

Writing a detailed text prompt did not mean the illustration work was finished. A “striking picture of war” and “the exact scene from the manuscript” are different deliverables. Because image-generation AI prioritizes the visual impression, it can invert relationships that matter most to the story, such as who is attacking whom and the direction in which people are fleeing.

I therefore inspected every illustration myself and compared the following details with the manuscript.

1. I checked whether the characters and equipment actually appeared in the manuscript.
2. I checked whether the directions of attack, pursuit, and evacuation were correct.
3. I checked whether the numbers of people, flags, vehicles, and ships matched the manuscript.
4. I checked whether the relative sizes of people, tanks, helicopters, and ships were realistic.
5. I checked whether objects from medieval Mars and equipment from near-future Earth were appropriately distinguished by period.
6. I checked whether the image prematurely revealed an event that had not yet occurred or a scene from the following chapter.
7. I checked whether the image maintained the human perspective without reducing the inhabitants of Mars to mere monsters.

Because images are understood more quickly than text, a single error in direction or scale causes the reader to accept the wrong situation immediately. In the end, the thirty images could not be completed through batch generation. They had to be reviewed and remade one by one, like revising a manuscript.

These problems did not reliably disappear in response to a simple request to “write well.” I reduced them by adding actual failures to the review criteria and repeatedly comparing the manuscript, setting, and images.

chapters.title: 03. Correspondence with *The War of the Worlds*
chapters.markdown:
# 03. Correspondence with *The War of the Worlds*

This document explains what happens in H. G. Wells’s *The War of the Worlds* and how *The Invasion of Mars* reverses those events by viewing them from a different perspective. Each scene is described so that the parallels remain clear even if you do not remember the chapter titles of the original novel.

## Principles of Correspondence

The novel does not reproduce the original’s prose or its distinctive machines. Readers unfamiliar with the source can read it as a self-contained story of invasion, while those who know the original can recognize how the functions of scenes involving the white flag, the evacuation, the Black Ship, and disease have been reversed.

The reason the book is titled *The Invasion of Mars*, and the question that grew out of the original novel’s ending, are recorded separately in the [Author’s Note](authors-note.md).

## Scene Correspondence Table

| Structure of the original | What happens in the original | Parallel in this novel | Reversed meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Book One, Chapter 1: The Eve of the War | The people of Earth go about their peaceful lives, unaware that the Martians are watching them and preparing an invasion. | In Chapter 1, “The Eve of the War,” Earth openly prepares an expedition to Mars and selects those who will depart. | The daily life of unsuspecting victims becomes the departure of invaders who have devised their own justification and procedures. |
| Book One, Chapters 2–3: The Falling Star; Horsell Common | A Martian cylinder falls in England, and residents and scientists gather to see it, believing it to be a meteorite. | In Chapters 2–3, Earth’s transport ships approach Mars, and the military secures the landing zone. | The people of Earth who once looked upon an object from the sky become the beings descending through the Martian sky. |
| Book One, Chapter 4: The Cylinder Opens | The cylinder opens and the strange body of a Martian emerges, turning human curiosity into terror. | In Chapter 4, the lander opens and unloads tanks, armored vehicles, robots, and troops. | Instead of a monster’s body, familiar military hardware from Earth becomes the terror of alien machinery to the inhabitants of Mars. |
| Book One, Chapters 5–6: The Heat-Ray | The Martians kill a human delegation carrying a white flag with their heat-ray. | In Chapters 5–6, Earth forces open fire on orc envoys carrying a white flag and crush the counterattack with modern firepower. | The human delegation and the Martian heat-ray are replaced by orc envoys and Earth’s military firepower. |
| Book One, Chapters 7–10: The Battle Spreads | The narrator tries to flee with his family, while the army is driven back by Martian fighting machines. The front lines and the evacuation become entangled amid storms and darkness. | In Chapters 7–10, Earth forces advance into the Red Forest but encounter problems with terrain, storms, maintenance, and supplies. | The victims’ flight becomes the invaders’ advance, yet even overwhelming firepower cannot dispel every fear. |
| Book One, Chapters 11–13: Observation and Companionship | From windows and roads, the narrator catches only limited glimpses of the destruction of towns and travels with a curate. | In Chapters 11–13, Seo Yujin and Menon witness cities, farmland, funerals, and evacuation through orbital footage and field investigations. | The survivor’s limited perspective becomes the record of a war correspondent and an investigative team, but greater access to information does not guarantee empathy. |
| Book One, Chapters 14–16: London and the Evacuation | Londoners learn the scale of the invasion too late and flee, while roads and rivers collapse under the flood of refugees. | In Chapters 14–16, Earth consumes news of the war as stories about investment and migration rights, while the inhabitants of Mars evacuate toward the Inland Sea. | The inhabitants of Mars take the place of London’s refugees, while the people of Earth regard them as populations moving within an operational theater. |
| Book One, Chapter 17: The Thunder Child | The British warship Thunder Child charges the Martian fighting machines pursuing refugee vessels, buying time for them to escape. | In Chapter 17, “The Black Ship,” an aging orc warship holds off Earth’s landing craft, buying time for the refugee vessels. | The sacrifice of a British warship resisting the invaders becomes the sacrifice of a Martian warship resisting Earth’s invasion force. |
| Book Two, Chapters 1–3: Under Foot; Ruins; Days of Confinement | The narrator and the curate are trapped in the ruins of occupied territory, hiding from the Martians and enduring hunger and fear. | In Chapters 18–20, an Earth forward company is isolated in the Southern Gorge and cannot receive supplies from orbit. | The survival of people trapped under occupation becomes the survival of Earth troops isolated in the land they invaded. |
| Book Two, Chapter 4: The Death of the Curate | When the curate, broken by fear, makes a noise, the narrator subdues him to avoid detection, and the curate dies. | In Chapter 21, Earth forces debate whether to use the bodies of dead orcs as food and order their controlled preparation. | An individual’s collapse into killing a companion for survival becomes an institutional decision to use the bodies of the occupied. |
| Book Two, Chapters 5–6: Silence; The Work of Fifteen Days | The Martians’ activity abruptly ceases, and when the narrator ventures outside, he finds the invaders fallen for reasons they never understood. | In Chapters 22–23, red swellings spread through the forward company and the orbiter, and biological signals vanish over the course of fifteen days. | Discovering the invaders’ silence from outside becomes a direct experience of incubation and collapse within the invasion force. |
| Book Two, Chapter 7: The Man on Putney Hill | The artilleryman speaks of gathering the strongest survivors, building an underground community, and seizing the Martians’ machines. Yet the tunnel he has actually dug is paltry, and he is easily distracted by food, drink, and card games. The narrator realizes that the plan is fantasy without action and leaves. | In Chapter 24, “The Strategist on the Hill,” Tomasz Nowak identifies food standards, relay stations, drone drops, helicopter fuel, and quarantine protocols as concrete areas for improvement. His report is used by the follow-up force. | The survivor’s unrealized plan for resistance becomes an invader’s logistical improvements put into practice. In the original, the plan is powerless because it is fanciful; here, it is more dangerous because it is realistic. |
| Book Two, Chapters 8–9: Dead London; Wreckage | In an empty London, the narrator sees dead Martians and motionless machines, then hears another person’s voice and realizes that humanity has survived. | In Chapters 25–26, Seo Yujin sees quarantine lines, empty helmets, immobilized equipment, and sealed samples. | A city liberated by the invaders’ deaths becomes a base emptied by disease, where the invasion force has fallen but the occupation has not ended. |
| Book Two, Chapter 10: Epilogue | The narrator reunites with his wife and reflects on the post-invasion world with relief that humanity has survived. | In Chapter 27, the advance force’s deaths become an improvement report, and Earth prepares for the next launch window. | The survivor’s reunion and relief become the conclusion of an invasion system that learns from failure. |
| After the original | The original ends with the Martians felled by pathogens and the surviving people of Earth looking to the future. | In Chapters 28–30, the records are sealed, vaccines and Green Corridor equipment are prepared together, and the follow-up force departs twenty-six months later. | The pathogen becomes not the end of the invasion but a correctable flaw. |

## Source Novel

* [H. G. Wells, *The War of the Worlds*, Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/36/36-h/36-h.htm)

chapters.title: 04. Adversarial Review Criteria
chapters.markdown:
# 04. Adversarial Review Criteria for the Expanded 30-Chapter Edition

## 1. Setting Continuity Criteria

* Maintain the Earth forces’ point of view exclusively. The orcs’ inner thoughts, translated dialogue, and Earth-style names are prohibited.
* Show evidence that the orcs are an intelligent species through funerals, farmland, carts, evacuation, military discipline, citadels, and maritime activity.
* The Earth forces must already have recognized the possibility that the orcs are an intelligent species. The inability to communicate is no excuse.
* The initial departure point is the expanded launch complex at Sriharikota, India. It fails if it appears to be an operation launched from Florida or conducted solely by the South Korean military.
* South Korea takes part in the invasion not as a virtuous exception, but in keeping with its stake as an advanced military and economic power.
* The debate over AI/AGI belongs in the background. It fails if it becomes the central conflict.
* The Moon is not an intermediate rest stop but a long-term supply base.
* The disease is not Earth’s Black Death but a red swelling similar to the plague.
* Return to Earth is blocked, preventing the disease from spreading there. Its effects extend only as far as the orbital medical section.
* The ending is not the cancellation of the invasion, but the departure of a follow-on force after vaccines, quarantine, and supply systems have been improved.

## 2. Military and Logistics Criteria

* Armor, aircraft, drones, and robots are overwhelming but not unlimited.
* Tanks and helicopters are constrained by assembly, inspection, fuel, maintenance, and ammunition.
* Once guns are fired, replacements and supplies must be imported. Repeatedly show the labor involving dust, barrels, magazines, filters, socks, batteries, and similar necessities.
* When helicopters fly low, their noise and rotor wash must become sources of terror.
* Heavy weapons are not cinematic props but horrifying forces that tear through bodies and spaces.
* Even a medieval army creates terror through numbers, terrain, adaptation, fire pots, and attacks on waterways and relays.
* Supply failures occur not because orbital stockpiles are insufficient, but because of the final leg, relays, weather, landing zones, fuel, and robot malfunctions.

## 3. Style and Literary Criteria

* Chapters unfold through concrete scenes rather than summaries. However, do not begin every chapter with a contextless description of an object.
* Each chapter briefly identifies its time and place, and if the location, time, or viewpoint character has changed since the previous chapter, the reader must be able to understand how the transition occurred.
* Check that narrative methods borrowed from other works do not conflict with this work’s spatial structure. It fails if the surface form of a reference style is turned into a mechanical requirement.
* If a named character reappears after a long absence without any reminder of their role or distinguishing marker, making them seem like a new character, it fails.
* Incorporate reports and briefings within scenes, and do not let the entire text read like a briefing.
* Do not convey characters’ ethical judgments through lengthy exposition; reveal them through speech, actions, omissions, and file structures.
* Yujin is not a moral commentator. She is an observer, but she is also part of the system.
* Hale, Nowak, and Vosrov are not villains. Show how rational language sustains the machinery of invasion.
* Dubois and Menon say what is right but do not prevail. Do not write them with a sense of moral triumph.
* Han Doyun’s hesitation is not an excuse but evidence of his responsibility.
* Kenji Nakamura’s survival must not be used as a happy ending or as absolution for an opponent.
* Homages to the source novel should emerge through scene structures readers can recognize, but pare back excessive direct explanation.

## 4. Illustration Criteria

* One illustration per chapter, for a total of 30.
* Maintain a consistent style: black-and-white pen drawings with the texture of illustrations from an old science-fiction magazine, allowing limited spot color only for the red planet.
* Earth forces’ equipment should resemble next-generation versions of present-day weapons. Giant robots and laser superweapons are prohibited.
* Orcs should appear as inhabitants and soldiers of a civilization, not as monsters. However, maintain the sense of distance inherent in the Earth forces’ point of view.
* Depictions of blood and corpses should suggest brutality without becoming excessively graphic.
* Place names and legends within map images should be written in English so they can be reused in the translated edition. Do not change place names in the main text to English.

chapters.title: 05. Setting Adversarial Review
chapters.markdown:
# 05. Setting Adversarial Review — Expanded 30-Chapter Edition

## Verdict

Conditional pass. The current manuscript preserves the core setting. However, there is still room to increase the length of each chapter to novella scale, and in some chapters, conveying function still takes precedence over scene density.

## Confirmed Passes

* The point of departure remains fixed at the expanded launch complex in Sriharikota, India.
* The Moon is treated not as a stopover but as a long-term supply depot.
* Korea appears not as a virtuous exception, but by virtue of its stake as an advanced military and economic power.
* Han Doyun remains a male former member of Korea’s 707th Special Mission Group, a frontline commander, and the officer responsible for the limited cooking order.
* The journalist Seo Yujin is a Korean observer, but that does not absolve her.
* The Earth forces press ahead in operational language despite knowing that the orcs may be a sapient species.
* There is no orc POV, no orc names, and no translated orc dialogue.
* The Red Swelling is treated not as the Black Death itself, but as an indigenous Martian infection with similar symptoms and speed of progression.
* Contamination of the orbital medical section is included, while the suspension of return travel to Earth prevents the infection from spreading there.
* The ending concludes with the departure of a follow-up contingent after improvements to vaccines, logistics, and quarantine procedures.

## Issues Found and Corrected

1. Chapter 16 contained the meta phrase “readers of the source novel,” which broke immersion.
   * Action: Replaced it with a scene in which Yujin recalls an old illustration.
2. The phrase “Korean military experience” in Chapter 7 risked suggesting an operation conducted solely by the Korean military.
   * Action: Rephrased it more modestly as “his military career in Korea.”
3. The setting file lacked a blank line between the character table and the following header, which could cause rendering issues.
   * Action: Added a blank line.

## Remaining Risks

* Chapters 24\~30 have a strong concluding function and contain many report-like sentences. This currently serves the intended coldness, but to give the work greater literary weight, it would be advisable to add one more scene of character action to each chapter.
* Chapters 3\~10 have sufficient combat and maintenance density, but making each chapter longer would require giving one individual soldier a recurring action in each.
* The structural homages to the source novel are sufficient, but to strengthen the pleasure of recognition for readers, it would be safer to make them more explicit in each chapter’s illustration caption and in the appendix concordance.

chapters.title: 06. Military and Logistics Adversarial Review
chapters.markdown:
# 06. Military and Logistics Adversarial Review — Expanded 30-Chapter Edition

## Verdict

Conditional pass. The causes of weapons-system and supply failures do not significantly conflict with the current setting. It captures both forms of terror: “overwhelming firepower” and “overwhelming numbers, terrain, and supply instability.”

## Passing Points

* Equipment remains limited to next-generation versions of existing systems, including the Abrams M1A3, CV90, Boxer, AH-64F, UH-60V, M4A2, M250/M240L, drones, and quadruped robots.
* The text contains no equipment names, such as the K2, that would suggest the force is exclusively South Korean.
* Tanks and helicopters are not immediately available for unlimited operations; they are constrained by assembly, maintenance, fuel, and ammunition.
* Helicopter noise and rotor wash are portrayed as sources of terror.
* Heavy weapons are overwhelming but not treated as expendable. Weapon intake, barrel changes, dust, magazines, and filters recur throughout.
* The orcs’ flame canisters are not exaggerated weapons capable of penetrating tanks. Instead, they target vulnerable rear-area assets, burning sunshades, relays, fuel bladders, drone-charging stations, and irrigation pipes.
* Supply failures are attributed not to shortages of orbital materiel but to last-mile bottlenecks, relay losses, terrain, weather, failed drone landings, and helicopter fuel constraints.

## Remaining Risks

* The depiction of operations involving the full battalion-strength force of 700 personnel could be expanded further. The principal scenes currently center on the forward company, landing zone, and orbital craft.
* Some equipment—including mortars, Javelin, Spike, and Stinger systems—appears in the setting reference but rarely in the main text. Including all of it could make the narrative overcrowded, so the current scene-driven approach is preferable.
* The AH-64F designation feels sufficiently like a plausible next-generation model, but illustrations should not exaggerate it into an overly futuristic science-fiction aircraft.

## Recommendations

* During the final literary review, retaining a few more lines in Chapters 6, 9, and 10 about “post-fire maintenance” and “unintended incendiary damage” would better reflect the user’s requirements concerning military experience.
* Image prompts should explicitly prohibit super robots and lasers.

chapters.title: 07. Style and Literary Quality Review
chapters.markdown:
# 07. Adversarial Review of Style and Literary Quality — Expanded 30-Chapter Edition

## Verdict

Conditional pass. The draft feels considerably less like a summary, but in some chapters, “reportorial detachment” still takes precedence over literary scene-building. That detachment is necessary to the work’s intent, but if every chapter maintains the same temperature, the characters’ lived experience may begin to feel flat.

## Strengths

* Recurring bureaucratic language serves to conceal the violence of the invasion.
* Words such as “hazard,” “local vegetation,” “settlement security,” and “preservation” clash with the physical objects in each scene.
* Seo Yujin works well as someone who loses the record rather than as a whistleblower.
* Han Doyun is not absolved through repentance; he remains a figure burdened with command responsibility.
* The Black Ship scene clearly inverts the structure of the Thunder Child episode in the source novel.

## Weaknesses

* The object-centered openings that worked effectively in *The Legend of Dragonia* were carried over without considering the distinct demands of this work, causing some chapters to introduce objects before establishing the time, place, or viewpoint character. In the earlier work, dates, maps, and continuous geography gave each scene its coordinates. Here, Earth, the transit vessel, Martian orbit, and the Martian surface differ so radically in character that the same approach resulted in abrupt scene breaks.
* The latter part of Chapters 24–30 moves through a succession of reports, meetings, and document-centered scenes, creating a similar rhythm throughout.
* The early battles in Chapters 3–6 have a strong sense of scene, but recurring actions by individual soldiers would make them feel more fully novelistic.
* Menon and Dubois voice their opposition clearly, but if they keep delivering arguments with such precision, they may come across as purely functional characters.
* Yujin’s lines sometimes state the author’s conclusions outright. In the final polish, one or two of them should be replaced with objects and actions.

## Immediate Revisions Applied

* The mandatory rule that “the first sentence of each chapter must begin with the physical substance or movement of the setting” was abolished. It was replaced with a standard requiring a brief time-and-place marker in each chapter and, for major spatial transitions, an explanation of the journey or a clear scene connection first.
* The adversarial review criteria were strengthened so that stylistic references are assessed not merely by their surface prose but also by the conditions that made them effective within the original work.
* The meta-homage sentence in Chapter 16 was removed and replaced with Yujin recalling an old illustration.
* The wording in Chapter 7 that gave the impression the Korean forces were acting alone was toned down.

## Direction for the Final Polish

* Reduce direct statements of judgment and let objects—the file structure, denied permissions, quarantine lines, empty helmets, and green culture tanks—carry the conclusions.
* Preserve the rhythm of short sentences. However, ensure that every chapter contains at least one scene grounded in smell, sound, or the movement of hands.
* Avoid overexplaining the homage in the main text. Reinforce it instead through the appendix’s source-comparison table and the arrangement of the illustrations.

chapters.title: 08. World and Forces
chapters.markdown:
# 08. The Invasion of Mars Part One Setting

## State of the World

Earth has embarked on a large-scale migration program in response to climate collapse, resource depletion, and the long-term loss of habitable land. Behind this collapse lies the unchecked competition for energy and runaway circulation of capital that began in the early twenty-first century. Nations recklessly expanded power grids, rare-earth extraction, water resources, and coastal industrial zones to secure data centers, semiconductors, automated military production, and climate-control technology. At the time, some claimed that a little more investment and a little more power consumption would bring superintelligent AI within reach. An economy predicated on cheap energy and endless returns on investment suffered repeated repercussions, followed by wars intended to conceal or reorder the damage. In some regions, even localized nuclear wars broke out. Humanity gained more powerful automation and predictive systems; what remained was a devastated Earth and a world polarized to extremes. Earth’s science and technology are roughly thirty years ahead of the present day, allowing it to operate low Earth orbit refueling systems, long-term lunar stockpiles, uncrewed interplanetary cargo vessels, Mars orbiters, and reusable landers. The first major departure point is the expanded launch complex at Sriharikota, India. Built upon existing space-launch infrastructure near the Indian Ocean, it combines low-orbit transports, cargo vessels, and migration-control terminals in one facility. The transport system resembles today’s large reusable spacecraft. Guns and missiles, armor and helicopters, however, remain no more than improved versions of present-day equipment.

Mars has an atmosphere dense enough for helicopters and vehicles to operate, as well as low gravity, but it is not entirely safe for humans. Long-term residents must use filtered respirators and follow quarantine procedures, and local water, plants, and animals are not to be consumed. Contrary to observations from Earth, a medieval civilization exists here. The forests, mosses, farmland, aquatic vegetation, and other plant life of Mars naturally run to shades of red, and the orcs are an intelligent species with fortresses, armies, ships, families, funerals, and a political order bound to that red ecosystem. Their language is wholly unintelligible, and the forces from Earth never fully decipher the phenomena unique to Mars.

Earth’s settlement plan includes **localized terraforming**. Green mosses, lichens, and cyanobacterial colonies from Earth are to be released around landing zones, supply routes, and areas intended as future agricultural bases, altering the soil, retaining water, and laying the groundwork for terrestrial crops. Earth’s documents call this the deployment of ecological starters, but to the Martian ecosystem that depends on red vegetation, it is an invasive-species catastrophe.

### Martian Quarantine Disaster — Red Swelling

Some dormant cysts of the indigenous Martian microorganisms living symbiotically in orc blood, organs, and bone marrow survive even after heating. In humans, symptoms begin two to six days later with high fever, chills, and exhaustion. The lymph nodes in the groin, armpits, and neck swell into hard, dark-red masses. Without prompt treatment, the disease progresses to bloodstream infection and pneumonia, causing black hemorrhagic lesions on the fingertips and mucous membranes before respiratory failure sets in. Earth’s forces call it **Red Swelling**.

It is not the bacterium responsible for plague on Earth. Yet when the orbiter’s medical records are compared with Earth’s historical infectious-disease data, the symptoms, speed of onset, and short-range droplet transmission prove strikingly similar to the pneumonic form of the plague eradicated on Earth. This fact is first revealed in a medical report later in the story.

Ingestion and contact with bodily fluids are the initial routes of infection. Patients in the pulmonary stage can transmit it to other humans at close range. As soon as Earth’s forces realize this, they seal off the front and quarantine sections both on the surface and aboard the orbiter. By then, however, eleven people evacuated before showing symptoms have already reached the orbital medical section, and of the first battalion’s 700 personnel, 246 are removed from active duty through infection, quarantine, or contact management. Combining deaths from direct infection with losses in combat and withdrawal, the first expedition loses about 80 people. All return to Earth is prohibited, preventing the disease from spreading there.

Using sealed samples, the orbiter develops diagnostic methods and antiserum, while Earth uses transmitted genetic and protein data to develop vaccine candidates and handle mass production. Confirming the vaccine’s safety and duration of immunity takes seventeen months, followed by several more months to replenish equipment and crews and rebuild the quarantine system. The follow-up force departs with the vaccine during the next low-energy window, twenty-six months later.

Earth chose Mars for more than its proximity. Within humanity’s immediate reach, Mars is the only destination that possesses water, a pressurized atmosphere, broad plains and soil, and an already functioning ecosystem. Earth’s governments call this “settlement suitability.” The fact that people already live there is not treated as reducing that suitability; in public documents, it is classified merely as a risk factor.

Earth still has cities and controlled habitats where people can survive from day to day. But its seas, climate, drinking water, and agricultural systems are collapsing on a generational scale, leaving no future in which everyone can continue to live. The journey to Mars is therefore both an evacuation and a territorial seizure conducted by selected people and nations. AI is not a protagonist in this world. It is merely background infrastructure supporting selection, prediction, logistics, reconnaissance, public-opinion management, and uncrewed production. It failed to save Earth; it only allows the system that consumed Earth to conduct the invasion of Mars more efficiently. The operation is carried out in the name of all Earth, but real decision-making power is concentrated among advanced nations and conglomerates that control orbital infrastructure, capital, military industries, and launch sites. Some nations are excluded. They are mobilized as climate refugees, low-wage spaceport workers, raw-material suppliers, and political signatories, yet pushed to the back when it comes to migration rights, boarding passes, and seats in the orbiter’s conference rooms. Earth’s racial, national, and religious conflicts have not disappeared, but the work does not overexplain them as central themes. They appear only in announcements delivered in different languages, differing military backgrounds, small tensions around food and prayer spaces, nationality-based migration priorities, and the question of who is left off the list for Mars. Once the humans reach Mars, their internal conflicts do not serve to blur responsibility for the invasion. They are used only as evidence that the logic of capital and power belonging to advanced nations operates under the borrowed name of all Earth.

## Geography

All names are provisional operational designations assigned by Earth’s forces. They do not understand the place names used by the orcs.

| Location | Characteristics | Role in the Story |
| --------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Lunar Supply Base | Long-term stockpile of propellant feedstock, spare parts, and uncrewed cargo | Not a physical stopover, but a base that sustains preparations for the next supply window and the departure of the follow-up force |
| First Mars Orbiter | Hub of communications, reconnaissance, and cargo recovery | Earth’s eye, recording the war without being able to intervene on the surface |
| Eastern Landing Zone | First base, where landers, fuel, and medical facilities are concentrated | The starting point of the war and the place left empty at the end |
| Red Forest | Dense forest and hills between the landing zone and the Inland Sea | Where the forward company loses its supply route |
| Red Inland Sea | A broad sea across which the orcs’ evacuation ships escape | The setting of the warship’s charge |
| Western Citadel Belt | A region of connected orc cities and walls | The site of the first victory that makes occupation seem real to Earth’s forces |
| Southern Gorge | Deep terrain where communications and supply-drone flights are unreliable | Where the final stretch of the supply route is severed |
| Green Corridor | A zone seeded with ecological starters to connect the landing zone to the gorge | Future farmland and supply territory to Earth’s forces; to the orcs, the beginning of the death of the red land |

## Time and Logistics

* Large transports depart for Mars after repeated refueling by uncrewed tankers in low Earth orbit. The lunar base maintains long-term stockpiles of propellant feedstock, parts, and uncrewed cargo, but it is not an intermediate station through which every cargo vessel must pass.
* The movement of heavy cargo and troops is timed to Earth–Mars low-energy supply windows. A window occurs roughly every 26 months.
* Small emergency cargo can be sent outside these windows, but only medicines, electronic parts, data, and similar payloads. Such vessels cannot carry enough troops, food, or ammunition to save a force.
* Even when cargo is available aboard the orbiter, field units starve if the final link—uncrewed supply craft → landing zone → ground supply route—is severed.
* Even if some oxygen, water, and fuel can be produced locally, food, medicine, ammunition, and precision parts cannot safely be procured on Mars.
* Uncrewed cargo includes not only food and ammunition but ecological starters, soil-treatment machinery, and equipment for localized atmospheric and moisture control. Even after the war begins, the equipment continues operating in the name of the settlement plan.

## First Mars Landing Battalion

Its total strength is approximately 700 personnel. Smaller than a carrier strike group, it is nevertheless a reinforced battalion intended not for reconnaissance but to secure a landing zone and establish an occupation bridgehead.

| Formation | Personnel | Mission |
| ------------ | -----: | ------------------------- |
| Battalion headquarters and security detachment | 54 | Command, military policing, landing-zone security, and control of prisoners and civilians |
| Orbital and transport detachment | Approx. 120 | Operation of the orbiter and landers, recovery of uncrewed cargo, and communications |
| 2 mechanized infantry companies | Approx. 200 | Landing-zone defense, approaches to the citadels, and supply escort |
| Heliborne company | Approx. 100 | Reconnaissance, rapid deployment, and casualty evacuation |
| Armor, fire-support, and drone detachment | Approx. 80 | Direct fire, mortars, reconnaissance drones, and loitering-munition operations |
| Engineering, signals, medical, and logistics personnel | Approx. 120 | Base construction, relays, quarantine, and field supply |
| Scientific survey team | 24 | Ecological, quarantine, linguistic, geological, and meteorological surveys |
| Embedded press team | 2 | Reporting and video documentation. The embedded reporter is the principal observer |

## Equipment Principles

Weapon names remain largely the same as they are today. To avoid the impression of futuristic weaponry, they are presented as next-generation versions of existing equipment, improved only in targeting, sensors, communications, and uncrewed operation. The main text prioritizes abbreviations and functions; the detailed versions below serve only as setting references.

| Category | Equipment |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Individual and squad | M4A2-series rifles, M250A1- and M240L-series machine guns, M110A2, M107A2, M320A1 grenade launchers |
| Anti-materiel and indirect fire | AT4 CS Gen.2, Carl Gustaf M5, Javelin FGM-148G, Spike LR3, Stinger Block II, M252A2 81mm mortars, smoke grenades, smoke rounds, incendiary rockets |
| Drones and autonomous systems | Black Hornet 5-series micro-reconnaissance drones, VTOL fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, Switchblade 700-series loitering munitions, 40kg-class short-range cargo drones, uncrewed transport vehicles |
| Armor | 2 Abrams M1A3-series tanks, 4 CV90 MkV-series infantry fighting vehicles, 8 Boxer A3-series armored vehicles |
| Aviation | 4 UH-60V Black Hawk-series transport helicopters, 2 AH-64F Apache-series attack helicopters |

Armor and aircraft are transported first aboard several large cargo landers, then assembled and inspected at the landing zone. The problem is not bringing them in the first time, but replenishing aviation fuel, ammunition, and parts. Spacecraft propellant and helicopter fuel are not interchangeable. When supplies are cut off, tanks become heavy gun batteries fixed to the base, and helicopters can no longer fly.

Drones have advanced far more than ground weapons. Micro-reconnaissance drones fly alongside squads, providing thermal imaging, low-light video, and automatic target tracking, while VTOL fixed-wing drones map gorges and coastlines for hours at a time. Cargo drones can carry roughly 40kg of blood, medicine, or ammunition, and several can form a relay network that allows them to fly behind terrain. The system, however, depends on outdoor landing points, terrain maps, relays, battery or fuel charging, and recovery routes. When the canopy of the Red Forest, the gorges, fog, and destroyed relays combine, it cannot become a supply network capable of carrying food for an entire battalion.

## Shared Systems for Soldiers and Robots

| System | Functions Seen in Part One | Limitations |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Skeletal augmentation suit | Powered assistance for the back, waist, knees, and ankles; carries 35\~45kg of equipment; drags casualties | It is not full-body armor that stops bullets. When the battery or joint actuators fail, only a heavy burden remains. |
| Soldier’s tactical helmet | Thermal and low-light vision, maps, friendly positions, drone feeds, biometrics, and recording | It cannot translate the orc language. When the relay is lost, only local maps and direct vision remain. |
| Squad support AI | Marks people, equipment, and fires in video feeds; suggests routes and casualty priorities | It does not make lethal decisions. It does not understand Martian organisms, language, or intentions. |
| Quadruped supply robot | Carries 80\~120kg, pulls stretchers, and transports batteries, ammunition, and water-purification membranes | It stops in narrow gorges and fires, or when batteries and relays are lost. |
| Bipedal work robot | Uses ladders, doors, valves, and tools designed for humans; installs relays; handles hazardous materials | It depends on batteries and communications, while Martian dust wears down its joints and sensors. |
| Uncrewed engineering equipment | Excavation, loading, mine detection, and installation of irrigation pipes in the Green Corridor | It is effective at the landing zone and in the corridor but cannot resolve the supply crisis at the front. |
| Power and emergency systems | Portable fuel cells, folding solar membranes, micro-component printers, automated hemorrhage control, portable ultrasound, and blood substitutes | They cannot produce food, semiconductors, or complex parts, nor can they provide a treatment for an unknown symbiont. |

Infantry generally wear lightweight composite protective suits capable of stopping arrows, crossbow bolts, blades, spears, and fragments. Heavy ballistic plates are issued only to personnel at particular risk from friendly firearms and explosions, such as landing-zone guards, vehicle crews, and ammunition-depot staff.

## Fire and Smoke

The Martian army’s fire canisters cannot penetrate tank armor from the front. Instead, they burn external fuel bladders, drone-charging stations, communications relays, solar membranes, medical tents, ammunition crates, and the irrigation pipes of the Green Corridor. Earth’s forces also use smoke grenades and incendiary rockets. Smoke conceals retreats and the defense of the landing zone, while incendiaries burn forest paths, ambush sites, and ships carrying fire canisters. These weapons burn the rear areas, which are far more vulnerable than tanks, leaving lasting scars across the Red Forest and farmland.

## Scientific Survey Team

| Field | Personnel | Position in the Conflict |
| -------- | -: | --------------------- |
| Planetary science and geology | 4 | Surveys of the landing zone, roads, and groundwater |
| Atmosphere and meteorology | 3 | Analysis of flight conditions and local storms |
| Ecology and food | 5 | Assessment of the safety of local plants, animals, and water |
| Astrobiology and quarantine | 4 | Biological opposition to the consumption of orc meat |
| Medicine and pharmacology | 3 | Response to unknown toxins, infections, and injuries |
| Language and anthropology | 3 | Establishes in the official record that the orcs are an intelligent species |
| Surveying and data analysis | 2 | Converts orbital imagery and surface data into supply routes |

## Character Profiles

For character information, including nationality, role, appearance, and distinguishing traits for readers, use the [character sheet](characters.md) as the canonical source.

## Mandatory Scene Principles

1. Earth’s forces know that the orcs are an intelligent species. The absence of a shared language is no excuse.
2. The consumption of orc meat is not colonial administration but a choice made in the field by a forward company trying to survive after its supplies are cut off.
3. Soldiers, astrobiologists, and anthropologists oppose it. Their opposition is right, but it does not prevail over command authority.
4. The warship scene is observed from the human perspective. To Earth’s forces, the ship is an enemy vessel that must be sunk; only the reader understands from its actions that it is aiding an evacuation.
5. Never include the orcs’ point of view, translated dialogue, or explicit inner thoughts.
6. Mars’s red ecosystem is natural, and Earth’s green moss is the invasive species. Terraforming begins not across the entire planet but within the occupied corridor, yet to the orcs it is already a catastrophe.

chapters.title: 09. Definitive 30-Chapter Structure
chapters.markdown:
# 09. Definitive Structure of *The Invasion of Mars*

## Overarching Interpretive Lens

This work reverses the event structure of *The War of the Worlds*, while grounding its emotional and political framework in the expansion and destruction wrought by the great powers of the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries. Earth’s forces are at once a futuristic space force and an amalgam of an East India Company-style contract army, an imperial navy, survey expeditions, naturalists, a civilizing discourse without missionaries, and migration companies. The crucial point is that they are not simply setting out after discovering new land. They have damaged Earth themselves through the runaway energy competition and capital circulation of the early twenty-first century, and now seek to shift the resulting costs and burden of survival onto another world. Overinvestment, competition for electrical power, struggles to secure resources, and the ensuing economic fallout led to several wars, while localized nuclear conflicts in some regions further reduced Earth’s habitable territory. Some investors and bureaucrats of the time claimed that general-purpose AI had been just within reach if they had only pushed a little further, but the text does not judge whether that claim was right or wrong.

The homage appears in the underlying structure of the scenes. The historical critique appears in the logic of power through which those scenes are interpreted. The Black Ship recalls the warship episode in the original novel, but it is also a scene in which an imperial navy classifies a local vessel as a military target. The Green Corridor is terraforming, but it is also ecological destruction conducted in the name of plantations, survey lines, and land improvement. The scientific expedition sometimes uncovers the truth, but when that truth is relegated to an appendix in a conference room, it becomes a form of colonial knowledge.

The text does not overexplain this lens. It makes it visible through company logos, cargo manifests, map colors, insurance language, migration priority, quarantine reports, and launch sites that resemble trading ports. Earth’s destruction is shown not through abstract slogans but through leaking pipes, water rationing, abandoned coastal cities, insurance exclusions, rejected migration applicants, and the bodies of low-wage workers around the launch sites.

## Length Targets

* Target chapter count: 28\~30 chapters.
* Basic structure: Reconfigure all 27 chapters of the original novel in reverse correspondence, then add 1\~3 chapters set after its ending.
* Minimum completion point: 28 chapters. 27 chapters corresponding to the original + Chapter 28, “The Next Window.”
* Recommended completion point: 30 chapters. Chapter 28, “The Sealed Original”; Chapter 29, “The Vaccine and the Corridor”; Chapter 30, “The Next Window.”
* Target per chapter: 4\~6 scenes. Advance through scenes on the ground, dialogue, supplies, orders, and changes to bodies—not summary.

## Part One: The Landing and the First Victory

### 01. The Eve of the War

Corresponds to Part One, Chapter 1 of the original. Shows Earth’s migration terminals and the expanded launch complex at Sriharikota, India. Yujin reports on it not as a war but as a settlement operation. The citadels of the Red Planet and the first green ecological growth appear in the same frame.

### 02. The Light from the Sky

Corresponds to Part One, Chapter 2 of the original. Cargo ships and landing craft enter Martian orbit. To Earth’s forces, it is a successful orbital insertion; from the Martian surface, it appears as an ominous sign in the heavens.
